articles.title_orig: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.title_zh: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.content_orig:
People seen through a window inside a bar in La Cabrera, on the outskirts of Madrid, Spain, watch a televised speech by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez from La Moncloa Palace announcing national elections, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Bernat Armangue/AP hide caption
MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections Monday after his government suffered a bruising legislative defeat last week on emergency measures related to the country's housing crisis.
The vote will be held Nov. 29.
In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees in Parliament that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation. The setback sparked wide speculation that Sánchez could consider moving up a national election that would have otherwise taken place next year.
In a televised address, Sánchez argued that a broader progressive coalition in Parliament would allow Spaniards to tackle the biggest issues facing the country today.
"The time has come, therefore, for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country," Sánchez said.
Sánchez, 54, has been Spain's prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe's longest-standing leaders.
He has become one of the leading international progressive heads of government thanks to his defense of migration, his diplomatic efforts to defend Palestinians and his criticism of the American and Israeli war against Iran.
He has also enjoyed one of the fastest growing economies in the developed world in recent years.
But back home, the Spanish leader has been hemmed in by a series of legal cases involving his Socialist party as well as his wife and brother, who both deny wrongdoing.
He has also struggled to account for this summer's border crossing by tens of thousands of mostly Moroccans into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta, where a humanitarian crisis remains two months after the initial crisis.
He has led a coalition minority government along with the left-wing junior partner Sumar since 2023. But his reliance on several smaller parties to get anything done has hamstrung his legislative ability.
Throughout his political career, Sánchez has earned a reputation as a political escape artist capable of winning elections he looked set to lose.
Speculation around whether he would call snap elections centered on the momentum that his party may now have around issues of affordability, while the opposition Popular Party — which holds the most seats in Parliament already — is likely to define the contest around corruption.
"Sánchez is choosing this moment because it is arguably the best time to do so, given that the issue of housing frames the electoral conflict or debate in terms that are highly favorable to (his party's) position," said Oriol Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
"Sánchez can frame the election — or has realized he can frame it — in very classic left-versus-right terms," Bartomeus said."
The Socialist leader will face Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who aims to take control of the government.
"At last, the Spanish people will decide," Feijóo said Monday after the announcement of the the snap election. "These aren't elections like the previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez," he said.
The formal dissolution of parliament will need to be approved by the Cabinet, which Sánchez has convened for later Monday.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Slips, Dollar Strengthens as Investors Look for Safety — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Slips, Dollar Strengthens as Investors Look for Safety — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite sailed to a fresh all-time high as traders looked past rising U.S. Treasury yields and digested new economic data.
The Nasdaq Composite was up 1.05% and hit an intraday of 27,544.07. The tech-heavy index posted a record close of 27,477.31. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 90.94 points, or 0.18%, to end at 51,267.90. The S&P 500 climbed 0.66% to 7,773.95.
Several stocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade led the way higher for the Nasdaq. SpaceX jumped more than 7%, while hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Microsoft ticked up almost 2% and more than 1%, respectively. Nvidia and Tesla rose 2% each.
Tech is "sort of like the inverse bond trade," Infrastructure Capital Advisors founder and CEO Jay Hatfield told CNBC. "It's buy tech, sell everything else, and so it's kind of an unstoppable juggernaut."
Hatfield added that tech has served as a kind of safe haven since the pandemic, citing the sector's high earnings-related growth and relatively low sensitivity to interest rates.
"It really doesn't matter what they pay for debt, and the demand for compute is so strong, [so tech is] not really impacted by interest rates," Hatfield said.
As tech stocks rallied, bond yields also advanced. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last up more than 3 basis points to 5.311%, while the 30-year rose more than 3 basis points to 5.664%. Both yields surged to multiyear highs in recent weeks, as traders fretted that inflation would lead the Federal Reserve to keep rates higher for longer.
Stocks and bonds moved as traders processed the Institute for Supply Management's latest report on economic growth in the services sector. The ISM report showed that the Purchasing Managers Index for services came in at 54.9% in September, or roughly in line with expectations. However, that figure came in modestly below the index's rate of growth for the previous month.
Investors now turn their attention the Fed, which will release the minutes from its September meeting — potentially shedding light on its decision to hike rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month.
Traders also monitored oil prices, which were lower on Monday. Brent crude futures settled down 1.89% at $100.32 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude was down 1.8% to settle at $89.43 a barrel.
Stocks are coming off a week defined by surging Treasury yields and a surprisingly lackluster jobs report that helped ease concerns about another Fed rate hike this month. The data provided some relief after a week of pressure from rising bond yields.
"Despite a growing list of headwinds (e.g., geopolitics, higher rates), global equities have climbed c12% YTD and are just below all-time highs," wrote Citi strategist Beata Manthey. "Does this relative calm suggest equity fundamentals will prove resilient to ongoing macro shocks, or will stocks eventually need to correct to more accurately reflect the current risk backdrop? While uncertainty remains high, we still find ourselves in the 'resilience' camp for now."
The Nasdaq Composite finished at a record closing level amid a broader market rally on Monday.
The tech-heavy index closed up 1.05% to 27,477.31, blowing past its former record high hit on Sept. 22.  The S&P 500 added 0.66% to finish the day at 7,773.95, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 90.94 points, or 0.18%, to 51,267.90.
S&P 500 companies are expected to report earnings-per-share growth of 27% on a year-over-year basis for the third quarter, according to Goldman Sachs.
That represents a decline from the broad-market index's realized growth of 33% in the second quarter of 2026, Goldman Sachs analysts said in note to clients dated October 2.
Brazil's post-election market rally is giving investors a reason to look at beer stocks with exposure to the country.
Ambev shares are jumping about 10% in U.S. trading, making the brewer one of the clearest equity plays. The company generates the bulk of its business in Brazil, where its beer division delivered first-half revenue of 20.8 billion reais and EBITDA of 7.1 billion reais. The underlying business was already gaining momentum before the election surprise.
In the second quarter, Brazil Beer volume rose 5%, revenue increased 8.9% and EBITDA grew 12.8%, driven by market-share gains and World Cup-related demand.
The stronger real could provide another tailwind. It has the potential to boost Brazilian consumers' purchasing power and reduce some FX and imported commodity pressures for a company that brews and sells locally.
AB InBev is up roughly 1.5% Monday. It offers investors a larger — but less direct — way to play the same idea through its controlling stake in Ambev. Brazil is an important market for the global brewer, though its U.S., Mexico, China and European businesses make it far less of a pure Brazil trade than ABEV.
Jefferies initiated a buy for Samsara with a $50 price target, implying about 22% upside from Friday's close.
Jefferies equity analyst Samad Samana expects roughly 22% annual revenue growth through fiscal 2029.
"We see the current valuation as a compelling entry point for a moated AI winner and expect positive revisions to power shares higher," Samana wrote.
The company's closed-loop data platform processes over 30 trillion annual data points, creating a flywheel effect that powers increasingly valuable AI insights, automation and new product innovation.
"We view this proprietary data asset as a durable competitive advantage and a key enabler of future AI monetization. Additionally, with pricing primarily tied to assets rather than users/employees, we see less seat displacement risk," according to the analyst.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) was up more than 13% in mid-day trading on Monday, pacing for its best day since March 2020.
The ETF's jump comes after the first round results of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, where challenger Flávio Bolsonaro narrowly edged out incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. However, neither received a majority of the vote, and thus will face voters in a runoff election on Oct. 25.
Polls before the first round widely expected Lula to receive the most votes in the initial tally, even though they also showed him trailing Bolsonaro in a potential runoff. Now, following Bolsonaro's overperformance on Sunday, he is seen as the overwhelming favorite to win the runoff.
Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSCM) advanced 2.5% Monday, reaching a 52-week high of $485 per share after Elon Musk suggested his chip venture, Terafab will be partnering with the company for semiconductor factories in Texas.
Musk tweeted a reply post of the report indicating that it was true. Shares of Intel , which had previously said it was partnering with Terafab, are down 4%.
Meanwhile, shares of Musk's SpaceX are up 5.5% after Morgan Stanley said the stock is "cheap and getting cheaper," in a note to clients Sunday. Another catalyst for SpaceX came from Musk proposing a rebrand of its AI unit, from "SpaceXAI" to "SpaceXSI" after President Donald Trump directed the U.S. government to use the term "Super Intelligence" or "SI" instead of artificial intelligence on Sept. 29.
The dollar fell against the Brazilian real on Monday following Sunday's elections in which the Brazilian right was ascendant .
The greenback-to-real exchange rate dropped to 4.99 in Monday morning trading, the lowest level since at least May.
While the presidential contest between incumbent Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, will head to a runoff later this month due to the closeness of the race, senate and governors' races saw wins by conservatives and center-right candidates.
"The result points to gains by the right and the centrão," Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo reported on Monday .

articles.title_orig: Irvine woman charged in China spy op
articles.title_zh: Irvine woman charged in China spy op
articles.content_orig:
The FBI arrested an Irvine woman Sunday for allegedly taking photos, recording videos and gathering license plate information related to family members of the Taiwanese president during their U.S. visit last year.
Federal prosecutors have charged Wanying Zhang, who also uses the name first-name Heather, with acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China. PRC officials allegedly directed her to travel to Seattle in 2025 and monitor the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government by sending photos, videos and license plate information.
Zhang, 34, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport as she was attempting to travel to China, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a social media post. She was expected to make her initial appearance Monday in LA federal court.
Zhang allegedly coordinated the trip with an associate, using spying techniques to evade detection, Essayli said.
She did not report her activity for a foreign government to the U.S. attorney general, which is a federal crime with a maximum prison sentence of 10 years.
FBI Director Kash Patel also announced the arrest on social media.
“Foreign adversaries take note: America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations,” Patel posted. “Allegedly surveil a foreign leader’s family on U.S. soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening.”
A spokesperson for Taiwan’s presidential office on Monday described Zhang’s suspected actions as a “classic case of transnational repression,” according to published reports.
“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
Former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang is awaiting sentencing after her conviction earlier this year for acting as an unregistered PRC agent.

articles.title_orig: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.title_zh: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.content_orig:
As the United Nations continues its search for a new leader , Binaifer Nowrojee, president of the nonprofit Open Society Foundations, described the kind of secretary-general that the world wants. But is it the same person that the five permanent members of the Security Council — Britain, China, France, Russia and the US — want, PassBlue asked her.
“We need a secretary-general that is bold, that is not scared to speak truth to power,” Nowrojee told PassBlue on Sept. 24, during an interview that touched on many global issues, including the race to choose the UN’s next top diplomat.
The 15-member Security Council ultimately recommends a candidate to the General Assembly for approval this year, as planned. But the process is currently going through an informal straw-poll phase to assess its candidate of choice.
The latest poll was held by the Council on Sept. 29, after three in July, August and early September, respectively, and like the others before it, the P5, as they are known, have yet to publicly show their hands on who they want to lead the 81-year-old UN. Each P5 has a veto, which can block a substantive Council decision despite majority support and thus end a candidate’s aspirations. A nominee needs to have at least nine votes from the Council and no veto to win the coveted recommendation to the Assembly.
Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the UN and the Council’s monthly rotating president, said on Oct. 1 that members would be consulted on using color-coded ballots in the next two straw polls, slated for midmonth and end of the month. The color ballots distinguish the P5’s votes from those of the 10 elected members, revealing whether a candidate faces opposition from a permanent member without identifying which country cast the no vote.
The candidates, now numbering seven, after Michelle Bachelet of Chile dropped out on Sept. 20, have been straddling a tightrope in their respective campaigns, avoiding statements that could put them at crossroads with the P5. Despite the balancing act, some P5 have publicly signaled reservations about candidates. Bachelet, Chile’s two-time president, announced her withdrawal after poor results in the first three informal ballots.
Opposition from Washington was a hurdle she could not surmount because of her perceived pro-abortion stance and other matters. (Relevant US officials, for starters, never met with her, according to a diplomat familiar with her campaign.) China has said it would prefer a woman secretary-general. That could complicate the bids of candidates like Rafael Grossi of Argentina, Macky Sall of Senegal and Olara Otunnu of Uganda. Grossi also faces a potential block from Russia, which has reportedly suggested it may oppose candidates with European Union or NATO citizenship.
Besides being Argentine, Grossi holds Italian citizenship. Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a candidate who is a former vice president of Ecuador and is backed by Antigua and Barbuda, has Spanish citizenship. So far, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett have led the informal polls, but neither has emerged as an obvious consensus choice for the Council to recommend to the General Assembly. Color-coded ballots will better reveal their chances.
The interview has been edited for clarity and condensed for brevity. Some questions have been reordered for better flow.
PassBlue: Given the UN’s financial crisis, political tensions and struggles to resolve conflicts and fund development work, would a woman secretary-general step onto a glass cliff?
Binaifer: The United Nations has carried us well for the last 80-plus years, and there’s been great steps forward on a variety of issues through the UN and a rules-based world order, and people still want that. Governments still want that, but we are now at a point where the world is different. When the UN was set up, it was four or five empires that actually set it up and have presided over it. So there are inequalities and privileges that were built in that no longer fit today’s world.
Today, we don’t have a world of four or five empires. We have a world of 193 countries that sit and want a place at the table. Demographics are different. Eighty-five percent of the world’s population is now sitting in the global majority, only 15 percent in Europe and the United States. The UN has reached the end of how it can function in the way it’s functioned, and a reset is required, and that is the case for any organization.
The most important thing we need right now is a secretary-general who is visionary and bold and is ready to take this organization into the future. As the first woman to lead the Open Society Foundations, it is incredible to me that over 80 years, not a single woman has served as the UN secretary-general.
It is symbolic of the types of exclusions that have limited the abilities of the UN, even as it has espoused equality, even as it espoused human rights principles; it’s an important thing that it walks the talk internally of what it needs to do. We need a secretary-general who will lead us into the future that this next generation is going to live in.
PassBlue: What does the world need from the next secretary-general that might conflict with the P5’s priorities?
Binaifer: We need a secretary-general that is not scared to speak truth to power, that substantively can identify the key issues we need to focus on in this next century and is not scared to make some of the hard decisions that will require. We also need a secretary-general that is a bridge builder. They still have to work with member states. They still have to build coalitions around the agendas. But let’s not have a secretary- general that relinquishes the entire reform agenda and limits it only to budgets and headcounts. We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to press a reset button. Let’s do it properly.
PassBlue: How do you see African countries engaging in multilateral, bilateral and trilateral AI discussions and using the technology?
Binaifer: First of all, we know Africa is the youngest continent, and every one of those young people has a phone in their hand, so we know that there’s a lot of familiarity and that young Africans are leaning into technology. They’ll lean into artificial intelligence. They may not be the architects of the structure, but they will be the users, and they will innovate and find ways to have this integrated into their lives.
What we want to ensure is that the harms that we are seeing in places where children or hate speech, those kinds of things, that African governments take steps to put in a regulatory environment, because now we know those lessons. We see Australia stopping social media for children under 16. We know that women politicians, for example, get much more hate and abuse online compared to male politicians. So African governments can actually make policy decisions to limit the harms but also benefit, to have their young people benefit from the good possibilities that that technology and artificial intelligence will bring.
PassBlue: How can African countries move beyond consuming technology to creating economic benefits for young people and for their national economies?
Binaifer: There’s huge innovation in Africa on many levels. Take a place like Kenya, where technology for money transfers with M-Pesa happened long before other countries were doing it, and you find very savvy tech people in Gen Z organizing protests on social media to call on the government to do things about their issues. We also see innovation in organizations like Gearbox in Kenya or others, and the difference between the US and Africa in terms of why does innovation actually appear in the US in the tech space. Because the US government has invested in providing funds for innovation.
Innovation doesn’t just pop out of thin air, and if African governments want to engage their citizens more and engage their young people with talent, they also need to invest in them, an

articles.title_orig: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.title_zh: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.content_orig:
As a new parasite with flesh-eating larvae threatens the nation's livestock industry, a team of Virginia Tech researchers will be on the frontlines of defense.
Led by Luis Escobar, an associate professor of fish and wildlife conservation, the team is working on one of 40 breakthrough projects funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an integrated preparedness and response system against the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in the Americas.
“Preventing a screwworm invasion protects food production, food prices, rural economies, family farms, wildlife populations, companion animals such as dogs and horses, and public health because the screwworms can also affect people,” said Escobar.
Earlier this summer, the USDA confirmed that the new world screwworm fly reached south Texas, threatening the livestock industry for the first time in decades.
Screwworm-related losses exceeded $200 million annually in the 1950s, the equivalent of roughly $1.8 billion today, before eradication efforts succeeded.
According to Escobar, mitigation measures include mandatory physical inspections and anti-parasitic treatments for cattle at southern border ports, as well as stricter movement requirements for animals entering Texas.
As part of the project, Virginia Tech will expand collaborations with Texas A&M, North Carolina State University, the University of Kansas in the United States, Universidad de San Carlos, and Universidad del Valle in Guatemala.
“Rather than addressing one aspect of screwworm control, this project creates a complete decision-support framework that connects surveillance, genetics, producer behavior, and predictive modeling,” Escobar said.
Luis Escobar is an associate professor in the College of Natural Resources and Environment at Virginia Tech. He is a member of the Pandemic Prediction and Prevention Destination Area, the Invasive Species Collaborative, and the Fralin Life Sciences Institute’s Center for Zoonotic and Arthropod- borne Pathogens and Global Change Center.
His research focuses on biogeography, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases across landscapes.
To schedule an interview with Escobar about the new world screwworm, its reemergence, and how to stop the parasite from threatening food systems and agriculture, email mediarelations@vt.edu .

articles.title_orig: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.title_zh: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.content_orig:
Author: Br. Murray Bodo, OFM
Date Published: October 05, 2026
In declaring 2026 the year of St. Francis , Pope Leo has once again called attention to the depth and breadth of the world’s interest in St. Francis. In this, the 800th anniversary year of his death , Francis has emerged as a saint who is as relevant today as he was in his lifetime.
We live in a time of division and upheaval in the world, with wars cropping up in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, and with hateful rhetoric and divisive decisions that are separating people. The good among us are longing and praying for peace daily: peace in the world and peace of heart. We long for models and look to saints for guidance about how we are to live our lives. Again and again, we turn to Francis of Assisi as the Christian example of a peacemaker who found peace of heart and preached peace and good by embracing Jesus and His Gospel of Peace and Love. “May the Lord give you peace,” and “Peace and Good” were the two mantras that Francis uttered his whole life long.
Ours is also a time of turmoil in nature. Our climate is warming yearly, and the excessive human consumption and use of fossil fuels are damaging our planet. There is the feeling that we are pushing the envelope of what our climate can take of human neglect and abuse.
And again, it is Francis of Assisi who emerges as a model of what it means to embrace all of creation as our brothers and sisters through whom and with whom we make our way to God. For St. Francis, it is because of the Incarnation of God among us that all creatures are redeemed, all creatures are seen as good. Francis embraced all creatures and called them Brothers and Sisters; and towards the end of his life he sang one of the great poems of the Middle Ages and of all time, his “Canticle of the Creatures.”
“Laudato si, mi Signore,” St. Francis sings, “Praised be You, my Lord,” through Brother Sun and Moon and the Stars; through Mother Earth, our Sister; through Brother Wind and Air, Brother Fire and Sister Water. In so taking the four elements of Medieval Cosmology: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, and embracing them and praising God through, with, and in them, St. Francis was embracing all creatures of the earth and praising and thanking God for them.
St. Francis of Assisi is the patron of ecology. (Photo courtesy of Br. Octavio Duran, OFM)
What a program for a renewal of the earth! What a program for peace of heart and peace among people and all creatures. And in his pursuit of that program for a peace-filled world, Pope Francis turned to St. Francis’s “Canticle” for the title and framework of his encyclical “Laudato Si,” in which Pope Francis stated that the most pressing need of the environment today is to address the human and social roots of the ecological crisis. For example, the encyclical calls for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels because climate change disproportionately affects the poor. Also, the wealthy consume and pollute excessively while the poor suffer the gravest consequences of environmental degradation, often being denied basic human rights like clean water.
The deepest crisis identified by “Laudato Si” is the placing of technology and economic profit above all else. Therefore, the most critical need of the world today is a profound and spiritual change that would lead to a more integrated vision of human beings, of their life, and their relationship with nature.
What a universal patron saint for these profound changes in our times is St. Francis! It has been suggested that the month of October, the month of his passing, be dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, who is already a universal icon of peace and love among us. Perhaps Franciscans could ask that favor of Pope Leo, could suggest that we need to be reminded every year of the gift we have in St. Francis for renewing relationships in our time: the relationship we have with ourselves, with others, and with the very planet we live upon. All people need to hear every year St. Francis’s Admonition to his brothers who would be peacemakers:
“The peace which you proclaim with words must dwell even more abundantly in your hearts. Do not provoke others to anger or give scandal. Rather, let your gentleness draw them to peace, goodness and concord. This is our vocation: to heal wounds, to bind what is broken, to bring home those who are lost.” (Legend of the Three Companions, 58)

articles.title_orig: Luke Littler: World number one knocked out of World Youth Championships in semi-finals
articles.title_zh: Luke Littler: World number one knocked out of World Youth Championships in semi-finals
articles.content_orig:
Littler is only 19 so can still take part in the youth events
Luke Littler missed out on the chance to hold the senior and youth world titles simultaneously after suffering a surprise semi-final defeat at the World Youth Championship.
The 19-year-old world number one was beaten 6-5 by world number 68 Cam Crabtree, who will face German Jan Schmidt in the final on 29 November.
That match will take place on finals day at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead â an event Littler has also yet to qualify for having skipped the majority of Pro Tour events this season.
He is currently ranked 126th in the Players Championship order of merit and only the top 64 qualify.
Four Players Championship events remain, but two of those are in Den Bosch in the Netherlands - where Littler withdrew from events recently after being subjected to boos by the crowds .
Littler has won successive full World Championships and won the youth title as a 16-year-old in 2023, but the semi-final loss to 23-year-old Crabtree was his second successive exit at that stage having lost to Beau Greaves in 2025. He could though enter four more times, with the tournament open to players aged 23 or under at the start of the season.
The loss is the latest in a series of surprise exits for Littler, who was knocked out of the World Grand Prix in the first round by Luke Woodhouse and lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts finals.

articles.title_orig: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.title_zh: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
So urgent had the departure been that some of the planes left before refuelling aircraft could be arranged to support them, US officials who wished to remain anonymous told the New York Times.
"So, what you saw there is the secretary of war [Pete Hegseth], out of an abundance of caution, trying to protect our guys," Vice-President JD Vance said as he left Washington for a trip to Alaska.
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
Washington, he added, "actually knows the people that made the threat", he but did not confirm who.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men , Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, was quoted as saying by Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump's safety pact
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says the world must accept AI’s ‘bad things’ as industry leaders sign Trump's safety pact
articles.content_orig:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.
During Politico ’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.
The comments come as a debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.
Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .
In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.
Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.
In the interview with Politico , Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative could be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of like misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.
Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
Concerns over the possibility for AI to escape human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
While much of the AI safety debate has centered around losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too.
“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.
The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground, instead.
“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

articles.title_orig: World Teachers’ Day 2026: Patrick Kiminza Nurturing a Young Generation of Conservationists in Tsavo, Kenya
articles.title_zh: World Teachers’ Day 2026: Patrick Kiminza Nurturing a Young Generation of Conservationists in Tsavo, Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Teacher and Wildlife Club Patron Patrick Kiminza with some of his students at Ngwata Comprehensive School in Makueni County, Kenya. © AWF
Through the Young Conservation Heroes project, African Wildlife Foundation and Wildlife Clubs of Kenya are equipping educational leadership and Wildlife Club Patrons with the skills, resources, and opportunities to make conservation education practical. This World Teachers’ Day story highlights how investing in educators can create meaningful opportunities for learners to explore, experience, and act for conservation.
For Patrick Kiminza, education extends beyond teaching the stipulated curriculum in the classroom. He sees it as an opportunity to help learners understand the natural world around them while building knowledge, skills, and confidence to act for conservation.
As a teacher and Wildlife Club Patron at Ngwata Comprehensive in Makueni County, Kenya, Patrick uses practical lessons and experiences to help learners understand connections between people, wildlife, and natural resources, while creating opportunities for them to participate in conservation. This connection is extremely important since the school is located near Tsavo East and Tsavo West National Parks, which makes nature conservation relevant to students’ everyday lives.
Patrick’s own journey into conservation grew from an appreciation of nature and a desire to address ongoing challenges, such as habitat loss, climate change, and biodiversity decline. Today, that commitment is reflected in his work as he mentors learners through tree planting, environmental clean-ups, wildlife awareness activities, educational visits, and school-based conservation projects.
“Conservation is not just an interest, but a responsibility that continues to shape my personal and professional goals. When the opportunity to become a Wildlife Club Patron arose, I saw it as an opportunity to combine my passion for education with my desire to nurture a generation of conservationists,” he says.
For him, one of the most rewarding parts of the role has been watching learners grow in confidence as they discover that conservation is something they can participate in and influence.
One learner who stands out is Samweul Onsongo, who joined the Wildlife Club as a participant and has since taken on leadership roles, first as club secretary and now as Wildlife Club President.
Patrick Kiminza with Samweul Ombongi Onsongo, student and Wildlife Club President at Ngwata Comprehensive School. © AWF
Patrick recalls a visit to Nakuru National Park when Onsongo asked why some wildlife species were endangered and what ordinary people could do to help protect them. The question stayed with Patrick.
“When we returned to school, Onsongo became one of the most active members of the Wildlife Club,” Patrick recalls. He participated in tree planting and environmental clean-up activities, encouraged his peers to take part in conservation, and shared what he had learned beyond the school environment. For Patrick, this is an important measure of effective conservation education.
“The goal is not simply to transfer knowledge but to help learners connect what they learn with the decisions they make in their own lives and communities,” he says.
Patrick Kiminza leads a conservation learning session with students. © AWF
Experiential learning has become central to Patrick’s approach. One of his most memorable experiences as a Wildlife Club Patron was taking students on educational trips. He stated that encountering wildlife and conservation efforts first-hand transformed concepts students had encountered in class into experiences they could see, question, and understand.
“They asked questions about wildlife, habitats and threats such as habitat loss and poaching. Back at school, that curiosity continued through tree planting, environmental clean-ups and conversations about conservation,” Patrick says.
At Ngwata Comprehensive School, Patrick has ensured that conservation learning is also embedded in practical, school-based projects. Learners in the school’s wildlife club raise indigenous and fruit tree seedlings in a school nursery, practice Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR).
This kind of learning matters because conservation challenges are rarely isolated. Land, water, food production, livelihoods, and wildlife are interconnected, and it is critical that young people have opportunities to understand those connections if they are to participate meaningfully in shaping the future of their communities.
Ngwata Comprehensive School also secured second place in the 2026 Shujaa Zone Competition under the Best Wildlife Club Project category. The competition, held under the Young Conservation Heroes project, provides a platform for learners and Wildlife Clubs to showcase their creativity, leadership, and practical action for conservation. The award recognised the club’s conservation initiatives and the active role students play in putting their knowledge into practice.
Patrick Kiminza takes a learner through a digital conservation learning platform in the newly established and equipped Information and Communications Technology lab supported by the Young Conservation Heroes project. © AWF
Through the Young Conservation Heroes project, supported by Bob and Emmy King, the African Wildlife Foundation and Wildlife Clubs of Kenya are equipping teachers, heads of institutions and Wildlife Club Patrons with training and resources to strengthen conservation education in schools.
As of September 2026, 266 teachers and 130 heads of institutions have received training in Education for Sustainable Development, supporting school-based Wildlife Clubs, strengthening their capacity to deliver conservation education, and support Wildlife Club activities in their respective schools.
As the world celebrates Teachers’ Day, Patrick’s experience shows what is possible when education creates space for curiosity, participation, and leadership. For him, success is not simply seeing a learner become a conservation enthusiast. It is seeing the values developed through the Wildlife Club, including responsibility, teamwork, leadership, and respect for nature, continue to shape the choices learners make in their lives and communities.
Through the Young Conservation Heroes project, teachers and Wildlife Club Patrons are creating opportunities for learners to understand conservation, put their knowledge into practice and take an active role in caring for the places they call home.
Lasting conservation will depend not only on protected areas, policies, and scientific knowledge, but also on the choices young people make today and the kind of relationships they build with nature, their communities, and the resources that sustain them.
Your gift helps safeguard iconic African species and the landscapes they call home—while working with communities to lead the way in conservation.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump told Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson on Monday that he thinks Iran was behind the attempted attack aboard a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight on Sept. 30.
“And on flydubai. Do you think Iran was responsible for that terrorist attack?” Tomlinson asked.
President Trump said, “I do, I personally do.”
The Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight had landed safely in Saudi Arabia after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who attacked the captain and tried to crash the plane.
Explosions were heard across the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Monday, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported on X.
Reuters also reported that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they carried out three military operations targeting several locations in Saudi Arabia , including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha International Airport and the Khamis Mushait military base.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia, the outlet reported.
U.S. sanctions successfully froze Iranian oil exports completely last month as the country's currency plunged to record lows, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday.
“Operation Economic Outcast is delivering results: the rial has plunged to record lows, Iran loaded zero crude oil onto tankers last month, and even Iran’s top security official has admitted the country is facing one of the most difficult periods in its history,” Bessent said on X .
“The Iranian regime allows its own people to suffer while it pours resources into terrorism,” he added before vowing that Operation Economic Outcast would not stop until the Iranian regime understands that Washington “will never allow the regime to fund terrorism and develop a nuclear weapon.”
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) is pushing back against claims that it purposely targets journalists in Gaza , stating that individuals "presented as innocent journalists" were actually in Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) and other terrorist organizations.
"They presented themselves as legitimate media professionals while serving terrorist organizations that regularly use propaganda and psychological warfare," the IDF stated on its website.
"Journalists are expected to report the unbiased truth," the IDF continued. "Yet these individuals concealed a fundamental truth about themselves: their own roles within military wings of terrorist organizations ."
The IDF noted that targeting journalists is a violation of international law, but said that many articles, opinion pieces and reports have misled the public.
As a result, the IDF launched an "in-depth investigation based on a wide range of intelligence sources, including open-source information, documents gathered in the field, interrogations of military operatives by Israeli intelligence bodies," to determine that claims the group violated international law do not tell the full story.
The IDF listed 170 alleged military operatives who were reportedly working as journalists.
This is an excerpt from a report by Fox News Digital's Brian Flood.
President Donald Trump issued a stark warning to Tehran on Monday, saying Iran would “suffer greatly” if it brought combat drones into the United Kingdom, while predicting the war with Iran will end shortly.
When pressed by reporters on the tarmac before departing for Grand Island, Nebraska, about whether Iran had brought combat drones into the United Kingdom, Trump replied: “I can't tell you that.”
“But if they did, they'll suffer greatly.”
The president also said the war with Iran “ is going to end very soon. One way or the other.”
President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington pulled its U.S. bombers from RAF Fairford in the U.K. because of a credible security threat.
“I think we can say that. I mean, they didn't fly out by accident,” Trump told reporters after being asked whether there had been a specific threat.
“There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy,” Trump said.
“But why should we leave him there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far,” he added.
The remarks came as Washington removed its heavy bombers from the base it had used to launch strikes on Iran , amid an investigation into a suspected plot to attack the base, in which six people were arrested and released on bail.
At least a dozen planes, including B-1 bombers, were redeployed to the United States from Royal Air Force Fairford, the Pentagon said.
Another tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, sparking a fire in its engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported.
The maritime organization said there were no reported casualties or environmental impacts.
“Authorities are investigating. Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO,” it said in a statement on X .
This was the third incident in the waterway in the last 48 hours.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert Monday warning Americans in Saudi Arabia of potential drone and missile attacks.
“Due to the ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia and the potential for aerial drone or missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, the U.S. Mission strongly encourages all U.S. citizens to remain vigilant and follow the guidance of national alerts released by Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense,” the embassy said on X .
The warning came amid rising tension in the region as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces launched a lightning advance, retaking the coast along the Bab el-Mandab Strait through the city of Mocha and driving Iran-backed Houthis from most of the territory they seized last month, the government said.
Iran’s army chief warned Monday that the country’s armed forces are ready to deliver a "crushing" response to any renewed U.S. military action while accusing Washington of turning to economic sanctions after losing the battle.
“After failing on the military battlefield, the enemy has resorted to other methods and, through sanctions and economic pressure, is trying to put the people under pressure, while at the same time pursuing many measures to create insecurity and unrest,” Hatami said, according to Fars , the state-affiliated news agency.
Hatami added that Iranian forces would deliver “a crushing and decisive response” if the United States makes “another mistake.”
Iran is adopting a mirror narrative, using President Donald Trump 's own claims to make their own.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian lashed out at the United States on Monday, saying negotiations have “no meaning” with an enemy that “terrorizes, sanctions, pressures and threatens on a daily basis,” according to Iranian state media.
The irony of the remarks are very close to what Trump and his administration has long claimed of Iran.
The comments signal Tehran’s hardening public stance as the Iran war continues to fuel attacks on global shipping routes, energy disruptions and growing threats to U.S. assets abroad.
They also come as Trump has said Iran wants to make a deal “quickly and badly,” while U.S. officials continue to press military and economic pressure on Tehran.
Retired Gen. Jack Keane said Monday that Saudi Arabia “cannot let” the Iran-backed Houthis maintain control near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, calling the waterway “strategically as significant as the Straits of Hormuz.”
“The Houthis escalated significantly when they took control of the Bab al-Mandeb Straits,” Keane told Monday's Fox News “ America’s Newsroom .” “That’s a waterway that is strategically as significant as the Straits of Hormuz, and the Saudis, in terms of its impact on them and their economy, they can’t let that stand.”

articles.title_orig: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.title_zh: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.content_orig:
The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.
The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Key details remain unknown, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people that came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media.
“Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine.
Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.”
“We need to understand that now,” he added.
The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is.
Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics.
It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization . All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body.
Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious.
Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said.
Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood.
Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes.
The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.”
It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO.
Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said.
“It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said.
Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet.
“It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said.
While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest.
“It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said.
It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm.
Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici.
People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Health care workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure.
“We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said.
Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague.
“This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said.
Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.”
Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.”
“The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said.
About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC . Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas.
Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen.
Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague .
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.title_zh: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

articles.title_orig: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.title_zh: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title_orig: Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform-FL: 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards Finalist
articles.title_zh: Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform-FL: 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards Finalist
articles.content_orig:
Quebec City — Technimount EMS (Technimount), a leading provider of mounting solutions for medical devices, is proud to announce that its Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL has been selected as a finalist for the 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards.
Designed specifically for critical care air transport, the Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL transforms a LifePort AeroSled TS stretcher, typically used for adult and pediatric patients, into a neonatal transport system within seconds. The platform securely mounts the Dräger Isolette TI500 incubator while allowing care teams to quickly return the stretcher to standard patient care when neonatal transport is no longer required. By eliminating the need to dedicate a stretcher exclusively to neonatal care, this solution helps air medical teams to optimize equipment utilization while increasing operational flexibility.
At the heart of the system is Technimount’s proprietary XClamp Technology, which remains installed directly onto the stretcher without interfering with its regular use. When neonatal transport is required, the platform can be rapidly installed without tools. A dual quick-release latch system, one securing the platform to the stretcher and the other anchoring the incubator, allows for fast installation and removal. Engineered with the space constraints of aircraft environments in mind, the compact platform remains within the dimensions of the AeroSled TS while providing a secure solution for neonatal transport. The system has been rigorously tested to meet applicable sections of FAA regulations 14 CFR §§ 23 and 25.
The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL is also designed for seamless compatibility with Technimount’s Xtension Pro Assistant – LP, a previous EMS World Innovation Awards-winning solution. Together, the systems provide teams with the ability to securely manage the incubator and essential medical devices required for neonatal critical care throughout transport.
“Being selected as an EMS World Innovation Awards finalist for a tenth year is an important recognition of the work our team continues to put into solving real challenges faced by critical care transport professionals,” said Carl Bouchard, Founder and CEO of Technimount System. “The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL was developed to give air medical teams greater flexibility without compromising safety or efficiency, and we are proud to see this innovation recognized by the EMS industry.” Concluded Mr. Bouchard
Technimount EMS is a leading provider of mounting systems designed to safely secure medical devices during transport. Technimount EMS addresses the safety needs of patients and staff during ground or air emergencies and Critical Care Transport, establishing itself as a standard in the Emergency Medical Services industry.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the US
articles.content_orig:
by MATTHEW DUCKWORTH | WHP
The Commonwealth has reported 977 total measles cases, up 34 since Sept. 30, according to the measles dashboard. (FILE)
PENNSYLVANIA (WHP) — Measles cases continue to climb in Pennsylvania, surpassing a grim milestone as the state continues to be at the center of the 2026 outbreak.
The Commonwealth has reported 1,004 total measles cases, up 61 since Sept. 30, according to the measles dashboard.
Hospitalization numbers continue to climb as well, as 198 total Pennsylvanians have been admitted to the hospital since the start of the outbreak. The 22 new hospitalizations mark an increase of around 10% in under a week, according to data.
Additionally, the Department of Health said, "An unvaccinated Lancaster County resident with confirmed measles has died."
This is the fifth reported measles-associated death in Pennsylvania this year. The Department of Health previously reported two infant deaths in Lancaster County , the death of an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, and the death of a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported only two measles deaths on its website.
Current data show that 391 of the 1,004 cases in Pennsylvania have been reported in Lancaster County, accounting for almost 40% of total cases in the Commonwealth. The only other county in Pennsylvania with more than 100 reported cases is Mifflin County, with 118.
