articles.title_orig: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.title_zh: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.source: The University of Alabama at Birmingham
articles.content_orig:
Margaret Canter, Ph.D (left) and Maree Jones (right) There was a time when the internet was a briefly visited place. People logged on, did what they needed to do and logged off. That time is gone, and society’s attention now has completely shifted to the online world as digital technology has evolved.
As director of Social Media Strategy at the University of Alabama at Birmingham , Maree Jones has watched the shift happen in real time. Spending 16 years in a field that never stops, Jones has seen technology go from sitting on desks to riding in people’s pockets from the moment they wake up until they go to sleep. Drawing on her years of expertise in an always-online world, Jones provides insight on how to protect attention and focus in the workplace.
The challenge of protecting attention is a workplace concern, and it also is a critical component in mental health and emotional well-being.
Margaret Canter, Ph.D., clinical psychologist and professor of pediatrics in the UAB Marnix E. Heersink School of Medicine and Children’s of Alabama, speaks on the connection between attention and mental health, and shares her insight on attention protection and focus recovery. Canter’s work focuses on providing integrated behavioral healthcare to the pediatric clinic's patient population, which is children from birth through 18, and their families.
According to Canter, attention is a valuable resource because humans can give their attention to only one thing at a time, meaning what individuals choose to focus on and attend to must be worth it.
“When someone is able to focus and sustain their attention, they learn more and can be more efficient in completing their work or tasks,” Canter said. “If we are stressed or anxious about things getting accomplished, we may be preoccupied with those things’ getting done, which would negatively impact our attention.”
Difficulty paying attention and trouble focusing are symptoms of both anxiety and depression. If one already has difficulty paying attention, feelings of anxiety can become heightened, with mood and self-esteem being negatively impacted.
“In the age of social media, productivity isn’t just about how much work gets done. It’s also about how often we’re asked to stop what we’re doing and mentally shift to something else,” Jones said.
Likewise, if someone is already having feelings of anxiety and depression, individuals may not have the motivation to make the effort in their work, tasks and other responsibilities.
Jones says that part of what makes constant connectivity so draining is not the volume of work; it is the volume of decisions. With access to all kinds of information, the mind can be easily susceptible to burnout, and it can be hard to determine which information should be attended to. This persistent hum of pressure can be especially draining for people whose jobs depend on staying informed.
“ Burnout has become an increasingly important conversation because we’re finally beginning to understand what long-term exposure to that pace feels like,” Jones said.
Smartphones allow access to all kinds of information at any time and place, including consuming the news via social media instead of traditionally. Because news segments are delivered in 30-second to three-minute intervals, sustaining attention for longer can be more difficult.
“When they’re wanting to read about a news topic or event, I encourage individuals to find one or two sources or individuals they trust and limit their exposure,” Canter said. “If we are intentional about our attention, we will not have the constant stream of information negatively affect our productivity and mood.”
In her role, Jones has the potential to be exposed to thousands of notifications a day. Each one, she says, carries a hidden cost of deciding on what and which information needs to be attended to.
For Jones, she has learned to recognize the warning signs that technology has taken the wheel. The antidote starts with treating attention as a resource worth guarding.
“By the end of the day, people who largely do digital work can feel exhausted because they’ve spent the day managing interruptions and making thousands of tiny decisions,” Jones said.
“Protecting my attention has become just as important to me as managing my calendar, because attention is what allows me to do meaningful work.”
For many people, including Jones, simply spending less time online is not an option. Being online is the job. So instead of avoidance, she recommends building boundaries around intention and learning to let technology work for her, instead of against her.
“I’ve adopted a mindset of being intentional with my time online rather than constantly immersed in it,” Jones said. “Sometimes that means giving yourself permission to mindlessly scroll but setting a timer. Sometimes it means unfollowing accounts that consistently leave you feeling anxious or discouraged.”
Some recommended ways to protect attention include the following:
When people are feeling stressed, they often seek distractions to take their minds off whatever is stressing them. While often associated with unproductivity, distractions can be a tool for attention protection and getting through a tough moment.
“Distraction is an excellent coping skill and one that I often use with children and teens in therapy,” Canter said. “Sometimes we need to get through a tough moment without doing something that would make the situation worse. However, it is important to remember that sometimes you need to come back to whatever is upsetting you and work through it, so it does not cause future problems.”
Having to respond to multiple people, whether digitally or in-person, can be taxing on the mind and attention. To balance responsiveness and attention, Canter encourages having windows of time when they are truly offline. This powerful strategy helps rebuild attention stamina and allows individuals to have higher-quality responses when coming back online.
“As a parent, I try to not have my phone with me during the time I’m helping my kids get ready for bed,” Canter said. “When I’m successful, I’m able to be more present for my kids, which feels good, and we are more efficient in completing the bedtime routine because I am not distracted by whatever it is I’m looking at or whoever I’m talking to on my phone.”
One of the biggest barriers to setting boundaries in terms of responsiveness, Jones says, is the fear of seeming unavailable.
“In workplace culture, we sometimes unintentionally equate responsiveness with value,” Jones said. “Responding quickly doesn’t always mean you’re doing your best work.”
According to Jones, the healthiest teams she has worked with communicate expectations and preferred boundaries clearly. Everyone understands what requires immediate attention and what can reasonably wait. That creates trust without requiring individuals to be constantly interrupted.
“For any communication methods, expectations should be discussed with your manager and your team,” Jones said. “Different jobs require different response times, and having those expectations clearly defined removes a lot of unnecessary stress.”
Digital fatigue is real, and much of it is fueled by the belief that instant communication should always be the norm.
“Just because technology makes instant communication possible doesn’t mean every conversation needs to happen instantly,” Jones said. “Digital work is cognitive work, and sometimes what feels like burnout may actually be decision fatigue.”
Away from work, Jones guards her attention just as carefully, keeping few apps on her phone and even fewer with permission to send notifications.
“Every notification is essentially asking, ‘Can I interrupt what you’re doing?’ Very few apps deserve that permission, especially in my free time,” Jones said. “Just because I work in social media doesn’t mean I have to live in social media.”

articles.title_orig: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.title_zh: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Since it initially published in 1997, the Japanese manga series ONE PIECE has surpassed 600 million copies in its circulation, on par with the biggest superhero comics and most popular wizarding-world books. To call creator Eiichiro Oda’s series a cultural behemoth would be like calling ONE PIECE ’s legendary “Blue Sea” a mere body of water — technically true, but wildly short of it.
Dr. B’s Research Lab at Nike’s Harajuku pop-up, recasting Bill Bowerman as a scientist studying the Devil Fruit–inspired Air Max Plus collabs. Here, the three models hang suspended like specimens.
You can call it manifest destiny that the world’s most popular manga and the world’s largest sports company would join forces at some point . But for Nike to honor the legacy of a pop culture landmark so robust and influential that fans literally name their children after characters, it couldn’t just be a simple merch collaboration. Instead, Nike answered with three Air Max Plus silhouettes, each inspired by a Devil Fruit (from ONE PIECE lore), apparel stitched with references only the faithful will catch, and a globe-trotting rollout meant to be explored like the story it came from. With a mythology this deep and only one shot to engage with the canon, Nike Virtual Studios’ .SWOOSH team knew it had to come correct.
“When a brand collabs with ‘ONE PIECE,’ they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story.”
“When a brand collabs with ONE PIECE , they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story,” says Ashwin Shinde, .SWOOSH's Senior Manager, Energy Gaming Product Merch on Nike’s ONE PIECE Collection. “So, we lean on the thing that’s always going to set us apart from other brands. What is a story that only Nike could tell?”
For .SWOOSH, the answer started with a conceptual parallel. “We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential and essentially have superpowers,” says Bryce Wong, Senior Manager, Gaming Footwear Product Design.
Bridging the two brand universes, the team landed on a single idea: “If Devil Fruits existed in our world, they would be Nikes.” From there, the task became choosing the right shoe to bring it to life. Wong proposed the Air Max Plus, an iconic model whose expressive cage and dimensional upper made it, in the words of Senior Designer Yuchung Chen, “a perfect design to blend with the whimsical world of ONE PIECE .”
Translating a superpower-inducing fruit into the shoe meant reworking every surface. “Each Devil Fruit design posed its own challenge of maintaining the motion and directionality of the original shoe’s cage design while keeping it light and open,” says Chen, who wrapped the fruit pattern across the mudguard, cage and shank. Each upper got its own finish: gummy and rubber-like for Gum Gum, a velvety peach-fuzz for Ope Ope, and an on-fire sunset for Mera Mera that nods to the OG Air Max Plus.
The deepest cut is on the medial shank: a contrasting color bites a chunk clean out, a reference to the panel where rubber-limbed hero Monkey D. Luffy accidentally eats the Gum Gum fruit — or, as Chen noted in a wink for the heads, it has another, real name — thinking of it as dessert.
“We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil
Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential. If Devil Fruits existed
in our world, they would be Nikes.”
The apparel scaled the same logic up: mythical fruit into tangible object, rendered on fabric. “Following that same approach, the patterns, colors and textures of the Devil Fruits that inspired the footwear are enlarged and abstracted into layered graphics,” explains Lead, Global Brand Digital Designer, Sarah Kim. This makes each piece a “wearable abstraction of the shoes and, by extension, the fruits themselves.”
She built the graphic tees around Laboon — the whale character who waits years for the promised return of his old friends, making a promise with Luffy  — because of the way his endurance speaks to both sides of the collab at once. “We wanted the choices to ultimately communicate the shared ethos of a Nike athlete and a shonen manga hero: resilience, perseverance and the ability to keep going.”
The building takeover in Shanghai, including a Straw Hats’ Jolly Roger reworked with a Swoosh for crossbones, beside a flaming “WANT ’EM” ad wrapping the space.
The team also used canonical deep cuts to inject the collaboration with inside jokes that will make loyalists salivate. This includes a vest that nods to one of the manga’s core rules, that Devil Fruit consumers trade their ability to swim for their powers. “The vest was an addition that emerged as a meta and cheeky way to play into the lore as we got deeper into development and more immersed in the ONE PIECE universe,” says Kim.
Inside Dr. B’s Research Lab, including the “hated by the sea” vest.
The same investment into authenticity even shaped the release’s packaging. Open the shoebox and your reflection stares back from a “Wanted” poster printed inside, casting buyers as pirates with bounties on their heads, like so many of the ONE PIECE heroes. “The idea behind the mirror was to make the person opening the box part of the story,” says Global Brand Experience Designer Heena Chung. “Your reflection completes the poster and, for a second, you become part of the ONE PIECE world.” She designed the packaging as a “treasure chest” with a staged reveal, down to a reward for completists: line up all three boxes and the Devil Fruit graphics connect into a single panoramic artwork.
The unboxing was intentionally designed to unfold in stages, like a treasure chest built to reveal itself over time. Printed tissue gives way to a trading card; the shoes wait beneath as the prize.
Between the lid and the shoes, printed tissue paper hides its own ONE PIECE iconography. “There’s a deliberate progression to the reveal,” says Chung. “The exterior establishes the collaboration, the tissue introduces another layer of the world, and the mirror creates the final interaction by placing you directly inside the Wanted poster.”
The IYKYK references are dense and intentional, but they aren’t the raison d'être. “The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ONE PIECE rather than simply collect Easter eggs,” says Chung. “The box becomes part of the collaboration itself — something worth keeping and exploring rather than just a container for the product.”
“The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ‘ONE PIECE’ rather than simply collect Easter eggs.”
A collection this considered could have simply dropped, no problem. Instead, the deep bench of the global .SWOOSH team took it off the shelf and into the wild by staging physical activations across nearly two dozen cities worldwide, turning the release into something fans can travel to and track down. The blueprint came straight from the source. ”“Creatively, the table was already set by Oda’s story of the ONE PIECE protagonist and his crew, known as the Straw Hats, traveling the world and searching for treasure,” says Wong. “We wanted to parallel that with the world of sneaker collecting, giving people a reason to find their crew, discover, and experience something different along the way.”
Dr. B’s mobile lab, parked in Harajuku and rigged out. Nike’s answer to Dr. Vegapunk, the ‘ONE PIECE’ scientist who studies the Devil Fruits.
That hunt materialized city by city. In the Harajuku district of Tokyo, a Nike-branded Poneglyph — one of the manga’s ancient, indestructible tablets inscribed in a lost language — appeared on Cat Street, teasing the release with no explanation unless you’re fluent in the saga. Below the Nike store there, the team built out Dr. B’s Research Lab, a nod to Dr. Vegap

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s presidential race goes to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.content_orig:
Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro put in a stronger than expected showing, with Lula calling the result ‘unexpected’
Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
With 99.9% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1%. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m.
Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.
Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.
Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.
Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.
​Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.” Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld , including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.
Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.
Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo , but want to vote Lula out of power.
As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.
Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.
“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.
Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.
Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.
Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.
But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.
Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, ​a 31​-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round​. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”.
Donald Trump became a key election issue , with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
articles.content_orig:
Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now. ”
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro .
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, has yet to comment on Sunday’s result, although writing on his Truth Social network, he praised the speed of the vote count. But the US president will be delighted by the strong rightwing showing, a major boost to his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo , and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups ,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

articles.title_orig: New Supreme Court term begins with justices stumped by climate change case
articles.title_zh: New Supreme Court term begins with justices stumped by climate change case
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court kicked off a new term Monday, with the justices wrestling with an attempt by oil companies to throw out lawsuits alleging they should pay damages for the impacts of climate change .
Although the case concerns a specific lawsuit the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, brought against Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, the ultimate decision could have broad ramifications for more than two dozen similar lawsuits brought by cities and counties around the country.
The justices — lacking a ninth member because Justice Samuel Alito’s recused — asked tough questions of both sides as they tackled broad legal questions raised in the case. Alito’s absence raises the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling that would leave the legal issues unresolved while allowing the Boulder case to move forward.
Boulder officials say they face increasing costs because of the impacts of climate change, including efforts to minimize risks from wildfires. Just this summer, Colorado has experienced extreme heat, drought and multiple fires .
The lawsuit, bringing claims under state law, says Exxon and Suncor misled consumers about the impact that greenhouse gases produced by their products would have on the climate.
The companies deny the allegations and warn that if the Boulder lawsuit and others like it are able to move forward to trial, they and other energy companies could face crippling damages in the billions of dollars. They also argue climate change is such an inherently national and international issue that it cannot be the subject of litigation in state courts.
There was some sympathy from the bench toward the oil companies and the potential for substantial damages.
Chief Justice John Roberts, one of the court’s conservatives, wondered how many more cities and counties would launch similar lawsuits if the court allows the Boulder case to continue.
“Just to make sure I have a correct understanding. Presumably, if you prevail, the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit,” he told Boulder’s lawyer, Kevin Russell.
Although Boulder’s claims are based on consumer deception, Roberts also seemed skeptical that the lawsuit was anything other than what he called “an effort to reduce emissions.”
On the other hand, Roberts, in an exchange with the oil companies’ lawyer, Kannon Shanmugam, said litigation brought in state court against out-of-state companies over an alleged harmful product is commonplace.
Other justices also seemed conflicted. Liberal Justice Elena Kagan at one point compared climate litigation with the wave of lawsuits against tobacco companies and drug manufacturers that sold opioids, which were allowed to proceed.
The oil companies have pushed back on such comparisons, saying that in the tobacco and opioid litigation there was a much more direct connection between the product and alleged harm to consumers.
But Kagan also wondered if, as the oil companies argue, the Clean Air Act that was enacted by Congress to regulate air emissions nationwide could foreclose the Boulder claims. A ruling saying that state lawsuits are preempted by the federal law could be “the more natural and simpler route” of deciding the case if the court sides with the companies, she said.
A decision on those lines would be the narrower of two paths to victory for the oil companies, with Shanmugam pushing for a broader ruling that state lawsuits are prohibited under the Constitution.
Liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor pointed out that even if the Clean Air Act bars states from seeking to cap emissions, the lawsuit does not seek to do that. “The Clean Air Act does not regulate marketing or advertising of fuel, correct?” she said.
The most vocal justice in backing the oil companies was conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who cited several court precedents that he said were “crystal clear” that air and water pollution are matters of federal law that the states cannot regulate.
“We don’t have to reinvent the wheel because we’ve said this multiple times,” he added.
Overall, there appeared to be a lack of consensus on the bench as to how to resolve the case, with one possibility that the court simply dismisses it, which would allow litigation to continue.
Lurking in the background are recent efforts by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency to eliminate greenhouse gas regulations under the Clean Air Act, an issue being litigated that could reach the justices in a later case.
“I think it is difficult to decide whether the Clean Air Act preempts these claims when we don’t know whether the Clean Air Act applies to greenhouse-gas emissions when the EPA is saying it lacks the statutory authority to do that,” Russell told the justices.
The Boulder case was the first to be argued in the courtroom as the justices began a new nine-month term after a summer break. Other major cases already on the docket involve a challenge to bans on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles and two about the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies .
Alito announced last week he was stepping aside from hearing the Boulder lawsuit but did not say why. Liberal groups have said for months that he should recuse himself because he owns stocks in other oil companies that could benefit from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor. Alito’s decision was a surprise, as the court had told NBC News in May there was no need for him to step aside.
The litigation is playing out amid a broader battle between oil companies and their allies on one side and groups advocating for action on climate change on the other.
State courts have become a focus, in part, because of a lack of action at the federal level, with the Trump administration rolling back Obama- and Biden-era policies seeking to reduce carbon emissions and speed up the transition to cleaner energy. The administration, which filed a brief backing Exxon and Suncor, has also sought to block renewable energy projects, with President Donald Trump calling climate change a “hoax.”
In a ruling in 2011 , the Supreme Court shut the door to making certain claims against energy companies over climate change in federal court, saying they were displaced by the Clean Air Act.
The proxy war over the issue has also focused attention on a chapter about climate science in a reference manual for federal judges. It was abruptly withdrawn this year after conservatives alleged the authors had a conflict of interest. Some also called for Kagan to recuse herself in Monday’s case because she wrote a foreword to the manual. She later said she did not even read the climate chapter.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

Getting to space is no longer just a matter of building a rocket and launching it once. Reusable boosters, new launch vehicles and a growing commercial space industry are reshaping the path to orbit — a transformation that will take center stage during this year's World Space Week.
World Space Week (WSW) 2026 runs from Oct. 4 through Oct. 10, with this year's theme, "Rocket Revolution," highlighting the technologies and organizations changing how humanity reaches and uses space. The global celebration brings together space agencies, companies, educators, students, museums, astronomy clubs and space enthusiasts for events and activities around the world.
The annual celebration of WSW is tied to two important milestones in spaceflight history. Oct. 4 marks the anniversary of the 1957 launch of Sputnik 1 , the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, while Oct. 10 marks the signing of the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, which established principles for the peaceful exploration and use of outer space. The United Nations General Assembly established WSW as an annual observance in 1999.
This year's theme "recognizes how increased space access and falling launch prices have stimulated the space ecosystem and exciting new space applications," Dennis Stone, WSW Association president, said in a statement from the organization, adding that the theme is also intended to inspire student interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, or STEM.
For decades, reaching orbit required enormous amounts of hardware, fuel and infrastructure — and rockets were generally designed to fly only once. That model has increasingly begun to change.
Reusable rockets have demonstrated that portions of a launch vehicle can return to Earth and fly again, while a growing number of commercial companies and countries are developing new ways to put satellites, spacecraft and other payloads into orbit.
The change is about more than simply building bigger or more powerful rockets . Reusability and new launch architectures could alter the economics and cadence of spaceflight, while smaller launch vehicles are opening additional options for organizations looking to send spacecraft into orbit.
The result is a space industry with more participants and a wider range of missions — from communications and Earth-observation satellites to scientific spacecraft and human spaceflight. Just last month, SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time during its Sept. 28 test flight , successfully deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites in a major milestone for the vehicle's development. The mission was ultimately cut short after an engine issue, but achieved its primary objectives of reaching orbit and deploying its payload.
More frequent and diverse access to orbit supports an expanding ecosystem of satellites and spacecraft that already plays a role in everyday life. Space-based systems provide communications, navigation, weather information and Earth-observation data, while satellites are increasingly used for environmental monitoring, disaster response and connectivity. That broader impact is part of what WSW aims to highlight.
This year's rocket theme also comes with educational resources designed to bring the subject into classrooms and homes. Estes Education partnered with WSW to develop a Rocket Revolution Toolkit, with activities for classrooms, families and clubs that encourage students to explore rocket science and engineering — including the challenges of designing reusable launch vehicles, according to a statement .
WSW events are expected to take place across 100 nations this week, with activities ranging from talks and exhibitions to classroom activities, movie nights, astronomy events and hands-on STEM projects.
Among the activities planned for 2026 are events from major space organizations and companies. The European Space Agency (ESA) and The Pokémon Company International are teaming up on a Europe-wide space-themed exhibition and Pokémon GO event, while the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida will host a WSW Expo on Oct. 9 featuring NASA and industry partners.
The rocket theme will also take a hands-on approach, with students and rocket clubs encouraged to launch model rockets using equipment provided by United Launch Alliance and Estes. The BBC StoryWorks Commercial Productions will also launch an exclusive online "Space Renaissance" event, featuring the world premiere of the series' first film and a discussion on how storytelling can bring space closer to global audiences. A full list of events, both local and virtual, can be found online .
For those who can't make it to an organized event, the night sky offers plenty of ways to mark the week, with Saturn at opposition on Oct. 4, the moon near Mars on Oct. 5, the moon near Jupiter on Oct. 6, the Draconid meteor shower peaking around Oct. 8-9, and a New Moon on Oct. 10.
So while "Rocket Revolution" is focused on the technology carrying humanity beyond Earth, celebrating WSW doesn't require a launchpad, a laboratory or even a telescope — you can simply step outside after dark. Be sure to check back here over the coming days for our WSW coverage of global events.
Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! You can follow her on Twitter @Sam_Ashley13.

articles.title_orig: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.title_zh: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.content_orig:
Quarantine measures in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya Shipilova
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has said the US is closely monitoring the case of a Russian laboratory worker who died last week after a reported accident at a plague research institute in Siberia.
“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio said on Monday before leaving for a trip to Europe . “I ⁠don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an ⁠eye on it.”
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, became ill at work. She died two days later on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov.
It remains unclear how she became unwell. Unconfirmed reports in Russian media have suggested Shipilova may have been infected after a mishap at the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed that account.
Local media have reported that the institute has subsequently been locked down, with staff forced to sleep on the floor and on chairs. “They’ve been isolating everybody since Friday – more than 60 people,” one relative, Roman, told the news portal Siberia.Realities .
He said family members were allowed to drop off food at a checkpoint while tests were carried out inside the building. Similar quarantine restrictions have been placed on several other hospitals in and around the city.
Rubio, citing what ‌Russians have released about the death, said it seemed a worker in the lab became ​infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.
“There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously,” he said. “But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads.”
Senior Russian officials have added to public disquiet by sending conflicting messages. Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the Buryatia region, which neighbours Irkutsk, initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” . It insisted that tests found no micro-organisms linked to her professional work and described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the area as stable.
Authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to avoid travelling to Shelekhov and surrounding settlements after what they said was unofficial information about a possible plague infection. They later deleted the post from social media.
“There are no obvious changes to daily life on the streets, but people are worried and anxious. Locals are angry that they are not being told anything,” said Elena Trifonova, a journalist with People of Baikal , an exiled Russian media outlet specialising in Siberia.
Despite the lack of a confirmed diagnosis, precautionary measures appear to have been introduced across the region. The US-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on Monday that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine.
The outlet confirmed that staff from Shipilova’s workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had been kept inside the institute since 2 October.
Patients at Irkutsk city clinical hospital No 1 and the Ivano-Matreninskaya children’s hospital said relatives were not being allowed to visit and people inside were not permitted to leave.
On social media, local residents described some of the precautions being introduced.
Ulyana Gavryunina, who went on Monday to one of Irkutsk’s main maternity hospitals for a routine check-up on Monday, said doctors refused to allow her mother in, citing a quarantine imposed over the suspected plague case. Gavryunina said staff member checked her for flu-like symptoms and asked her to fill out a screening form for infections, on which “plague” was listed. She posted a photograph of the form on Instagram.
Elsewhere, a mask requirement was introduced at the Irkutsk aluminium smelter in Shelekhov. The plant’s director, Artyom Fominykh, called it a preventive measure , saying: “Better safe than sorry.” Over the weekend several public events in Irkutsk were cancelled.
Shipolova’s death has prompted intervention from senior federal health officials. Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary doctor, travelled to Irkutsk on Friday.
She attended an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission over what officials called a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection”.
Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, urged residents to remain calm after meeting Popova to coordinate the response. “All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none is showing signs of illness and laboratory tests have returned negative results,” he wrote on Telegram.
Kobzev made no reference to reports that a laboratory worker had died.
US politicians have raised concerns about the incident, which follows longstanding and unfounded allegations by the Kremlin that Ukraine has secretly carried out biological weapons research with the support of Washington.
A Republican representative, Don Bacon, a senior member of the House armed services committee, wrote on social media: “I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs.”
Plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian far east, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents and their fleas.
But human cases in Russia are rare. Before the suspected Irkutsk case, the country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in Siberia’s Altai Republic contracted plague after helping butcher a marmot.
“This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further,” Prof Ian Jones, a professor of virology at the University of Reading, in the UK, said. “Although it is true that pneumonic plague is directly transmissible, the contacts of the primary case are known and can be treated if they show any sign of infection.”
He added: “Plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia, but the living conditions associated with previously spread plague are no longer generally true, antibiotics are available and its potential is therefore limited.”

articles.title_orig: Africa's gold powerhouse bypasses US dollar to clear trade with China as Beijing unlocks zero-tariff access for 53 African nations
articles.title_zh: Africa's gold powerhouse bypasses US dollar to clear trade with China as Beijing unlocks zero-tariff access for 53 African nations
articles.content_orig:
Ghana has begun allowing importers to use the Ghanaian cedi to pay for eligible imports from China, in a move aimed at reducing businesses’ reliance on the US dollar for bilateral trade.
Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama disclosed the development at the 132nd Monetary Policy Committee press briefing, saying Stanbic Bank Ghana is already piloting the payment arrangement.
“ As we speak, if you want to buy anything from China, just go to Stanbic Bank with your cedis. You are able to do that,” Asiama said.
Ghana Commercial Bank (GCB) is also developing a similar arrangement, according to the governor, as the central bank seeks to facilitate payments between Ghanaian importers and Chinese suppliers without requiring businesses to first source US dollars.
DON'T MISS THIS: China’s push for a global yuan gains ground in one of Africa’s biggest oil economies
The initiative is being supported by Stanbic’s access to China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), a payment network authorised by the People’s Bank of China for settling eligible cross-border transactions in Chinese yuan.
Stanbic says businesses can initiate eligible yuan payments from their Ghana cedi accounts, meaning they do not necessarily need to maintain a yuan-denominated account. Customers select Chinese yuan as the payment currency and submit the required documentation.
Eligible payments submitted by 2:00 p.m. GMT can be processed for next-business-day settlement, subject to regulatory and compliance requirements.
Stanbic Bank Ghana CEO Kwamina Asomaning said CIPS provides a more direct payment route to Chinese counterparties, reducing the need for US correspondent or intermediary banks.
“ With CIPS, businesses can access a more direct payment route to Chinese counterparties, reducing the need for US correspondent or intermediary banks, ” Asomaning said.
DON'T MISS THIS: Africa’s shift toward China’s yuan gathers pace as Angola’s banking sector embraces Beijing’s payment network
The bank said payments between Ghana and China have traditionally passed through intermediary banks, including US correspondent banks, potentially increasing costs and processing times.
Stanbic’s CIPS service is therefore designed to allow eligible businesses to trade more directly in yuan, reducing the number of foreign-exchange conversions required for China-related transactions. CIPS does not replace SWIFT, with Stanbic continuing to use existing payment rails for transactions in currencies such as the dollar, euro and pound.
The development comes as Ghana seeks to deepen its economic relationship with China. Stanbic said China accounted for 22.3% of Ghana’s imports in 2024, while the Bank of Ghana has said it is also looking to engage Chinese counterparts on opportunities created by Beijing’s expanded zero-tariff policy for African countries.
DON'T MISS THIS: The world’s second-largest economy just decided, with one of its top African partners, to do away with the use of the US dollar
From May 1, 2026, China extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, creating new opportunities for African exporters seeking access to the Chinese market.
For Ghanaian importers, however, the immediate benefit of the new payment arrangement is on the other side of the trade relationship: the ability to fund eligible Chinese yuan payments from cedi balances without first having to source US dollars.
The Bank of Ghana said it will continue working with relevant institutions to support the growing Ghana-China trade relationship, while GCB prepares to offer a similar payment option.

articles.title_orig: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
Preschoolers at The Goddard School in Plymouth recently got a hands-on introduction to broadcast journalism during a special visit from CCX News anchor Emily Haugen in honor of World News Day.
During the visit, the young students stepped behind the anchor desk, practiced using real microphones and tried their hand at interviewing. The interactive session gave them a taste of how news reporting works, featuring lighthearted conversations about their favorite colors, sports and pets at home.
“So I just asked all of them what their favorite color is, so I’ll ask that to you, too,” Haugen asked one student during a practice interview. “What is your favorite color?”
“Purple!” the student replied.
“Why is purple your favorite color?”
The activity aligns directly with the school’s focus on inquiry-based learning, according to school owner Anthony Miller.
“I think any time you can add curiosity to anything, kids learn well with that,” Miller said.
The Goddard School frequently hosts visitors from various professional backgrounds to introduce students to different career paths and foster early curiosity about the world around them.

articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.content_orig:
About / Offices / Vocations
About / Offices / Vocations
Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_orig: Midterm Election Updates: Democrats Target More GOP Strongholds as They Fight for Control of Congress
articles.title_zh: Midterm Election Updates: Democrats Target More GOP Strongholds as They Fight for Control of Congress
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four weeks out from Election Day, the Senate battleground map is growing after signs of improvement for Democrats in several red-leaning states.
For the first time this year, CNN’s list of 9 Senate seats most likely to flip expands to 10 to include Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years . A new wave of polling also shows Democrats ahead or competitive in red states like Ohio, Alaska and Texas. All four states went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024.
To win the Senate majority, Democrats will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while defending three of their own, including Michigan.
Trump’s approval rating stands at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls, amid high frustration over the economy and the war he launched against Iran. Democrats have also seen surging enthusiasm in special elections since Trump returned to office and early signs of elevated turnout in early voting.
But they have also expressed unease over the massive amount of spending coming from the GOP. From the start of October through Election Day, Republicans are poised to outspend Democrats on advertising in eight of the ten most competitive Senate races, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, even though that advantage will be blunted by GOP-aligned outside groups having to spend more for ratings points than Democratic campaigns will.
Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states. The rankings are a snapshot of where the contests stand at this point and can shift as the midterm election season enters its final month.
North Carolina remains the state most likely to flip this year. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, who has made affordability issues a centerpiece of his campaign, has a strong position over GOP nominee Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and Trump ally vying to replace Sen. Thom Tillis.
An Elon University/YouGov poll released last month showed Cooper up 11 points over Whatley among likely voters. The Senate Leadership Fund, a key Republican outside spending group, is pausing its ad campaign there. Over the weekend, Republican outside groups cut more than $15 million from their remaining ad bookings, according to AdImpact data.
Still, Trump campaigned with Whatley in North Carolina last month in an effort to turn out his base in a state he won three times.
Ohio moves up two spots on this list, a reflection of the prime position of former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Brown, who lost reelection to a fourth term by less than four points two years ago, has led GOP Sen. Jon Husted in most polls. A New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters conducted at the end of September showed a tight race, Brown at 49% and Husted at 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A Marist poll of registered voters in Ohio showed Brown up eight points over Husted last month.
In the NYT/Siena University poll, Husted’s favorability is at 37% while Brown is at 46%. That’s perhaps a reflection of Brown having a longer history with many Ohio voters than Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed to take Vice President JD Vance’s seat last year.
Brown’s attacks on Husted over data centers – calling him “the face of data centers in Ohio” – have proven particularly potent as Republicans’ campaign arm in Washington has warned the issue is an “anchor” on Husted’s campaign.
Senate Democrats last week blocked a Husted-sponsored bill that would have recommended states take action on data center-related energy costs. And campaigning for Husted on Saturday, Trump defended data centers in southwestern Ohio, a reflection of the president’s longstanding opposition to pausing their construction.
In one buzzy digital spot released last week, Brown’s campaign also featured voters using expletives as they reacted to Husted’s past comments suggesting people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” (Brown’s campaign is running an expletive-free version of the ad on TV.)
Republicans have pulled from a 2024 playbook to run ads attacking Brown on transgender politics, hoping that will move the needle in the state. Brown has responded with a TV spot of his own featuring voters talking about how Ohio already has laws addressing transgender policies and wanting candidates to focus on other issues.
One big question heading into the final stretch is whether GOP spending could help tighten this race. Republican groups are set to spend more than $80 million there from the start of October through Election Day while Democrats have allotted more than $50 million.
Alaska moves up two spots. The enormous and sparsely populated state is notoriously hard to poll, but a NYT/Siena poll of likely voters released Saturday found Democrat Mary Peltola up seven points over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, 50 to 43%.
November’s contest will be determined by ranked-choice voting, and two others join Sen. Sullivan and Peltola on the ballot, including another GOP candidate named Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher. The possibility of voters confusing the same-name candidates has been a point of concern for Republicans ahead of November.
Democrats consider Peltola, a former congresswoman, as one of their strongest recruits, and she’s kept some national Democratic politicians like former Vice President Kamala Harris at arm’s length at a time when her opponent attempts to tie to her to “lower-48 liberals.”
Sullivan stood beside Trump in the Oval Office to tout a $54 billion investment from South Korea for the Alaska LNG pipeline project just weeks before the election. Peltola also moved quickly to praise the president’s announcement, saying she looks forward to “continuing this bipartisan work” with Trump.
Peltola’s demeanor towards aides and use of vulgar rhetoric came under scrutiny last month with a New York Times report detailing allegations of hostile behavior from some former aides. Her campaign denied any pattern of abusive pattern but acknowledged that Peltola has struggled at times to deal with the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, also came to her defense , noting Peltola’s personal struggles.
Maine drops two spots on our list. But the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson remains extremely competitive as the two prepare to debate for the first time this week.
A University of New Hampshire poll conducted last month found Jackson slightly ahead of Collins among Maine likely voters – 51% to 47% - marking the first public survey showing the Democrat with the advantage in the state. Other recent polls, including a CNN survey conducted by SSRS and a NYT/Siena poll , have shown no clear leader.
Collins remains in a vulnerable position given Harris won her state by 7 points in 2024. Polling has indicated the contest hinges more on negative views of the Maine senator and Trump than it does on perceptions about her Democratic opponent.
Democrats have hammered Collins for siding with Trump on consequential votes even as she’s struck out on her own on issues like tariffs and the Iran war. They have also seized on a ProPublica report alleging Collins’ office was involved in a pay-to-play scheme during her 2020 campaign. Collins has forcefully denied the allegations as a “political hit job.”
Collins has survived tough reelection battles in the past, and Republicans are leaning hard on reminding constituents of what she’s accomplished for the state. GOP groups also have spent millions on corruption ads of their own against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, along with TV spots hammering the Democrat on tax policy .
Starting Tuesday, Collins and Jackson will have four debates over ten days.

NORTHAMPTON, MA / ACCESS Newswire / October 5, 2026 / DP World and Fundación Verde Profundo are expanding their mangrove restoration work in Boca Chica after achieving a 86% survival rate among more than 400 seedlings planted in the area's reef lagoon. The partnership now aims to reach 1,000 planted mangrove seedlings by the end of 2026.
Launched in 2025 , the partnership focuses on restoring coastal ecosystems near DP World's Caucedo terminal while strengthening biodiversity and the natural resilience of Boca Chica's coastline. The program includes ongoing monitoring and maintenance to support the long-term growth of restored mangroves.
Monitoring shows that approximately 48% of the planted mangroves have already developed aerial roots, an important sign of growth and adaptation. Mollusks, crustaceans, and juvenile fish have also been observed in restored areas, using the mangroves as shelter and nursery habitat.
The latest restoration activity on September 15 brought together 35 DP World employees and representatives from Fundación Verde Profundo for hands-on conservation work and education about the role mangroves play in protecting marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
"Economic development and environmental protection must advance together," said Manuel Martínez, CEO of DP World in the Dominican Republic . "Our two years of work with Fundación Verde Profundo show how strong partnerships can deliver measurable environmental results. We remain committed to supporting the recovery of coastal ecosystems and helping build healthier, more resilient communities".
Tasha Gough, CEO of Fundación Profundo, highlighted the progress achieved through this collaboration. "Mangrove restoration is a long-term process that requires technical monitoring, continuity, and collaboration among the public, private, and social sectors. One year after the first planting, the high survival rate of the seedlings and their continued development indicate that we are moving in a positive direction. Our goal is not simply to plant mangroves, but to support their establishment and assess how the ecosystem responds over time," she said.
Building a More Sustainable Logistics Hub
The mangrove program forms part of DP World's broader sustainability work in the Dominican Republic. In 2026, the company commissioned a 5,120-kW solar installation expected to reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 3,500 tons annually. DP World is also electrifying its terminal fleet , with now 41 fully electric internal transfer vehicles currently in operation at Caucedo.
The partnership with Fundación Verde Profundo also extends to environmental education. For example, during DP World's Global Volunteer Week , held in connection with the UN's International Volunteer Day, employees, customers, and community partners in the Dominican Republic take part in activities focused on mangrove conservation, biodiversity, and coastal resilience.
Together, these efforts reflect DP World's "Our World, Our Future" sustainability strategy and its approach to reducing the environmental impact of port operations while protecting the ecosystems surrounding them.

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans executive order seeking to bring down high diesel costs
articles.title_zh: Trump plans executive order seeking to bring down high diesel costs
articles.content_orig:
The move would allow broader use of red dyed diesel, which carries no federal excise tax, but is not expected to boost overall supply
President Donald Trump is preparing to ease restrictions on the use of red dyed diesel, a tax-exempt variety of the fuel typically limited to off-road purposes, according to Bloomberg .
The administration is expected to announce the plan on Monday, according to Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources. Red dyed diesel is chemically identical to on-road diesel but is exempt from the 24-cents-per-gallon federal excise tax, so broadening its permitted use in on-road vehicles would effectively deliver a tax cut to drivers.
The measure is aimed at cutting costs for users of on-road vehicles such as pickup trucks, but would not directly lower expenses for farm equipment operators who already run on tax-exempt red diesel. It is also not expected to increase the overall supply of diesel, according to Bloomberg. Red diesel is drawn from the same national stockpile as conventional on-road fuel, and that stockpile is currently at a record seasonal low.
Retail diesel averaged $6.32 per gallon on Sunday, well off the all-time peak of $6.53 reached last month, yet nearly double the $3.76 a gallon that drivers paid on Feb. 28, the day the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins $ROL wrote on social media Monday that Trump "is taking action to deliver short-term relief for farmers and ranchers, including prioritizing diesel in the release of 100 million barrels of crude oil." Rollins separately told Fox Business that Trump would make an announcement on relief for farmers later Monday, without elaborating.
That move was preceded by a deal reached Friday in which Group of Seven nations and partner countries agreed to collectively release up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks, an outcome that followed sustained U.S. pressure on European allies.
Trump had previously floated banning U.S. diesel exports as a way to bring down domestic prices, a position that drew sharp opposition from industry groups including the American Petroleum Institute. Following the G7 agreement, Trump said he would not restrict foreign diesel sales. The administration has also pressured European nations including France and Germany to draw down their emergency petroleum reserves, with the U.S. at one point signaling the threat of an export ban if they refused to comply.
Monday's trip takes Trump to Grand Island, Nebraska, where the GOP is working to turn out farm-state voters before November's midterm elections.
