articles.title_orig: Celebrating World Teachers’ Day: The Mentors Who Help Young Scientists Find Their Voice
articles.title_zh: Celebrating World Teachers’ Day: The Mentors Who Help Young Scientists Find Their Voice
articles.content_orig:
Today, October 5, communities around the globe are celebrating World Teachers’ Day, a moment to recognize the teachers who show up every day to spark curiosity, build confidence and help young people imagine what they can become.
Educators do far more than deliver lessons. They notice the quiet student with a big question, bring to their attention opportunities students didn’t know existed, and stay late to help an experiment finally work.
At Society for Science, educators are at the heart of so much of what we do. Behind nearly every young researcher who steps up to a science fair board, enters a competition or presents their findings to a judge, there is a teacher or mentor who encouraged them. Anna Pawlow, the Society’s Director of STEM Literacy & Curriculum says, “Our STEM Outreach programs recognize that teachers are the experts in effective STEM education and student research. That is why the peer-to-peer learning model is at the core of our teacher professional development programming. We celebrate educators’ immeasurable impact by creating meaningful opportunities for them to learn from one another, build community and inspire new possibilities for their students.”
This World Teachers’ Day, we asked three educators who work closely with Society for Science to share their thoughts on STEM education.
Allyson McFalls ELA & Science Teacher, Blowing Rock School Blowing Rock, North Carolina
Allyson has participated in the Society’s Advocate Program as an Advocate and a Lead Advocate. She is also a former Western North Carolina STEM Research Ambassador, leading the Society’s NC STEM Research Fellow Program. Allyson participates in the Science News Learning program and has mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
For many students, especially adolescents, time in the classroom can feel like an obligation, not a joy. My goal with implementing independent research experiences is to provide students the opportunity to explore in depth a subject that matters deeply to them, and in the process discover that there is joy in deep learning. Helping students discover the project that fits them is key to helping them engage with the rest of our science content and helps them see that I care about them as more than a data point—as an individual with unique interests and passions.
Can you tell us about a time when a student’s confidence or trajectory changed because of a research experience?
I’ve had the joy of teaching students in both 6th and 8th grade in a small rural school. There are a few girls who entered 6th grade very hesitant about their science skills and aptitude, worried about whether they could “do it” when it came to science fair projects. Watching them discover their passion through science fair has been incredible, and now, as 8th-grade students, they are not only confident in their own research, but are actively seeking out opportunities and connections to build their science education. I can’t wait to see how their lives unfold!
Milene de Farias Teacher, Southcrest Christian School Lubbock, Texas
Milene has participated in the Society’s Research Teachers Conference, received a STEM Action Grant, served as an Invention Fellow and participates in the Science News Learning program. She has also mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF, as well as in Thermo Fisher JIC, Regeneron ISEF and Regeneron STS.
What drew you to teaching, and specifically to teaching a STEM subject? Was there a teacher or mentor in your own life who shaped how you teach today?
In 6th grade, I moved to a traditional public school, where my science teacher introduced me to a real lab for the first time and I took part in a science fair. I was shy, but when it came to my projects, I could talk with anybody who asked about them, and I couldn’t wait to start researching for my 7th-grade project.
The science fair changed my plans of becoming a model, a surfer or a crime novel writer, and I chose to attend a technical STEM high school. There, my math teacher, Armando, made a lasting impact on how I teach. He taught with empathy and always used projects. I still remember learning trigonometry by going outside to measure the height of our four-story school building, which is why I love hands-on activities today.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
Information is everywhere today, and students can find an answer in seconds, but personal experiences are what truly shape them. When students choose a problem they care about and work to solve it, they build critical thinking, curiosity and grit, because real research does not always go as planned. They learn to ask better questions and keep going when the results surprise them. Independent research also connects students to the needs of their community, which teaches them to think beyond themselves and see that science can make a difference.
Oktay Ince Director of Teaching and Learning, Concept Schools Columbus, Ohio
Oktay has participated in the Society’s Advocate Program as an Advocate and a Lead Advocate. He has also attended the Research Teachers Conference as an attendee and a Captain, participated in the Science News Learning program and mentored students who competed in science fairs affiliated with Regeneron ISEF.
What drew you to teaching, and specifically to teaching a STEM subject? Was there a teacher or mentor in your own life who shaped how you teach today?
I believe teaching is rewarding both personally and professionally. I think it is especially rewarding when you are teaching in a STEM field. You know that you are making a difference in the lives of students—their life trajectories, their families and the communities around them.
Witnessing this makes my heart full of joy. It makes me think that I am leaving a legacy in this world, even after I am gone. That is what makes teaching so meaningful to me. This servant mindset was instilled in me by my parents, teachers and coaches. They taught me that our purpose is not only to be successful ourselves, but also to help others become successful. That is the mindset I try to bring to my students every day.
Why do independent research experiences matter for kids right now?
I believe acquiring skills through the experience of conducting independent research is one of the highest forms of education we can give to students.
Students do not have to choose a career in STEM, but the skills they develop through the research process can set them up for success in almost anything they choose to do. They learn how to ask questions, solve problems, think critically, communicate, persevere when things do not work and defend their ideas.
Independent research experiences are both transformative and transferable.
If we want our students to be prepared for a constantly changing world and to be competitive in that world, I believe students from all backgrounds need opportunities to experience independent research. We are not just preparing them for a science fair or a STEM career. We are preparing them to become thinkers, problem-solvers, and people who believe they can make a difference.

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.content_orig:
U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”
You can read more about The Princeton Review’s methodology here .

articles.title_orig: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.title_zh: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.content_orig:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.
However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade.
"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.
When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.
"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."
According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country.
High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according AFP, with around 85% of them minors.
The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected.
Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted.
But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets.
Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest.
In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced.
Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October.

articles.title_orig: Inventors of optogenetics win Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
articles.title_zh: Inventors of optogenetics win Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth , Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for “their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.
Optogenetics is a method that uses light to characterize and manipulate the activity of neurons in a living brain. Hegemann and Nagel discovered the light-sensitive protein channelrhodopsin, while Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” says Per Svenningsson , chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.
Speaking in the press conference following the announcement, neuroscientist Abdel El Manira from the Karolinska Institute described how the breakthrough began with the study of a single-cel­led green alga, Chlamydomonas, known for its ability to swim towards light using a tiny “eyespot” on its surface as a sensor. Hegemann was intrigued as to how this simple organism could transform light into action.
Using electrical measurements to solve this mystery, Hegemann discovered that the eyespot contains a light-sensitive protein that almost instantly converts light into an electrical signal, enabling the alga to move. Hegemann next teamed up with Nagel, who used the gene for Chlamydomona to produce the protein in frog egg cells. They discovered that the protein itself was a light-gated ion channel that opens when exposed to light, allowing positively charged ions to flow into the cell and rapidly generate an electrical signal.
“Nagel and Hegemann realised exactly what they had found. They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of – a light-gated ion channel they named channelrhodopsin,” says El Manira.
Appreciating the potential of this discovery, Deisseroth – at the time studying ways to establish causal links between specific brain circuits and behaviour – decided to test whether channelrhodopsin could be used as a switch to control the activity of neurons with light. By introducing the DNA encoding the protein (supplied by Nagel) into mammalian neurons and illuminating them with light, he observed a remarkable response: the neurons reacted on command, instantaneously and with millisecond precision.
The real test was whether channelrhodopsin could control neurons in living animals. Deisseroth and colleagues demonstrated that this was possible. By introducing the gene for channelrhodopsin into specific nerve cells in the brains of living mice and illuminating these cells via a thin optic fibre, they activated selected group of neurons and elicited a distinct behaviour.
“For the first time, causal links between specific brain circuits and behaviour had been achieved. The technology, which soon became known as optogenetics, transformed neuroscience,” notes El Manira. “Optogenetics was rapidly and widely adopted all over the world.”
The field of optogenetics has now enabled researchers to establish causal links between neural activity and behaviour, identifying, for instance, neural circuits associated with pain, social behaviours, thirst, food consumption, reward and attention. Beyond the healthy brain, the technique also sheds light on how specific brain circuits can be disrupted and how this impacts psychiatric and neurological conditions.
And while optogenetics is primarily a tool for basic research and understanding of disease, optogenetic therapy is also showing early promise as a medical treatment. In particular, a landmark study has demonstrated partial recovery of visual function in a blind patient with retinitis pigmentosa , by insertion of a channelrhodopsin-like protein in their retina.
“In this disorder, retinitis pigmentosa, patients lose their photoreceptors, the rods and cones in the retina,” explains Svenningsson. “But there are still healthy cells in the retina and researchers have used optogenetics to stimulate these healthy cells and thereby activate the optic nerve and generate vision perception in the brain. This has been done and there are several clinical trials ongoing with this approach.”
Elsewhere, optogenetics is also under investigation for applications including control of spinal cord activity and bladder activity in small animals, inhibition of nerve pain and guidance of morphogenesis in a living embryo.
Karl Deisseroth was born in 1971 and received his PhD and MD from Stanford University in the US, where he performed the work for which he was awarded the prize. He is currently an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and professor at Stanford University.
Peter Hegemann was born in 1954 and received his PhD at the Max-Planck-Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsried, Germany, where he made his prize-awarded discoveries. He is now a senior professor of neuroscience at Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany.
Georg Nagel was born in 1953 and received his PhD at the University of Frankfurt, Germany. His prize awarded discoveries were made at Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt. He is currently professor of molecular plant physiology at the University of Würzburg, Germany.
Plug me in: the physics of brain–computer interfaces
Thomas Perlmann , secretary-general of the Nobel Assembly, described his call to the laureates earlier this morning: “All three were very surprised and all three said the same thing, that it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two, called them ‘my friends’, and that it was such an honour to receive them together”.

articles.title_orig: United Methodist elected federation world vice president
articles.title_zh: United Methodist elected federation world vice president
articles.content_orig:
Patricia Petudzai Mapani, 61, a United Methodist from Harare, was elected world vice president of the World Federation of Methodist and Uniting Church Women on Aug. 27 at the organization’s world assembly in Auckland, New Zealand.
The Chisipiti United Methodist Church member has held several leadership positions in the organization over the past two decades.
She served as president of the South and East Africa Area 2022-2026 and vice president of the area 2016-2022. Before that, Mapani was The United Methodist Church in Zimbabwe’s unit coordinator for eight years.
“I am driven by passion to support, encourage, empower women and girls and being the voice of the voiceless,” she told UM News.
“It was a very tight election and I felt most humbled to have been chosen. I am still in awe. I am very thankful to the Almighty God for the opportunity to serve at a global level,” Mapani said.
As area president she expanded the area from eight to 18 units, increased attendance at seminars and established the Africa University Scholarship Fund, which enables disadvantaged young women to pursue higher education. She also introduced monthly dawn prayer meetings that are held virtually and have strengthened spiritual life of members in the area.
Her vision is to faithfully strengthen the federation by supporting the world president, coordinating materials and United Nations programs, promoting prayer, women’s empowerment and sustainable partnerships, and safeguarding and sustaining Christ’s transforming mission through hope, unity and love.
Chikwanah is a UM News correspondent based in Harare, Zimbabwe.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Becomes A Trillionaire—Again—After SpaceX Stock Jumps
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Becomes A Trillionaire—Again—After SpaceX Stock Jumps
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk rejoined the trillionaire ranks on Monday after SpaceX shares surged past 5%, reaching $167 by mid-morning, reclaiming a milestone he first hit in June, according to Forbes . Tesla stock rose more than 1% in the same session, contributing to a net worth gain of $30.6 billion over Friday.
The jump puts Musk's fortune more than $628 billion ahead of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who holds an estimated net worth of $371.5 billion, according to Forbes.
Morgan Stanley analysts had flagged SpaceX shares as undervalued, and the stock also got a lift from Starship's first successful trip to orbit the previous week, according to Forbes. Friday had already added $61 billion to Musk's fortune after Tesla's third-quarter delivery figures came in ahead of what analysts had forecast.
Musk said over the weekend that he would rename SpaceXAI — SpaceX's artificial intelligence subsidiary that operates the Grok chatbot — to SpaceXSI, aligning with President Donald Trump's push to rebrand the technology. An executive order Trump signed on September 29 instructed government agencies to drop the phrase "artificial intelligence" and adopt "super intelligence" and the abbreviation "SI" instead. Musk posted on X: "No more AI, SI, It's better," according to Forbes. By Monday morning, however, no official rebranding steps had been taken.
Musk first became a trillionaire in June when SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq at $135 per share , an 11% premium over the IPO price, briefly pushing his net worth to roughly $1.1 trillion. He lost that status within days as SpaceX and Tesla stock declined. Monday's close above $167 puts SpaceX stock roughly 24% above its IPO price.
The IPO itself set a record, with 555.6 million shares sold at $135 apiece to generate $75 billion in proceeds, surpassing Saudi Aramco's 2019 offering. Musk controls approximately 82.4% of voting power in the company after the offering.
SpaceX reported revenue of $18.67 billion in 2025, a 33% increase from the prior year, while swinging to a net loss of $4.94 billion from a profit of $791 million the year before.

articles.title_orig: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.title_zh: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.content_orig:
Chicago topped the list of the world’s most climate-resilient cities, as evaluated by AlphaGeo, a Singapore-based company that ranked 72 of the world’s largest cities based on their exposure to climate risks and ability to reduce adverse impacts from extreme weather events.
“The good news is they call us out and highlight what we have here in Chicago, which is plentiful, clean water and relatively good air quality,” says Aaron Durnbaugh, director of sustainability at Loyola University Chicago. “Although we’re seeing more extreme weather in Chicago, it’s not what folks deal with on the coasts with hurricanes and typhoons or in heavily wooded landscapes prone to wildfires.”
Durnbaugh, a former deputy commissioner in the City of Chicago’s Department of the Environment and one of the chief architects of its pioneering 2008 Climate Action Plan , says Chicago’s privileged geographical location only tells part of the story. The city’s decades-long focus on climate adaptation planning has paid off in infrastructure upgrades, power grid diversification, and emergency response systems that have helped Chicago brace itself for the hostile effects of shifting climate patterns.
Two measures, in particular, stand out.
—
                                    Gilbert Michaud, assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability
Following a heat wave in 1995 that led to the deaths of more than 700 Chicagoans, many of them older adults and people of color, the city invested in new cooling centers, launched wellness checks for at-risk residents, and fortified its power grid to prevent the kind of rolling brownouts that left tens of thousands of residents without power and air conditioning for days during the heat wave.
The city also bolstered its stormwater management infrastructure, widening piping conduits in its combined sewer system, leveraging plant-based infrastructure to absorb rainwater, and partnering with the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago to advance the development of the Deep Tunnel, a 110-mile-long infrastructure system begun in the 1970s and still underway that conveys water to reservoirs and treatment plants through massive underground tunnels.
“We’ve done a lot of things here in our region to improve our infrastructure, including our social infrastructure,” Durnbaugh said. “We’ve created cooling centers. We’ve created social service and public health programs that make sure that people are safe. At the same time, we’ve invested a lot in the hardening of our grid, so that electricity is available even under the most extreme or peak conditions.”
If the recognition comes as welcome news for the city, it is also an auspicious sign for Loyola, whose climate adaptation vision is guided by the Office of Sustainability and the School of Environmental Sustainability and closely aligned with Loyola’s Jesuit mission and commitment to integral ecology.
Under the leadership of Durnbaugh and others, Loyola’s 2015-2025 Climate Action Plan, A Just Future , positioned it to become the first university in the Chicago area to achieve carbon neutrality for its primary energy use. The University’s progress toward net-zero emissions has fulfilled several recent milestones, including a commitment to 100 percent renewable electricity ; $150 million invested in high-performing buildings and the long-term Campus Plan ; the growth of SES; and the inclusion of sustainability in the University’s core undergraduate curriculum.
“Both the city and Loyola have recent climate action plans,” says Gilbert Michaud, an assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability. “What I really appreciate is that we’re actually taking tangible steps to achieve them. One of the things you see with these roadmaps is the real rubber hits the road, in terms of implementation. And that’s what gets me excited about Loyola. We’re walking the walk, we’re achieving our targets, and the city is too.”
Durnbaugh cites several efforts that have helped Loyola draw national attention for its climate resiliency efforts—and they go well beyond decarbonization. In the 1990s, when erosion threatened the stability of high-rises south of campus, Loyola built a sea wall along Lake Michigan to fortify the shoreline near Santa Clara Hall, and raised several building foundations to prevent groundwater infiltration.
More recently, Loyola expanded a chiller plant to keep buildings cool in the face of warming temperatures, created text-based emergency alert systems, and implemented an extensive stormwater management system that includes 17 green roofs spanning more than 55,000 square feet , along with rain gardens, semi-permeable walkways, and underground stormwater infiltration vaults. The system diverts an estimated 19 million gallons of water from city sewers annually—enough to connect Chicago to Houston with one-gallon water jugs.
“Our stormwater system is not just taking pressure off of someone down the sewershed from us,” Durnbaugh said. “But also because we’re next to Lake Michigan, we can direct that water where, historically, it used to go, which is back out to Lake Michigan.”
Perhaps the biggest recent energy transition the University has undergone is a 12-year power purchase agreement with Constellation that began on January 1, 2025. Through the fixed-position contract, Loyola has agreed to buy an estimated 81,660 megawatt hours of electricity annually from the Double Black Diamond solar farm, the largest utility-scale solar project east of the Mississippi River.
The solar energy agreement, aligned with Illinois’ target for zero emissions by 2050 under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act , helps Loyola bring more clean, renewable energy onto the PJM regional transmission grid that feeds into ComEd’s local distribution network. Since electricity pricing fluctuates with demand, on hot summer days and cold winter days when electricity is in heavy use, Loyola can earn money back.
“We’re signing a contract to lock in the purchase of renewable energy at a fixed rate,” Michaud said. “Not only is it good from a climate and renewable energy standpoint, but it’s also a hedge against future fuel price increases.”
These efforts, along with students’ active role in biodiesel production, waste diversion, and urban agriculture programs, helped Loyola earn the Platinum rating —the highest possible—from the Association for the Advancement of Sustainability in Higher Education (AASHE) in their Sustainability Tracking, Assessment & Rating System (STARS). Loyola is the first institution in the Midwest to achieve the Platinum designation and joins only 10 other U.S.-based and seven international institutions in receiving the distinction.
Soon, Michaud says, that number could grow as other universities look to pioneering schools like Loyola as models.
“You have other colleges and campuses that are sort of looking at what we’re doing and having conversations with their faculty and staff, and maybe up to the president and board of trustees. Like, should we be doing this too? Should we also invest in solar? Should we also invest in high-performing buildings?”
Durnbaugh and Michaud are, of course, not the only climate resiliency experts at Loyola who have had a hand in shaping Chicago’s climate adaptation strategy.
Karen Weigert, the director of the Baumhart Center for Social Enterprise and Responsibility at the Quinlan School of Business, was the City of Chicago’s first chief sustainability officer, a position created under former mayor Rahm Emanuel. During her tenure, she led the development of the Sustainable Chicago Action Agenda that laid out 24 goals and more than 100 action items to help make the city more livable under changing climate conditions.
Though pleased by the city’s recent designation, she says there is plenty of work still to be done to prepare for growing climate hazards and extend resiliency efforts equitably across Chic

articles.title_orig: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.title_zh: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Broadcast Tools Inc., a manufacturer of specialty and “problem-solving” products for broadcast, will be acquired by Inovonics Broadcast.
Founder and President Donald Winget informed his dealers in a letter on Thursday.
“After nearly 40 years in business, I am finally ready to retire,” he wrote.
BTI is based in Sedro Woolley, Wash. Winget wrote that Inovonics will continue the Broadcast Tools name and product line, moving production to its location in Felton, Calif.
“Ben Barber and his team at Inovonics are fully committed to maintaining the excellence of our products and to nurturing the relationships of trust that have been built with you, our dealers, over these many years.”
BTI products include analog and AES routers, remote controls, satellite channel controllers, analog mixers and DAs, silence monitors and program schedulers.
Winget began in broadcasting as a gofer for the chief engineer of a radio station in Eau Claire, Wis., according to a company history on its website. He served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam war and later started an engineering contracting business, moving it to the Seattle area in the 1970s. Winget and engineer Lee Hurley created Sentry Systems, an early PC-based automation systems.
Winget founded BTI in 1989 while he was chief engineer at KXRX in Seattle. ( Read a company history .)
Inovonics was founded by Jim Wood and Mark Drake in 1972 to make drop-in, replacement tape recorder electronics assemblies for reel-to-reel machines. The company’s line today includes processors, monitors, RDS products, streaming gear and other specialty broadcast items.

articles.title_orig: Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation
articles.title_zh: Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation
articles.content_orig:
The death of a worker at an anti-plague laboratory in Russia has prompted officials to put at least one hospital facility under quarantine and nearly 200 people reportedly under medical observation as of Monday.
The female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week, according to the regional governor, Igor Kobsev.
He said no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body, and that there had been “no new cases” of illness among other employees of the lab.
“The sanitary-epidemiological situation” in the area “is currently stable,” Kobsev said.
On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation.
Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been confirmed by officials.
Meanwhile, there have been calls internationally for more information and greater transparency from Moscow.
“Many details have not been confirmed,” a State Department spokesman said. “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.” The spokesman said there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that despite there being “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.” So the United States government is “watching and monitoring it closely,” he added. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it.”
The World Health Organization said in a statement that it was aware of reports that a lab worker had died of “severe pneumonia” but that “no cause of death has been officially confirmed.”
Asked by NBC News in Moscow whether the Kremlin was following these events, President Vladimir Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s consumer welfare service, was handling the investigation.
“It is their official statements that should be relied upon— rather than paying heed to various rumors, speculations, and the like,” he said. “Rospotrebnadzor employs highly qualified professionals in this field, so let us heed their official statements.”
Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News that “much more” information and transparency were needed from Moscow. He said that if this is an isolated case of pneumonic plague and no one else dies, “it will probably end there.”
But “it’s actually very hard” for pneumonic plague to spread from person to person, Jha said. “We may see a few more people get infected, but the chances that this becomes a larger outbreak, let alone a global pandemic, is exceedingly low,” he said.
“If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me,” he said. “We need to understand that now.”
The pneumonic plague is caused by the same bacteria as the bubonic plague and can spread from person to person through airborne respiratory droplets, typically from sneezing or coughing. Medical experts say cases require rapid treatment with powerful antibiotics to prevent fatalities.
From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported more than 3,800 suspected human plague cases to the WHO, the agency said last week. Six of the countries ended up having confirmed cases, most of them in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, with 423 deaths.
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Janis Mackey Frayer is a Beijing-based correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.title_zh: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airline El Al aircraft is parked on the tarmac at Ben Gurion Airport near the city of Lod on Friday. Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is taking his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska on Monday, campaigning alongside GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats .
Trump is headed to Grand Island, Nebraska, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama . On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now he is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy , including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close. But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha , considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats.
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Navy and Air Force veteran Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee earlier this year, but Burbank specifically campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general elections in November, and she has since formally dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.

articles.title_zh: Old World Christmas Turns the Holiday Favorite Royal Dansk® Cookie Tin Into a Glass Ornament
articles.content_orig:
SPOKANE, Wash., Oct. 5, 2026
Old World Christmas has partnered with Royal Dansk ® to turn the Danish butter cookie tin into a hand-painted glass ornament, arriving just in time for the 2026 holiday season.
SPOKANE, Wash. , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For 60 years, the Royal Dansk® blue tin has been part of holiday traditions around the world. First filled with Danish Butter Cookies, it often takes a second life storing buttons, thread, and family keepsakes. Now, that beloved blue tin has been reimagined. Old World Christmas , the premier brand of hand-crafted glass ornaments, has partnered with Royal Dansk to turn its iconic Danish Butter Cookie tin into a mouth-blown, hand-painted glass ornament. The Butter Cookies Tin Ornament is available this holiday season at OldWorldChristmas.com .
Why this partnership matters Few cookies are as recognizable as the iconic Royal Dansk blue tin. Often repurposed to hold sewing supplies and treasured mementos, the tin has earned a lasting place in homes for generations. That's the nostalgia and tradition this ornament celebrates.
Old World Christmas has spent more than 45 years turning everyday objects and cultural touchstones into collectible keepsakes. Pairing that craft with one of the most recognizable tins in the world gives shoppers a way to keep the memory out year-round, not just for the few weeks the cookies last.
"The Royal Dansk tin is already in millions of homes. We just made a version you can hang on the tree," said Neal Applefeld, President and CEO of Old World Christmas. "We love taking the everyday objects and traditions people recognize and turning them into keepsakes they can enjoy year after year."
"For generations, the Royal Dansk blue tin has been a cherished holiday tradition," said Kris Nance, Brand Manager at Royal Dansk. "We've heard countless stories about families sharing our butter cookies and then finding new uses for the tin long after the cookies were gone. Seeing this iconic symbol reimagined as a holiday ornament is a wonderful way to celebrate those memories and the joy of the season."
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the Old World Christmas Royal Dansk ornament? It's a hand-crafted glass Christmas ornament shaped after Royal Dansk's iconic blue Danish Butter Cookies tin. Old World Christmas mouth-blows and hand-paints each one.
Where can I buy the Royal Dansk ornament? The ornament is available at OldWorldChristmas.com and Amazon in time for the 2026 holiday season.
How much does the Royal Dansk ornament cost? $27.99
Why did Royal Dansk and Old World Christmas partner up? Royal Dansk's blue tin is one of the most recognizable cookie tins around, and Old World Christmas has made glass ornaments since 1979.  Together, they turned a 60-year cookie tradition into a collectible ornament, with plans to expand the partnership.
Is the ornament made of glass? Yes. Like all Old World Christmas ornaments, it's mouth-blown from molten glass and hand-painted, using techniques inspired by 19th-century ornament-making.
When is the best time to buy it as a gift? It's a nostalgic pick for the 2026 holidays and pairs naturally with National Cookie Day on December 4. Order early, since these special partnership hand-crafted holiday ornaments tend to sell out.
About Old World Christmas Old World Christmas has made hand-blown glass ornaments since 1979. Each design is created in-house and handcrafted by skilled artisans, and the collection now spans more than 2,000 proprietary designs, from traditional to whimsical. Built to last and made to capture a memory, a milestone, a pet, or a person you love, the ornaments give everyone a way to tell the story of their lives one piece at a time. Learn more at www.oldworldchristmas.com .
About Royal Dansk Royal Dansk® Danish Butter Cookies have been elegantly crafted in Denmark since 1966, honoring traditional Danish baking from their origins in Helsingør. Produced exclusively in the Danish bakeries of Nørre Snede and Ribe, the cookies are made with real butter and contain no preservatives or artificial ingredients, staying true to the brand's commitment to quality. Royal Dansk offers a signature variety of artisanal cookie shapes, always presented in the iconic blue packaging. Keep up with the latest news at www.royal-dansk.com and on Facebook and Instagram .

articles.title_orig: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.title_zh: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.content_orig:
Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with cases that could reshape religious liberty, gun rights, immigration and the balance between state and federal authority.
While the last term was dominated by major cases testing presidential power — including Trump’s authority to restrict birthright citizenship, impose tariffs and fire independent agency officials — many of the court’s marquee cases this term span a wide range of issues, including federalism and individual rights.
"There’s a couple of religious freedom cases," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, told Fox News Digital. "We have a couple cases that touch on state and federal preemption, but I’m not sure there’s an easy theme for all of them."
The blockbuster case this term is Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, and it centers on whether Colorado officials can use state tort law to seek damages from oil giants Suncor and ExxonMobil for climate-related harms, or whether federal law blocks those claims.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with major cases involving executive power, gun rights, religious liberty and voting rules. (Photo by Leah Millis-Pool/Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION
"If Colorado actually succeeds on its nuisance claims and others against these companies, the upshot would not just be these companies changing what they do in a way to protect Colorado or remedy Colorado, but rather it would affect their operations far outside of the state," Adam White, senior fellow at American Enterprise Institute, shared during a Federalist Society Panel. "And the question is, can Colorado courts reach outside of their own state and try in effect to regulate?"
Suncor and ExxonMobil argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government authority over interstate and international emissions, leaving Colorado unable to hold them liable for conduct outside the state. But the state argues that it is seeking damages under state law and that the Clean Air Act preserves states’ authority to enforce their own laws.
The Supreme Court will decide whether federal law blocks Boulder’s climate lawsuit and whether the justices can hear the case.
Severino said the case is an effort by "climate lawfare activists" to regulate carbon emissions.
"If the court is viewing this as an effort to weaponize one jurisdiction's law to really regulate outside its borders, then I think they're going to be not very happy about this claim," Severino said. "If the court really views it as an attempt by Colorado to legislate worldwide actions of these energy companies, then I think they're going to say this is actually something that fits within the federal government's sphere of activity, not a single state."
The case marks the first oral arguments heard before the high court.
An Arizona election integrity measure is at the center of another Supreme Court case testing the balance of power between states and the federal government over how elections are run.
Smith & Wesson M&P-15 semi-automatic rifles of the AR-15 style are displayed during the National Rifle Association (NRA) annual meeting at the George R. Brown Convention Center, in Houston, Texas, on May 28, 2022. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)
THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA
Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota stems from an Arizona law requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship for certain voter registrations. Voters who register without that documentation may qualify as "federal-only" voters, allowing them to vote in federal elections but not state and local races. The law also allows the state to purge noncitizens off voter rolls close to an election. The dispute centers on whether the National Voter Registration Act prevents Arizona from imposing additional requirements on voters.
The Supreme Court will also hear major cases involving gun rights and religious liberty and will determine how far states can go in limiting those freedoms.
Colorado is up to bat twice before the Supreme Court this term, with St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy testing whether the state can exclude Catholic preschools from its universal preschool program because of religious policies barring same-sex couples and LGBT students from attending the schools, which conflicts with the state’s nondiscrimination requirements.
Colorado provides funding to private preschools that participate in the program but requires them to follow state anti-discrimination rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Catholic schools argue those rules clash with their religious beliefs and that they should not have to abandon their policies to receive the same funding available to other private schools.
"They don't agree with the state on things like allowing children to use the opposite sex bathroom if they identify with the opposite sex. So this is something the Supreme Court has been very favorable to religious organizations of and for not allowing states to just cut them out of otherwise generally applicable state benefit programs," Severino said.
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-world country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)
EXCLUSIVE: SUPREME COURT PRAYER GROTTO CASE COULD IMPACT 'EVERY SINGLE ZONING LAW' IN AMERICA, ATTORNEY SAYS
But Amanda Shanor, an attorney who helped represent the gay couple who were denied a wedding cake before the Supreme Court, said during a Federalist Society Panel there is concern that the case could chip away at anti-discrimination protections by expanding when businesses and institutions can refuse to serve people based on their identity.
"The schools are not saying, like in the earlier cases — like Masterpiece Cake Shop or 303 Creative — that they want to not serve somebody because of the expression that it would express with regard to a particular event, but instead that they don’t want to have the kids or the families because of the status of the kids or the families," Shanor said. "And will that then go spread over into other things, like will the bakery be able to say, ‘I don’t want to serve all X type of people?’"
Illinois and Connecticut have cases, with state laws restricting certain semiautomatic firearms facing challenges at the Supreme Court.
Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
"This is important because the Supreme Court, for the first time following its landmark Bruen decision, is going to be looking at how states or municipalities can limit particular types of weapons," Severino said. "What the court said it's going to look at is whether these are weapons that are in common use and have lawful purposes, and so this is the court's opportunity to look at things like the popular AR-15 type rifle and decide is this something that qualifies as something that's in common-use and therefore is protected by the Second Amendment."
And while presidential power may not be a major theme this term, the Supreme Court will still weigh the limits of the Trump administration’s authority in a case involving its push to deport illegal immigrants to third-world countries they are not from, and that are not listed in their removal orders.

articles.title_orig: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
articles.title_zh: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
articles.content_orig:
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.
The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.
He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.
Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".
More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.
Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.
He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.
The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.
The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.
There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.
But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.
Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".
Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.
In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter.
By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."
• The tiny island seized by Britain to foil the USSR
• The greatest sailing rescue ever made
• Queen Elizabeth II's secret night out on VE Day
Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
She’s a longtime Democratic officeholder, but she sounds like a Main Street conservative in her campaign for the state’s No. 2 job
Following concerns over how sensitive information is accessed, mayor’s new rules would shorten data retention, require documented searches and add oversight
Annual celebration of the US Navy is zooming back into The City for seven days of festivities and the return of the elite flight squad
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

articles.title_orig: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.title_zh: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.content_orig:
China’s state television CCTV News shared video footage on Sunday of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) counter-uncrewed aerial systems (C-UAS) units in training with laser weapons, integrated missile-gun systems and high-power microwave technology as a layered defence against hostile drones.
PLA troops conducted live-fire tactical drills involving multiple day and night scenarios, CCTV said, adding that radar was used to detect a “dense swarm of drones” at low altitude. The C-UAS units then used a combination of laser ‘dazzling’ and electromagnetic measures to disrupt the formation of the swarm. Interceptor drones were also deployed as well as anti-aircraft guns.
He Qing, a PLA serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the drills combined responses to different aerial threats with battlefield operations and the handling of unexpected situations in an unfamiliar, complex desert environment.
Image: A screenshot from CCTV via Global Times
The September issue of the 2026 Unmanned Airspace Global Counter-UAS Systems Directory is now available. The guide is the world’s only comprehensive, continually updated directory of global C-UAS companies and systems. It itemises over 1,000 C-UAS products and services with performance details, company sales and partnerships arrangements. It is updated every month and broken down into niche sub-sectors (net-capture, missiles, intercept drones, detectors etc) to give C-UAS procurement and industry personnel a unique perspective of global C-UAS technical capabilities and market positions. It is available in word, PDF and excel formats and Unmanned Airspace readers are eligible for a range of discounts. For more information about the Directory please contact the editor Philip Butterworth-Hayes at philip@unmannedairspace.info.
