articles.title_orig: AI researcher warns 'we are racing to build and grow our own adversary' in NYC hearing
articles.title_zh: AI researcher warns 'we are racing to build and grow our own adversary' in NYC hearing
articles.content_orig:
Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner warned that "misaligned" artificial intelligence could prove more dangerous than China's aggressive development push during a New York City Council meeting on Monday.
"China is not our only potential adversary," he said. "With reasonably high chance, we are racing to build and grow our own adversary here at home, which is misaligned AI. Misaligned AI is everyone's adversary, including our own, and one day may be more powerful than China."
The comments followed a question from New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin on how to balance frontier model development in the context of the technology race with China.
Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon, who raised early concerns about the dire risks of artificial intelligence , called out the industry's "extremely reckless" approach to development during the meeting.
"On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," he told a packed room.
Following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta testified under oath about the potential dangers of the technology and outlined current safety measures.
Anthropic sent Logan Graham, the head of its Frontier Red Team, to testify, while OpenAI was represented by Morgan Dwyer, the company's head of policy development and operations. Google's director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend, and Meta's AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill, also attended.
Menin appeared frustrated at times with the lack of direct responses to questions, including one on legal liability when AI models cause serious financial harm or even death.
"I'm going to take it then that neither of the four of you, no company here, can quantify the risk of something cataclysmic happening," she said, calling the answers "troubling at best."
Google's Friend spoke in support of a "comprehensive" federal framework to address mounting AI risks, citing national security concerns.
"As I said in my opening statement, we've long said if it's illegal without AI, it's still illegal with AI," she said.
Both Coxon and former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo warned of the dangers that the "move fast and break things" culture at the AI companies poses with such a transformative technology.
Coxon said that method works for a "photo-sharing app" but not "for building the most powerful technology ever built."
Kokotajlo called on the AI industry to increase transparency and slow the leading model development during his testimony, echoing the stark warnings raised by industry experts in recent weeks.
While Meta confirmed it would participate in the hearing late last month, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google only agreed to appear after the council threatened to subpoena them, Menin said.
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI was the only company called to testify not in attendance, even after the city issued a subpoena to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk last week, requiring that he or another representative of the company's AI unit, SpaceXAI, testify.
This is in "direct violation of the subpoena" issued by the council last week and the council plans to "pursue this matter in court," Menin said.
Top AI labs, most notably OpenAI and Anthropic, are facing heightened scrutiny over their safety and security practices after Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and set off a firestorm on social media by claiming that the company, and OpenAI , are " gambling with our lives ."
Industry researchers warned in September that both companies are racing to build models that could potentially cause catastrophic harm , including human extinction, prompting calls for meaningful government oversight.
Menin opened the meeting by singling out the federal government's light-touch approach to AI after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary accord with tech leaders in Washington last week.
"The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason," she said.
Rogue AI fears began swirling over the summer after OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face . Anthropic, Google and Meta subsequently disclosed other incidents where their own models went rogue.
Last month, Menin called for the rare "Council Committee of the Whole" to ask companies to explain the threats posed by AI and weigh in on potential legislative solutions.
"Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Menin said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.title_zh: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Energy Transition / Private Equity & Venture Capital / Sustainable Finance
Kenny Fisher October 5, 2026
Industrial heat and power solution provider Antora Energy announced plans for a new Kansas- based 5.8 GWh thermal battery storage project, anticipated to become one of the largest battery storage systems in the world once completed, with backing from investors including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Grok Ventures.
The new battery storage project will be based at renewable fuel producer Pratt Energy’s biorefinery in Pratt, Kansas. Alongside the new project announcement, Antora also announced an offtake agreement to supply around-the-clock energy to Pratt Energy.
Founded in 2018, California-based Antora develops thermal batteries that store low-cost electricity as heat in insulated blocks of solid carbon and deliver the stored energy around the clock as industrial heat or power.
The project’s third-party equity financing was led by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) as part of its credit platform investments, and included participation from Australian climate-focused investment firm Grok Ventures and University Pension Plan Ontario (UPP).
Reiner Boehning, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said:
“Antora has demonstrated something rare: sound technology, compelling economic fundamentals, and a clear path to repeatable deployment at scale. That gave us the conviction to partner with Antora on this project.”
Under the new offtake agreement, Antora will supply energy from the 5.8 GWh thermal battery system to Pratt Energy beginning in 2027. The battery will store low-cost electricity as heat in solid carbon blocks and supply that heat continuously to the biorefinery. The companies said that the project will improve Pratt’s operational efficiency and product competiveness, as well as supporting the company’s efforts toward producing 100% zero-carbon-intensity (CI) ethanol.
David Bierman, co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Antora, said:
“Our partnership with Pratt Energy delivers it, helping meet Kansas’s rising energy demand without increasing power bills for homes or businesses. This biorefinery project is creating jobs and spurring local investment without straining the resources the community depends on.”

articles.title_orig: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.title_zh: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

articles.title_orig: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.title_zh: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Washington may be about to get the Brazil it wants, a major piece of the hemispheric puzzle falling into place for the so-called “Donroe Doctrine. "
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, took 47 percent of the valid vote on Sunday to left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45 percent, setting up an October 25 runoff .
Trump has not formally endorsed him , but a Bolsonaro win would give the U.S. its friendliest government in Brasília since the elder Bolsonaro’s, just as Washington tries to loosen China’s grip on strategic supply chains.
China will look on nervously, but much of its groundwork in Brazil is already laid. Those foundations will be tough to break, even with a Trump-friendly Bolsonaro government in power.
The trade data shows why. In the first eight months of this year, Brazil exported $77.1 billion in goods to China, up 15 percent year-on-year, compared to just $24.1 billion to the U.S. , down 9.7 percent. That is a ratio of more than 3-to-1.
Two-way trade with China reached $128.6 billion, against $51.4 billion with the U.S. Brazil’s soybean sales to China alone outstripped everything it sold to America. And the gap is widening. A year earlier, the ratio was 2.5-to-1.
Brazil is physically closer to the U.S. and sits in the hemisphere over which Trump is asserting American hegemony. But Brasília is, in many ways, closer to Beijing than Washington.
To be sure, a Bolsonaro victory would be a real prize for Trump. But political alignment cannot repeal economic geography.
A new president can reset Brazil’s diplomatic posture in January. He cannot, at the wave of a hand, reroute the 305 million metric tons of cargo Brazil shipped to China in those eight months.
Trade on that scale doesn’t make Brazil China’s ally, though they are partnered through the BRICS bloc. But it means Beijing’s leverage depends less on who governs Brasília than on the material reality of who buys Brazil’s harvests and processes its minerals.
For evidence, look at Bolsonaro’s coalition. Brazil’s congressional farm caucus endorsed him days before the vote, and Mato Grosso, the heart of soy country, gave him about 65 percent .
Roughly 70 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports from January through August went to China. Washington cannot replace the Chinese customer. It competes with Brazil for it.
Trump’s 2025 deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping commits Beijing to buy at least 25 million metric tons of American soybeans a year through 2028. And since July, Washington has imposed a 25 percent tariff on most Brazilian goods .
Brazil has run this experiment before. Ahead of his 2018 election, Jair Bolsonaro visited Taiwan and accused China of buying Brazil . By October 2019, he was in Beijing , courting Chinese investment.
Over his term, trade with China grew, his government resisted U.S. pressure to shut Huawei out of Brazil’s 5G network entirely, and Brazil stayed in BRICS.
Rare earths, command of which will decide the great power competition in the 21 st century, make matters worse.
The younger Bolsonaro told CPAC in Texas in March that Brazil would be “the battleground where the future of the hemisphere will be fought,” and said he discussed rare earths with Trump in the Oval Office in May.
Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves but produced less than 1 percent of global output last year. The chokepoint isn’t the mine, but the refinery.
And here’s the difficult truth: China and Chinese-controlled firms handled 91 percent of the world’s rare-earth processing in 2024.
Pela Ema, a mine in the state of Goiás, is Washington’s showcase. About $5 billion in U.S.-backed loans, acquisition money, and price guarantees is converging on it, and last month a U.S. company bought its owner , Serra Verde.
Yet the mine yields only a mixed carbonate, an intermediate product. Separating its heavy rare earths requires a route the U.S. has not proved at commercial scale, so some output may be stockpiled.
Meanwhile, the company’s legacy contracts with Chinese processors run until the end of this year.
All of it unfolded on Lula’s watch, not a Bolsonaro. Washington’s push for Pela Ema was built on capital and guaranteed prices. No presidential sympathy needed.
What Washington still lacks is processing. No Brazilian president can conjure that. The reality is that America will rely on China for rare earths well into the 2030s .
Trump’s own January proclamation warned that even domestic mining does not safeguard national security if the U.S. “remains dependent on a foreign country for the processing.”
Washington’s has time, and it can move quickly. It assembled most of the Pela Ema package within months, and substantial new heavy-rare-earth separation capacity outside China is a few years away , roughly one Brazilian presidential term.
A Bolsonaro government could fast-track permits, court U.S. capital for new deposits, and deliver what Fernanda Magnotta of the Inter-American Dialogue expects: “ greater screening of investments in sensitive sectors .”
Pair that with U.S. tariff relief, and by 2030 Brazil could anchor a Western rare-earth supply chain even as its soybeans keep sailing to China.
The runoff can change the U.S.-China contest in Brazil without settling it. What happens next will take shape by the end of a Bolsonaro term, assuming, as all indications suggest, he will triumph in the next round.
If China’s share of Brazil’s exports, about 31 percent so far this year , has fallen below a quarter, Pela Ema’s heavy rare earths are being separated outside China at scale, and Chinese capital is screened out of strategic assets, then Washington won Brazil outright.
But if not, Trump won the palace and lost the ports.

articles.title_orig: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.title_zh: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.content_orig:
China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country.
Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis.
Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report , which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country.
The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles.
The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure.
The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added.
The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy.
China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

articles.title_orig: Live: Spanish Prime Minister Sánchez calls early election for November 29 after housing decrees rejected
articles.title_zh: Live: Spanish Prime Minister Sánchez calls early election for November 29 after housing decrees rejected
articles.content_orig:
Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election days after Congress voted against measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis
SÃ¡nchez's government had presented the measures in response to nationwide protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home for failing to pay a sharp rent increase
The woman's rent was raised from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since 2018. Spain was not due to hold a general election until summer 2027 - here's what happened last time
Most polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election, which will take place on 29 November
SÃ¡nchez clearly wants to take the initiative - but it's going to be very tough for him to remain in power, writes Guy Hedgecoe in Madrid
Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Imogen James
Dan Woodland Live reporter
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election on 29 November, bringing forward the vote which was originally scheduled for the summer of 2027.
The move follows weeks of protests across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants, sparked last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid following a sharp rent increase.
SÃ¡nchezâs leftist coalition government failed to pass emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis on Friday - but is now expected to approve measures on Tuesday.
The premier's position has also been marred by multiple corruption investigations in recent months involving former members of government and even his wife and brother.
Opposition parties welcomed the snap election, with the leader of the conservative People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o declaring Spain will "at last" say "what it thinks", and leader of the far-right Spanish party Vox Santiago Abascal saying he was "glad" about the announcement.
Meanwhile, members of SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians expressed confidence that they would be re-elected and the prime minister would "pull off a comeback".
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next vote, however they would be expected to need Vox's support to form a government.
This will be SÃ¡nchez's sixth election in 11 years, and if he is to remain in power, he needs to upset some tough odds, writes our reporter in Madrid .
We're ending our live coverage here, but you can read more in our news story .
With eight years in power, Pedro SÃ¡nchez is now Spain's second longest-serving prime minister in recent history.
His political career has been marked by dramatic twists and turns, including his resignation as Socialist Party leader in 2016 after losing the support of senior party figures. Just seven months later, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the leadership with the backing of grassroots members.
SÃ¡nchez has called an early election despite opinion polls suggesting he may struggle to secure enough support to remain in power.
Some analysts believe that focusing the campaign on Spain's housing crisis could help mobilise left-wing voters and steer the debate away from other challenges facing the government, including the situation in Ceuta and corruption allegations involving figures close to SÃ¡nchez.
It is not the first time SÃ¡nchez has taken a major political gamble. In 2023, he called a snap election after his party suffered heavy losses in regional and local elections.
Polls at the time also suggested he was heading for defeat.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, SÃ¡nchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to stay in office, thanks to agreements with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Opposition parties accused him of "selling out Spain" in order to remain in power.
The High Court of Justice of Madrid has rejected a request to disperse an encampment in Puerto Del Sol in the Spanish capital.
Protesters have set up tents in the famous square since 27 September, court documents show.
The court rejected the Community of Madrid's request for police to clear the square on Monday. A new hearing is expected to take place on Wednesday.
A trade union has also called on people to continue protesting in the street against issues with wages and housing ahead of the snap election.
The general secretary of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) trade union confederation, Unai Sordo, says: "We must continue with a path of mobilisation, of street protests as we had announced, regarding wages and housing measures, and that will be our course in the coming months."
People in the streets of Madrid say they welcome news of the snap election called by Prime Minister SÃ¡nchez this morning.
âI think itâs good given the situation thatâs arisen", Raomon Diaz tells Reuters.
"Young people have been given little prospect for the future. And Iâd like to see a truly left-wing government finally come to power.â
Protester Florencio Diaz described the election announcement as a "great victory for the protests in the streets".
Florencio Diaz says Spanish people are struggling with the cost of living
"Weâre in a very difficult situation, with the cost of living rising and, above all, the abuse taking place in the housing market", he says.
However, Sandra - who is also protesting against Spain's housing crisis - expressed reservations about what the future holds.
âTo be honest, Iâm a bit worried about what might happen. But itâs certainly true that with the government we have, things arenât moving forward.â
Sandra says she's worried about Spain's future
The Spanish government is expected to approve measures on Tuesday aimed at tackling the housing crisis that parliament rejected last week .
The measures include a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030 and an automatic renewal of rental contracts.
The government failed to pass them last week, after they were opposed by the People's Party (PP), Vox, and Junts.
Once the government approves the measures, SÃ¡nchez has 30 days to get them ratified. But the Madrid-based political newspaper Moncloa suggests that the prime minister's calling of a snap election could help him do this without congress, as parliament will be dissolved before those 30 days are up.
When congress isn't sitting, ratifying the measures falls to a committee which has a more favourable political make-up for SÃ¡nchez and doesn't require support from the Junts party, the newspaper says.
The deputy prime minister of Spain Yolanda DÃ­az has called for rent caps and a shortened workday
Members of Pedro SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians have continued to react to the Spanish snap election.
The deputy prime minister of Spain, Yolanda DÃ­az - who is part of the Sumar movement - says in a post on Bluesky: "We are going to win again."
DÃ­az says the group will cap rents, shorten the workday and raise the minimum wage.
Health minister MÃ³nica GarcÃ­a says in a post on X that the "Spanish people will rise to the occasion and prevail over the resentment of international hate".
Meanwhile Justice minister FÃ©lix BolaÃ±os says on X that the prime minister "will pull off a comeback" and leave the People's Party and Vox "without a government".
Catalan President Salvador Illa Roca says elections will be a "moment to decide between continuing to advance or going backwards". "Catalonia will stand with Pedro SÃ¡nchez," he adds.
SÃ¡nchez celebrates beside his wife Begona Gomez, after winning the general elections in 2019
These will be the sixth elections that Pedro SÃ¡nchez has contested as Socialist leader since 2015.
He has only won two of those - the 2019 ballot which was repeated after being inconclusive - and yet he has been in power since winning a no-confidence motion against his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, in 2018.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of French schools stay closed ahead of nationwide day of student protests
articles.content_orig:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco chief says replenishing global oil stockpiles could take two years
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco chief says replenishing global oil stockpiles could take two years
articles.content_orig:
The chief executive of Saudi Aramco said Monday it could take up to two years to rebuild global oil inventories, warning that the squeeze on supplies could yet get worse as the U.S.-Iran war drags on.
Speaking at the Energy Intelligence conference in London, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify until the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz fully reopens and confidence returns to energy markets.
The war has severely disrupted shipping through the strait, a narrow waterway that typically handles around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, sending shock waves through the global economy.
"Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years," Nasser said, according to Reuters.
His comments come shortly after G7 governments agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves, following pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump .
The G7 members are France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the U.S. France currently holds the group's presidency. The European Union also participates in its meetings.
Aramco's Nasser said nearly 3 billion barrels of oil supply had been lost since the U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in late February, while 1 billion barrels of oil had been released from stocks.
Most of the stock draw to date had come from commercial inventories, with the CEO of the world's largest oil company saying the remaining 6 billion or so in storage is "not practically available."
He added: "The system is already straining."
A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Monday was hailed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and instructed to turn back or risk being targeted, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO), a maritime security alert service.
The tanker complied with the instruction, UKMTO said, with the incident occurring about 11 nautical miles north of Oman's port city of Khasab.
Oil prices were mixed on Monday as Middle East crude exports rose, with flows through both the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia's key East-West pipeline reportedly trending higher.
International benchmark Brent crude futures with December expiry traded 0.7% higher at $102.92 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with November expiry stood 0.4% lower at $90.76.
— CNBC's Spencer Kimball contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX scrubs launch attempt for 21 data transport satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.title_zh: SpaceX scrubs launch attempt for 21 data transport satellites for the Space Development Agency
articles.content_orig:
Update 4:28 a.m. EDT (0828 UTC): SpaceX aborted the launch countdown in the final minute.
SpaceX will have to wait at least another day before launching a new batch of data satellites to low Earth orbit on behalf of the United States Space Force’s Space Development Agency (SDA). The launch planned for early Monday morning was scrubbed in the final minute of the count as rocket was shifting into its automated startup sequence.
SpaceX didn’t provide an immediate reason for the abort.
The mission, dubbed Tranche 1 Transport Layer A (T1TL-A), is the fourth mission sending production satellites into orbit for the SDA. This is one piece of a broad constellation — called the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) — designed to support the U.S. military and its allies through space-based capabilities, like missile tracking and secure communications.
Liftoff of the Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East is scheduled for no earlier than Tuesday, Oct. 6, at 1:17 a.m. PDT (4:17 a.m. EDT / 0817 UTC). The rocket will depart Vandenberg on a southerly trajectory.
The mission will use Falcon 9 first stage booster B1103. This will be its sixth flight following the launches of the SDA’s T1TL-E, NROL-179, and three batches of Starlink satellites.
Less than 7.5 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX plans to land B1103 at Landing Zone 4. If successful, this will be the 37th landing at LZ-4 and the 668th Falcon booster landing to date.
The T1TL-A mission is one of 23 missions awarded to SpaceX as part of the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 contract awarded in August 2020, which is managed by the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC). The previous missions from the SDA have already been launched:
The T1TL-B and -E missions featured satellites manufactured by York Space Systems and the T1TL-C satellites were produced by Lockheed Martin. Space Force Col. Ryan Hiserote, SSC’s division chief in Assured Access to Space, told Spaceflight Now back in September 2025 that these initial T1TL missions could be launched in any order.
The 21 satellites flying as part of the T1TL-A mission were manufactured by Northrop Grumman and delivered to Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 28.
Tranche 1 is the initial component of the PWSA constellation is expected to begin providing operational capabilities to the Department of Defense beginning in 2027. When complete, T1 will consist of 126 Transport Layer satellites, 28 Tracking Layer satellites, and four missile defense demonstration spacecraft.
With the three launches completed to date, there are 63 satellites in orbit.
“In close coordination with Space Systems Command (SSC) and Space Launch Delta 30, the deployment of Tranche 1’s proliferated capability will soon deliver continuous overwatch—neutralizing any first-mover advantage by delivering data to warfighters around the world, nearly instantaneously,” said GP Sandhoo, SDA Director and Space Force Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Missile Warning and Tracking following the T1TL-E launch in July.
The SDA said the Transport Layer will consist of between 300 to 500 satellites in low Earth orbit from 750 km to 1,200 km in altitude. The SDA said once complete, 95 percent of the globe will be in view of at least two of the T1TL satellites at any given time.
“The constellation will be interconnected with Optical Inter-Satellite Links (OISLs) which have significantly increased performance over existing radio frequency crosslinks,” the SDA wrote. “LEO orbits in conjunction with OISLs will reduce path loss issues but more importantly offer much lower latencies, which are deemed critical to prosecute time sensitive targets in today’s wartime environment.”
These satellites will be able to integrate with the Link-16 and Integrated Broadcast System (IBS) to allow for “timely threat warnings and situational awareness information”.
The launches of these satellites are managed by the SSC’s System Delta 80 (SYD 80) and the Space Fore Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Assured Access to Space.
In one of the strongest public endorsements of SpaceX’s initiative to put a reusable launcher on the commercial market, a top official from satellite communications giant SES said Tuesday that the company wants to fly one of its pricey payloads on a used Falcon 9 rocket, perhaps even without a test flight.
A pair of European-built, NASA-backed research satellites set for launch Tuesday from California will extend 15 years of global gravity field measurements collected by the GRACE mission before it ended last year, supplying scientists with data to help track the melting of Earth’s ice sheets and chart the impacts of floods and droughts.
Ready for a flight to the International Space Station, SpaceX’s first upgraded Dragon cargo capsule rolled out to pad 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida this week in preparation for launch on top of a Falcon 9 rocket.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump vs. Bernie Sanders—2 Sharply Different Views of America’s Role in the World
articles.content_orig:
One is an imperial gangster; the other seeks to create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
America’s century is over. History has not ended. This has become the new conventional wisdom even among the keepers of convention.
The challenge is how America finds real security in this new era. This month, we witnessed two strikingly different answers: one from the self-proclaimed most powerful man in the world, Donald Trump, and one from the champion of the rising populist movement on the left, Senator Bernie Sanders.
Trump’s address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly was a characteristically grotesque performance, essentially a raised middle finger to the 190 country representatives gathered before him and the UN itself. Amid the routine farrago of lies, boasts, threats, and resentments, he presented a stark vision of America’s emerging role: essentially an imperial gangster—that, if pursued, constitutes a clear, present, and harrowing threat to this nation’s security.
After a stump speech preening about America’s primacy—“Our economy is the envy of the world. Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet”—Trump turned to America’s role in the world.
He boasted about the bombing of Iran, the “peace” in Gaza, the kidnapping of Venezuela’s president and control of its oil—“to the victor go the spoils”—the bombing of fishing boats in the Caribbean designated as “foreign terrorists,” the blockade of Cuba, “failing like never before and it will fail.”
Each of these—from aggressive acts of war to aiding and abetting genocide to illegal blockade—represent a brazen and open violation of international law and the UN Charter. Trump is saying that America will continue to police the world, only not to enforce the law but to enforce its will and to take what it can get. In apparent acknowledgment of the lawlessness, he issued a scurrilous attack on the International Criminal Court, “an evil group of people,” calling on all members to resign from the “rogue institution.”
Ironically, this fool’s errand of brazen plunder isn’t Trump’s greatest disservice to US national security. As the UN secretary general warned in his opening remarks, the world is struggling with the growing costs of real and present dangers that can no longer be ignored and can only be addressed by greater international cooperation: catastrophic climate change, global pandemics, corrosive inequality that undermines democracy and savages the poor, an accelerating nuclear arms race accompanied by the collapse of arms control agreements, and the known unknown of AI, which requires international regulation.
Trump made clear that the United States, under his watch, will sabotage any international regulation. Climate change and efforts to regulate AI are dismissed as a “hoax.” He has pulled the US out of the World Health Organization that monitors emerging pandemic threats and crippled our own Centers for Disease Control. Having pocketed billions while in office, he is the tribune of oligarchs, torpedoing all efforts at imposing a minimal tax on multinationals or on carbon or efforts to shut down tax-free zones. “There is no global government,” he preached, and “while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” And, boasting about hiking America’s bloated military budget by one-third—to $1.5 trillion—and promising to build a “Global Dome” over America, he only adds fuel to the nuclear arms race.
At the dawn of the conservative era, Britain’s Margaret Thatcher asserted that “there was no alternative” to the neoliberal catechism. But there is an alternative course for the United States as it struggles to address new realities. It won’t come from a return to the failed “unipolar” globalism of the past decades. Instead, if there is an alternative to Trump’s gangsterism, it will come from the rising populist movement of the left.
Speaking on the eve of the UN General Assembly at Riverside Church in New York, Bernie Sanders offered a clear outline. He began with a tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King’s historic address at Riverside at the height of the Vietnam War, and his warning that “a nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense than on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death.”
He argued that not only is the US spending more and more on military weapons while turning its back on working people and the poor, but that “it is happening all over the world.”
To turn that around begins with a change in US policy, including “an end” to Trump’s “disastrous war on Iran,” termination of military aid to Israel and condemnation of “the genocide” in Gaza, work with grassroots activists to end “Putin’s disastrous war in Ukraine,” and denunciation of the UAE for aiding the genocide in Sudan’s civil war.
The growing violence, he argued, makes the United Nations more, not less, important, arguing that instead of arguing that “might makes right,” “our job is to strengthen the United Nations…and bring disagreements to the negotiating table…”
That would enable us to address the real and present security threats that we now face. At the top of that list, Sanders warns, is that “we are moving rapidly toward an extremely dangerous global oligarchy.” In nation after nation, we witness unprecedented levels of wealth and income inequality, illustrated by the fact that just as “the top 1 percent of America now owns more wealth than the bottom 94 percent,” the ratio is similar across the world.
“Children die of preventable diseases. People suffer every day. People give up hope. And 3,400 of the richest people on Earth became $4 trillion richer last year alone.”
The oligarchy, Sanders warned, “is ascending, working families are struggling to stay alive, and democracy is in retreat. The great challenge that we face in our country and all over the world is that that trend must be reversed.”
Sanders then turned to the other existential threats—focusing on the need to control the development of AI and to address catastrophic climate change.
The contrast is clear. For Trump, America strides the world. Our military will enforce our will. “The spoils” will go to the powerful, not to the people. Threats like AI and climate change are a “hoax.” International institutions are irrelevant if not evil.
For Sanders, militarism is a threat, not an answer. Basic security and democracy here and across the world are threatened primarily by an increasingly powerful and rapacious oligarchy. The emerging threats—climate change, AI (as well as pandemics and nuclear weapons, which he doesn’t mention)—require global cooperation. Changing our course depends not on building up the military but on building a progressive citizens movement here and across the world that can create a world “not based on greed but based on justice, on decency.”
Impossible? Perhaps, but Sanders reminds us of the “immortal words of Nelson Mandela: It always seems impossible until it is done.”
Katrina vanden Heuvel is editor and publisher of The Nation , America’s leading source of progressive politics and culture. An expert on international affairs and US politics, she is an award-winning columnist and frequent contributor to The Guardian . Vanden Heuvel is the author of several books, including The Change I Believe In: Fighting for Progress in the Age of Obama , and co-author (with Stephen F. Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers .

articles.title_orig: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung shares overview of WCC education, formation
articles.title_zh: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung shares overview of WCC education, formation
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation, shared a report on 5 October that offered an overview of the commission ’ s most recent work as well as a glimpse of future plans.
A major development during 2025 was the Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI) organised in connection with the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order under the theme “Where now for visible unity?” The programme included an online phase from 15 September to 12 October 2025 and a residential phase from 12–29 October 2025 in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt.
Chung described how GETI included theological lectures and facilitated group work, worship and community life, contextual and study visits, interreligious encounters, and direct interaction with the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order.
“ Ninety-five participants were admitted to GETI 2025, representing different regions and church traditions,” she said. “ A formal evaluation was undertaken following GETI. The results indicated a high level of overall satisfaction.”
Chung also described one of the major follow-up projects: the preparation of the publication GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity, which will be launched 8 October. “ The publication records the theological work undertaken through GETI and serves as a resource for future ecumenical theological education and formation,” she said. “ Another significant area of work has been the development of Ecumenism 101, an introductory online course on ecumenism.”
The course has been developed as a means of making basic ecumenical knowledge and formation more widely accessible beyond residential programmes.
“ The course content is complete, with public release planned through the WCC website,” said Chung. “ Work on Regional Ecumenical Theological Institutes has continued as part of the effort to strengthen ecumenical formation in different regional contexts.”
During 2026, particular attention has been given to North America and Latin America.
“ In 2026, Bossey marks its 80th anniversary, having been established in 1946,” added Chung. “ The 2026–2027 academic year began in September 2026 with a new cohort of 33 students.”
She described how the institute continues to combine academic theological study with residential, intercultural. and inter-confessional community life. "Work has also continued to strengthen networks connected with ecumenical theological education,” continued Chung. “ The GETI 2025 evaluation demonstrated strong interest among participants in remaining connected after the programme.”
The 2026 WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation is meeting at the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey from 5–9 October. The Commission will also participate in the celebration of the 80th anniversary of the institute on 7 October.

articles.title_orig: Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
articles.title_zh: Russia Cuts Coal Prices, Yet China and Türkiye Imports Keep Falling
articles.content_orig:
Russian coal exports to China fell 10.8% year over year in January-August 2026 as higher logistics costs, import duties, and stronger competition eroded Moscow’s position in one of its key markets.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) reported the figures on its official website on October 4. Russian suppliers delivered 53.15 million tons of coal to China during the eight-month period, losing ground to Mongolia and Indonesia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the agency, Mongolian coal imports surged 48.9% to 78.39 million tons, while Indonesia supplied 121 million tons. China imported 310 million tons of coal overall during the period.
Mongolia benefits from a shared land border with China and zero import duties, while Russian coal faces tariffs of 3% to 6%. Australia and Indonesia also receive zero-duty treatment under free-trade arrangements.
Russian producers are already offering discounts of around 10%, but further reductions could make exports unprofitable. Transport costs are adding further pressure, with the cost of shipping coal from Russia’s Vostochny port to China rising 45.5% from the start of 2026 through September 11.
Thermal coal exports could face the strongest pressure as Russian suppliers compete with Chinese mines while absorbing higher rail and freight costs. Russian railway tariffs increased again in October, while stronger demand for open freight wagons has raised transportation expenses.
The agency added that the pressure is also spreading beyond China. Russian coking coal exports to Türkiye fell 30% during the first seven months of 2026, with no shipments recorded in July, while coal deliveries to Russia’s southern ports dropped 33% that month compared with June.
The slump in southern deliveries coincides with mounting maritime risks in the Black Sea, where Ukrainian drone attacks on commercial vessels bound for Novorossiysk have driven up shipping costs.
Shipowners have pulled dozens of coal-transporting vessels from the region or halted operations altogether, and bulk carrier availability dropped by 21% in a single month. In early August, carriers serving the route raised freight rates by up to fourfold, while war-risk insurance premiums climbed to double or triple base freight rates.

articles.title_orig: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.title_zh: Season of Creation closes—but actions will continue
articles.content_orig:
As the Season of Creation officially closed on 4 October, people gathered online from across the world for a prayer service that not only recapped many green initiatives but also encouraged ongoing action to care for creation.
Speakers reflected on this year ’ s theme, "Living Water" (Ezekiel 47:9, 12): "Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live . . . Their fruit will be for food and their leaves for healing" (NRSV).
Analisa Ramsahai, environmental scientist and Catholic climate activist from Trinidad and Tobago, who serves as a board director and secretary for the global Laudato Si' Movement, focused on water as connection—our connection with each other, with the earth, and with God. “ Rain returns water to the earth, nourishing plants, animals and people,” she said. “ But before we explore these connections, I invite you to experience water for a moment.”
She then invited those gathered to imagine—and deeply appreciate—all the ways in which water touches their lives.
Elizabeth Trice, a UK-based wildlife and conservation professional and an active environmental organizer within the Church of England, and founder of “ The Seedlings Network,” expressed her appreciation for the gathering. “ It ’ s key to look back at our beginnings,” she said, referring to water being connected with the origins of all life.
“ It ’ s also important to remember that the voices of tomorrow are also the voices of today,” she added, noting that young people are not just carrying the future of the earth but also the present.
Fr Movses (Garen) Yosolkanian, Armenian Apostolic, with the Middle East Council of Churches (MECC), noted that water is a gift from God, a source of life, healing, and restoration. “ Yet we find ourselves in a thirsty moment in the struggle for global ecological justice,” he said. “ Across the world, our water sources are threatened. What should be a source of life is increasingly becoming a source of struggle, injustice, and division.”
Marí a Jos é Tejedor Gonz ález, with the ACT Alliance, thanked the speakers, those who began and continued earth-friendly initiatives, and all those who prayed. “ You all inspire us with your wisdom, hope, and witness throughout this season,” she said. “ You remind us that caring for creation is a shared calling. Although today marks the end of this year ’ s celebration, the journey continues.”
Season of Creation is the ecumenical world's month of prayer and action for creation. Beginning with “Feast of Creation in Christ” on 1 September, is a time of witness to God ’ s love and our human responsibility.
The season forms one chapter in the World Council of Church's Ecumenical Decade of Climate Justice Action (2025–2034), launched in Johannesburg in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties
articles.title_zh: Police investigating Flydubai co-pilot’s Australia ties
articles.content_orig:
Authorities have said they are investigating the links of the co-pilot of the Israel-bound Flydubai flight with Australia.
A multi-agency Australian police and intelligence team – the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team – is carrying out the probe, a spokesperson said on Sunday.
Mystery surrounds the co-pilot, who is accused of attacking the captain with an axe and attempting to seize control of Flight FZ1073 from Dubai as it approached Israel, and how he was able to acquire his seat in the plane’s cockpit.
He has been identified in media reports as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami .
He had been barred from flying in his own country because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views, The Associated Press news agency cited sources as saying.
While al-Hammami reportedly spent part of his life in the United Arab Emirates, the Reuters news agency, citing sources briefed on the Australian investigation, reported that he studied at a university in the Australian city of Melbourne.
A third unnamed source told the agency that he studied at RMIT University, a public research university in Melbourne, about a decade ago.
The Financial Times also reported al-Hammami’s links to Australia. Citing two sources familiar with the Australian investigation, the FT said al-Hammami had allegedly visited what it described as “radical mosques and extremist websites” while in the country.
Disaster was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot and a reserve pilot took over its controls and completed an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
However, the case has raised questions about security in Israel, which has some of the world’s strictest aviation security measures.
The prosecutor general of the UAE, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, has labelled the attack an attempted “terrorist act”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu said a “loophole” appears to have allowed the Omani pilot to take part in the Flydubai flight, and that Israel would now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest “terrorist” attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.

articles.title_orig: The mispricing of war
articles.title_zh: The mispricing of war
articles.content_orig:
The true price of war is rarely paid by those who start it. In a deeply interconnected world economy, the financial burden of conflict is increasingly exported through inflation, disrupted trade and slowing growth worldwide
In the space of just a few weeks, the throttling of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has revealed the true nature of the US-Israeli war with Iran. This is no regional conflict, because the entire world is being invoiced. While the size of the bill remains to be determined, it is already obvious that the belligerents won’t be the only ones paying the tab. War is typically framed in terms of national security, territorial integrity, humanitarianism, or even civilisational struggle. But such rationales obscure an unsettling truth: war is one of the most mispriced of human activities. Those who initiate it rarely bear the full costs, which tend to be displaced across borders, markets and time. Beyond the physical destruction, war generates massive negative externalities. The price paid by the perpetrator reflects only a small fraction of the social cost.
Of course, the intuition that war imposes downstream costs on others is deeply embedded in the political-economy literature, running from Adam Smith and David Ricardo to John Maynard Keynes and Karl Polanyi. But globalisation has transformed the effect into a structural feature of the modern economy.
Economic growth diminishing Consider the arithmetic of the current Iran conflict. Beyond the loss of life, direct US military spending may run into the tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars. Yet the broader economic cost – transmitted through energy, food and financial markets – runs far higher. The International Monetary Fund warns that the war is already diminishing many economies’ growth prospects, as energy shocks ripple outward and inflationary pressures intensify.
The transmission mechanism is brutally simple. When oil and gas prices rise, transportation and electricity become more expensive. When fertiliser costs increase, so do food prices. Central banks may respond by assuming a tighter monetary-policy stance. Ultimately, growth slows. Yet this domino effect is missing from the actual war ledger. Efforts to measure the true costs of war have consistently found that they lie beyond the battlefield. In their work on the Iraq war, Joseph Stiglitz and Linda Bilmes tallied a catalogue of costs in the trillions of dollars once macroeconomic effects were included. Similarly, both the IMF and the World Bank have found that violent conflict depresses growth in economies far removed from it.
Even under conservative assumptions, the US may bear only a modest share of the total global economic damage (much as the negative spillovers of the war in Ukraine far exceed the direct cost to Russia). As European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde recently cautioned, the rest is diffused across the system, absorbed by energy importers, emerging markets and households worldwide. War, in this sense, is globally subsidised.
Three mechanisms make this possible. The first is spatial. Modern economies are deeply interconnected. When war disrupts one node (particularly an energy chokepoint), the effects cascade outward. The Strait of Hormuz is not simply a geographic passage but a structural vulnerability in the global economy. The second mechanism is temporal. War typically requires the present to borrow from the future. Governments finance conflict through debt, deferring its cost to generations not yet politically represented. The fiscal consequences of past wars continue to unfold decades later, showing up in public debt, constrained policy options, and obligations that outlast the politics that created them.
The third mechanism is distributive. War concentrates decision-making while dispersing the costs. Those who decide are not the ones who pay. This last insight lies at the heart of modern conflict economics. The Oxford University economist Paul Collier has shown that wars persist not because they are collectively rational, but because they are privately beneficial. Small groups capture the gains as the broader population absorbs the losses. Today’s networked economy amplifies this asymmetry.
When the world pays the price As Edward Fishman of the Centre on Global Energy Policy argues in his book Chokepoints, power today flows through global systems such as energy routes, financial networks and supply chains. But conflict turns these into channels for economic contagion. The result is a peculiar inversion. War appears expensive in theory but affordable in practice, because much of the bill is paid by others. This mispricing has predictable consequences. When goods are subsidised, we get more of them. When their price is too low, we get oversupply: too much pollution, too much risk and too much war.
The policy challenge is therefore familiar, even if the politics are not: to discourage war, its costs must be internalised. Those who initiate conflict must bear a greater share (or, even better, the entirety) of its true costs. Ensuring that outcome requires an effective global institution that can align the private and social costs of conflict more effectively than global markets can. Until the world can come up with such an institution, the incentives will remain perverse, because one of the most destructive activities imaginable seems so affordable to those who undertake it.

articles.title_orig: Chester County has more measles cases than most entire states in the country
articles.title_zh: Chester County has more measles cases than most entire states in the country
articles.content_orig:
Nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with measles will get sick.
In late June, Chester County reported two cases of measles, as an outbreak in bordering Lancaster County crossed into the farmlands that blend into the suburban sprawl of Philadelphia’s collar communities.
Case numbers grew tenfold in July, and by late August, three dozen people had gotten sick up and down the county’s western border.
The latest numbers now show 83 measles cases in Chester County , more than most entire states have seen all year, making it a locus in Pennsylvania’s largest measles outbreak in more than three decades.
Chester is the first county in the Philadelphia region to grapple with wide circulation of a highly contagious virus that could spread like wildfire if it reaches other under-vaccinated communities, especially densely populated ones closer to the city.
As cases rise in Chester County, public health officials are ramping up educational outreach, scheduling pop-up clinics, and even bringing doses of the vaccine to people’s homes, all in an effort to contain known hot spots in the outbreak.
At Chester County’s schools, homecoming parades, and grocery stores, many families say they are aware of the outbreak, but are not deeply concerned. Those who are vaccinated worry more that their social and school lives may be disrupted, as they were during the COVID-19 pandemic, if the virus continues to spread.
Anne Nemeth, who lives in Paradise in Lancaster County, feels only a little worried, given that her two sons are vaccinated.
At a time of declining vaccination rates , she isn’t sure whether some of her closest neighbors, who the family regularly gets together with, are vaccinated.
They are Amish, and she has read that many of the people getting sick in her area were part of the Plain community. Two Amish infants in Lancaster County died in August after contracting measles in the state’s first deaths linked to the outbreak.
“I’m hoping they would tell us if they were sick,” she said. “It’s a lot of trust.”
Pennsylvania has reported five deaths associated with measles. A 20-year-old Amish woman who died lived just over the Chester border in Lancaster County. She wanted the vaccine after her parents and eight siblings got sick, but couldn’t get it because she was being treated for leukemia.
Close to 1,000 people statewide have been sickened by the virus, marking one of the most robust outbreaks the United States has seen in years. And experts say the cases that have been reported are likely an undercount, as many people do not seek medical care for their symptoms and some have been reluctant to speak with the health department.
“Public health is now in a race with the disease,” said Dale Weiser, the clinical services supervisor for Chester County’s health department. “It’s going to either burn through all the susceptible people, or we’re going to make fewer people susceptible through vaccination. That’s the only way it ends.”
Measles is so contagious that nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with the disease will get sick.
That’s how a county like Chester, with one of the highest vaccination rates in the state, has also come to log the third-most cases in the outbreak.
Chester County’s kindergarten measles vaccination rate falls just below the 95% threshold that scientists say is necessary to keep the virus from spreading widely. Kindergarten vaccination offers a view into a community’s protection because the vaccines are required for school attendance.
But the county — like the rest of the Philadelphia region — is pockmarked with areas where vaccination has dropped well below the so-called herd immunity threshold, leaving families vulnerable to severe illness.
In eastern Chester County, for instance, five elementary schools in West Chester had kindergarten measles vaccination rates below 95% — one of the vulnerable areas in the region identified by an Inquirer analysis of 2025-26 school-level data.
Farther east, Chester City in Delaware County , and neighborhoods in West and North Philadelphia have also similarly seen measles vaccination rates drop below so-called herd immunity.
In Chester County, the health department seeks to limit the virus from spreading from west to east across the county, where it would reach more densely populated communities, said Jeanne Franklin, Chester County’s health director.
“If it finds that pocket of unvaccinated individuals, it’s going to popcorn until it finds no one left,” Franklin said.
The health department began reaching out to hospitals and schools months before Chester County reported its first cases, because public health leaders knew it was likely only a matter of time before the virus spread from Lancaster County, Franklin said.
Hospitals were asked to develop a measles screening protocol, if they didn’t have it already, so that early symptoms, such as fever, cough, and runny nose, wouldn’t be dismissed as seasonal illnesses.
Schools were urged to start tracking vaccine status among staff. When a school identifies a measles case, the county requires any student or staff member who is unvaccinated or does not have proof of vaccination to stay home for 21 days, Franklin said. Since many adults don’t have their vaccination records handy, that could create a major staffing disruption.
As case counts in Chester County grow, pop-up vaccine clinics have been scheduled across the county.
The health department has administered more than 500 doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine so far this year, most of them since the outbreak began in April.
The health department’s nurses will bring doses of the vaccine to homes and farms of residents who don’t travel. Vaccines are also available at the county’s health clinics.
Many of the parents lined up along Atglen’s Main Street last week for the local school district’s homecoming parade said they did not feel a reason to be deeply concerned about the outbreak because their families are vaccinated.
“I guess I have the same level of concern as I have for all sickness with kids in public schools,” said Sandi Wrigley, a Cochranville mother whose children, ages 9 and 11, are vaccinated. “If we take the time to worry about that, it’ll be an endless worry.”
Until recently, measles was considered eradicated in the United States, and despite declining vaccination rates, most families are still choosing to vaccinate their children.
Some were angry that measles is even a conversation.
Michael Lavender, from Parkesburg, said vaccinating his 12-year-old daughter was an “easy decision.”
“I really feel like there should be no reason to even talk about it,” he said.
On the other side of the county, families lined up inside the Great Valley Middle School gymnasium in Malvern for flu and COVID-19 vaccines.
Kevin Wrabley, of Malvern, doesn’t worry about his 11-year-old son contracting measles because he is vaccinated. But he does worry about other children and adults who aren’t able to get vaccinated.
“It’s discouraging, things we thought were safely behind us are coming back,” he said.
In Chester County, public health educators have the task of trying to untangle the myriad reasons people are opting out of a vaccination. Many have little to do with science: Two doses of the measles vaccine provide 97% protection — better than most vaccines.
The MMR vaccine is among those long required to attend school in Pennsylvania and every other state. But families here have increasingly been deciding against vaccination for religious and philosophical reasons, as state law permits, often by simply printing and signing a form noting their objection.
Some fluctuations in kindergarten vaccination rates are typical from year to year, but the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric in federal leadership and a growing distrust in public health authorities has exacerbated fears about vaccination.

articles.title_orig: The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026
articles.title_zh: The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four weeks out from Election Day, the Senate battleground map is growing after signs of improvement for Democrats in several red-leaning states.
For the first time this year, CNN’s list of 9 Senate seats most likely to flip expands to 10 to include Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years . A new wave of polling also shows Democrats ahead or competitive in red states like Ohio, Alaska and Texas. All four states went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024.
To win the Senate majority, Democrats will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while defending three of their own, including Michigan.
Trump’s approval rating stands at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls, amid high frustration over the economy and the war he launched against Iran. Democrats have also seen surging enthusiasm in special elections since Trump returned to office and early signs of elevated turnout in early voting.
But they have also expressed unease over the massive amount of spending coming from the GOP. From the start of October through Election Day, Republicans are poised to outspend Democrats on advertising in eight of the ten most competitive Senate races, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, even though that advantage will be blunted by GOP-aligned outside groups having to spend more for ratings points than Democratic campaigns will.
Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states. The rankings are a snapshot of where the contests stand at this point and can shift as the midterm election season enters its final month.
North Carolina remains the state most likely to flip this year. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, who has made affordability issues a centerpiece of his campaign, has a strong position over GOP nominee Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and Trump ally vying to replace Sen. Thom Tillis.
An Elon University/YouGov poll released last month showed Cooper up 11 points over Whatley among likely voters. The Senate Leadership Fund, a key Republican outside spending group, is pausing its ad campaign there. Over the weekend, Republican outside groups cut more than $15 million from their remaining ad bookings, according to AdImpact data.
Still, Trump campaigned with Whatley in North Carolina last month in an effort to turn out his base in a state he won three times.
Ohio moves up two spots on this list, a reflection of the prime position of former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Brown, who lost reelection to a fourth term by less than four points two years ago, has led GOP Sen. Jon Husted in most polls. A New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters conducted at the end of September showed a tight race, Brown at 49% and Husted at 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A Marist poll of registered voters in Ohio showed Brown up eight points over Husted last month.
In the NYT/Siena University poll, Husted’s favorability is at 37% while Brown is at 46%. That’s perhaps a reflection of Brown having a longer history with many Ohio voters than Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed to take Vice President JD Vance’s seat last year.
Brown’s attacks on Husted over data centers – calling him “the face of data centers in Ohio” – have proven particularly potent as Republicans’ campaign arm in Washington has warned the issue is an “anchor” on Husted’s campaign.
Senate Democrats last week blocked a Husted-sponsored bill that would have recommended states take action on data center-related energy costs. And campaigning for Husted on Saturday, Trump defended data centers in southwestern Ohio, a reflection of the president’s longstanding opposition to pausing their construction.
In one buzzy digital spot released last week, Brown’s campaign also featured voters using expletives as they reacted to Husted’s past comments suggesting people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” (Brown’s campaign is running an expletive-free version of the ad on TV.)
Republicans have pulled from a 2024 playbook to run ads attacking Brown on transgender politics, hoping that will move the needle in the state. Brown has responded with a TV spot of his own featuring voters talking about how Ohio already has laws addressing transgender policies and wanting candidates to focus on other issues.
One big question heading into the final stretch is whether GOP spending could help tighten this race. Republican groups are set to spend more than $80 million there from the start of October through Election Day while Democrats have allotted more than $50 million.
Alaska moves up two spots. The enormous and sparsely populated state is notoriously hard to poll, but a NYT/Siena poll of likely voters released Saturday found Democrat Mary Peltola up seven points over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, 50 to 43%.
November’s contest will be determined by ranked-choice voting, and two others join Sen. Sullivan and Peltola on the ballot, including another GOP candidate named Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher. The possibility of voters confusing the same-name candidates has been a point of concern for Republicans ahead of November.
Democrats consider Peltola, a former congresswoman, as one of their strongest recruits, and she’s kept some national Democratic politicians like former Vice President Kamala Harris at arm’s length at a time when her opponent attempts to tie to her to “lower-48 liberals.”
Sullivan stood beside Trump in the Oval Office to tout a $54 billion investment from South Korea for the Alaska LNG pipeline project just weeks before the election. Peltola also moved quickly to praise the president’s announcement, saying she looks forward to “continuing this bipartisan work” with Trump.
Peltola’s demeanor towards aides and use of vulgar rhetoric came under scrutiny last month with a New York Times report detailing allegations of hostile behavior from some former aides. Her campaign denied any pattern of abusive pattern but acknowledged that Peltola has struggled at times to deal with the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, also came to her defense , noting Peltola’s personal struggles.
Maine drops two spots on our list. But the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson remains extremely competitive as the two prepare to debate for the first time this week.
A University of New Hampshire poll conducted last month found Jackson slightly ahead of Collins among Maine likely voters – 51% to 47% - marking the first public survey showing the Democrat with the advantage in the state. Other recent polls, including a CNN survey conducted by SSRS and a NYT/Siena poll , have shown no clear leader.
Collins remains in a vulnerable position given Harris won her state by 7 points in 2024. Polling has indicated the contest hinges more on negative views of the Maine senator and Trump than it does on perceptions about her Democratic opponent.
Democrats have hammered Collins for siding with Trump on consequential votes even as she’s struck out on her own on issues like tariffs and the Iran war. They have also seized on a ProPublica report alleging Collins’ office was involved in a pay-to-play scheme during her 2020 campaign. Collins has forcefully denied the allegations as a “political hit job.”
Collins has survived tough reelection battles in the past, and Republicans are leaning hard on reminding constituents of what she’s accomplished for the state. GOP groups also have spent millions on corruption ads of their own against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, along with TV spots hammering the Democrat on tax policy .
Starting Tuesday, Collins and Jackson will have four debates over ten days.
