articles.title_orig: U.S. shipwreck, laden with World War II munitions, is a time bomb near London
articles.title_zh: U.S. shipwreck, laden with World War II munitions, is a time bomb near London
articles.content_orig:
SHEERNESS, England – In the mouth of the River Thames, just downstream from London, a team of elite marine salvors has been busy trying to stabilize one of the world’s most dangerous shipwrecks.
The SS Richard Montgomery, a U.S. military cargo ship, dragged anchor, broke its back on a sandbar, flooded and sank in late summer 1944, a few months after D-Day, with 1,500 tons of explosives still in the holds.
The Monty, as the locals call the ship, has been disintegrating, slowly but surely, on the shallow seafloor for the last 82 years.
Though a precise manifest is elusive, there are still thousands of World War II munitions inside the Montgomery’s broken hull, including 2,000-pound blockbusters, fragmentation bombs, white phosphorus smoke ordnance and crates of pressure fuzes.
Old bombs, even underwater, can still detonate under the right conditions, and one thing certain about the Monty is that its conditions constantly change in the fast-moving tides and shifting sands of the estuary.
“It’s not just the explosives on the wreck that we’re worried about,” said Nolan Conway, who is leading the salvage operation from a high-tech Dutch barge that sits, ever so gently, alongside the wreck.
“It’s the stuff around the barge that we want to be careful about,” Conway said. “Things could create a sympathetic detonation at the wreck.”
The wreck has stood for all these years as a kind of war memorial, its three masts visible above the waterline, and clearly marked on nautical charts. You can see it from land. Tour operators take day-trippers out to circle it. Local communities remember the sacrifices – the bravery and the terror – of the earlier generations.
The wreck serves as a reminder, too, that the lethal detritus of war often lingers on, whether those ships and bombs are sunk off seaside towns on the English coast or in the Persian Gulf.
The Montgomery is a time capsule and a potential time bomb. And, after much delay, the British government decided that it was time to do something to prevent a catastrophic collapse of the ship’s degrading steel hull.
On a recent afternoon, Conway, the project leader for Resolve Marine, a company based out of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, was aboard a launch vessel that shuttles crew out to the barge.
His team members are masters of disaster. A recent assignment had them dealing with a fire in a torpedo room of a submarine operated by the Indian navy. In 2024, they were hired to disentangle the container ship that struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore Harbor. They routinely deal with groundings, capsizes, cargo losses, spills and fires.
The trip from the dock to the wreck takes just 20 minutes.
A first impression? How crowded the scene. The wreck lies a couple of miles from shore and just a few hundred meters from active shipping lanes. Thousands of vessels pass by each year, including bulk freighters, container ships, tugboats, liquefied natural gas carriers and cruise ships bound for London, plus many fishing craft and pleasure boats.
The wreck is marked by buoys denoting an off-limits exclusion zone. The masts were the remains of the derrick cranes that once were used to load and unload its lethal cargo.
The British government initiated the $12 million project to remove the three masts after experts concluded the steel structures might collapse onto the decomposing decks below – and that could be very bad.
Asked if the work on the Montgomery was dangerous, Conway explained how carefully they approached their task – the extensive surveys using radar, magnetometers and sonar to form a deep understanding of the wreck and seafloor around it, which is littered with UXO and PXO, terms of art for unexploded ordnance and potential unexploded ordnance.
Over the years, the wreck has collected additional dangers. The seafloor around it is dotted with half-buried objects, possibly defensive mines and antiaircraft ordnance left by the British navy, and unexploded offensive mines and bombs dropped by the Germans.
To put it very simply, the salvors really don’t want to bump into anything.
A shock wave could set off an explosion, which could be lethal to a diver, or could spark a larger conflagration.
Though some British government assessments remain classified, experts with the Royal Military College of Science estimated in 1970 that a “top event” – meaning essentially the worst case, in which the whole cargo goes kaboom! – could produce a blast of water and debris 3,000 meters high and set off a five-meter tsunami-style wave that could threaten local towns and industry, including nearby oil and gas facilities.
The British government, in its reports, has calculated the risk of a top event as “remote.”
Remote, however, does not mean unfathomable, let alone completely safe.
In 1967, salvors attempted to stabilize munitions inside the wreck of another American-built ship, the SS Kielce, that was being used by the Polish navy, which had sunk soon after the war near the English port of Folkestone.
Using mines, the salvors somehow ignited the hold, sparking an explosion equaling a 4.5-magnitude earthquake.
“If the Montgomery were typical salvage job, we would simply rig to the mast, cut the mast using traditional techniques and pull it free – simple and done,” Conway said. “But because of the sensitive nature of the wreck, we went with special tools.”
Those special tools include a barge that dropped three legs into the silty sand to position itself in place, just inches above the waterline and inches from the wreck. Divers enter the water one at a time, careful not to step onto the fragile deck below.
“Visibility is measured in inches,” said Jeff Cornish, one of the divers. “We work by feel.”
To cut the mast, the salvors deployed a diamond wire saw, “because it produces lower vibrations, with a lower potential for something to go wrong,” Conway said.
“We don’t do anything that would upset our mothers,” he added, meaning they plan to come home from work.
The Montgomery was a Liberty ship, designed for convoy duty in the North Atlantic. It was built at the U.S. Navy’s direction by the St. John’s River Shipbuilding Co. in Jacksonville, Florida, and took on its last load of high explosives at Hog Island, today the site of Philadelphia International Airport.
After surviving the ocean crossing and German U-boats, the ship was destined for an American air base in newly liberated Cherbourg, France. The Montgomery arrived at what became its grave in late August 1944, two months after the Allied landing on the beaches of Normandy.
People in nearby towns – and those following a live stream online – watched as the masts were removed this past week.
The cut masts, covered in rust and sea growth, now lie aboard the salvage barge. They were in surprisingly robust shape. But the structures around them were not. Some of the steel could be knocked apart with a single bang by a hand scrapper. “It’s paper thin,” Conway said.
David Alexander, an emeritus professor of emergency planning at University College London, has studied the wreck and its cargo.
“It is a rare case,” Alexander told The Washington Post. In a research paper, he wrote that the Montgomery “exemplified a very visible, alarming risk, but one which cannot be analyzed with any degree of sophistication and accuracy because there are simply not enough reliable, accurate data.”
“It’s impossible to say with any certainty what the explosion risk is,” he said, but that the risk is far from zero.
Alexander worried aloud that the wreck lies close to active shipping, that windsurfers have been recorded in the exclusion zone, that divers probably have sneaked out to the site and in years past, fishermen were photographed on the wreck at low tides.
Locals have reported seeing strange lights on the water above the wreck at night, probably phosphorous munitions that shook loose from their crates and ignited on the surface, he said.

articles.title_orig: Apple MacBook Pro Release Schedule: What To Expect When
articles.title_zh: Apple MacBook Pro Release Schedule: What To Expect When
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s major MacBook Pro overhaul is just around the corner, and should debut within a month or so. It’ll be the first touchscreen MacBook, as well as the first with Tandem OLED. Beyond that, though, the new MacBooks should be ‘significantly’ lighter than their predecessors, according to the latest issue of the Power On newsletter .
The newsletter reiterates that the new MacBook Pro should debut ‘by next month,’ so we should see these new machines before the end of November. These machines should offer the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, as Apple has opted to skip the higher-end part of the M6 family in favor of accelerating the M7 launch.
Despite the fact that these MacBooks have been rumored for quite some time, we haven’t really known too much about them besides specs on paper: OLED, touch, Dynamic Island, and so on. In the past, reports have described the computer as thinner, but we haven’t really had much of a visual. We still don’t, but we do have one major new detail on what this machine will feel like:
The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry. The current 16-inch MacBook Pro weighs as much as 4.8 pounds, compared with 3.3 pounds for the 15-inch MacBook Air, so any meaningful reduction would be immediately noticeable.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman doesn’t specify exactly how much lighter it will be, but if you’re someone who uses a current-generation MacBook Pro, especially the 16-inch, you might find that it’s heavier than you’d like it to be. Apple is reportedly working to improve on that.
I’m excited to see a new, lighter design for these machines as long as they don’t sacrifice the outstanding cooling performance of the current MBPs. If they’re going to sacrifice performance, then make the OLED touchscreen MBP a separate product line and keep the old design around as well.
Beyond that, Gurman also mentions that there will be some changes in macOS Golden Gate to support touch and the Dynamic Island, alongside the debut of macOS 27.2.

articles.title_orig: Brit-born rock singer & Canadian Idol star Sass Jordan dies aged 63 as heartbreaking tributes flood in
articles.title_zh: Brit-born rock singer & Canadian Idol star Sass Jordan dies aged 63 as heartbreaking tributes flood in
articles.content_orig:
Sass Jordan, the Montreal-raised rock singer whose career spanned nearly four decades, has died at 65.
Jordan died Friday surrounded by those who loved her most, said a statement from family spokesperson Eric Alper.
The statement described Jordan as an inimitable force of nature and an irreplaceable being of light and joy.
A cause of death has not been released.
Jordan's debut album, Tell Somebody , was released in 1988, and she won the Juno Award for most promising female vocalist of the year in 1989. Her second album, Racine , released in 1992, included hits like Make You a Believer .
She was nominated several times for a Juno Award for best female vocalist. She was also a judge on all six seasons of the reality television competition show Canadian Idol .
Then and now: Sass Jordan on the 30th anniversary of Tell Somebody
She was born on Dec. 23, 1960 in Birmingham, England, and raised in Montreal, according to the statement.
Geoff Kulawick, former president of Stony Plain Records, which released Jordan's last two albums, described her as "bold, beautiful and brave."
Jordan recorded her 2020 album, Rebel Moon Blues , and her 2022 album, Bitches Blues , with her husband Derek Sharp while signed with Stony Plains.
Kulawick said he was a fan even before Jordan signed to his label, and that he convinced her she could "really belt out the blues" on her final two records.
"Her voice really stood out and the way she was able to connect emotionally … brought her tons of fans," he said.
Canadian producer and songwriter Derek Downham said they "really hit it off" when they first met at Toronto's Massey Hall a few years ago.
"She was a ray of light and a really hilarious person," said Downham, who also played drums alongside Jordan last December at singer-songwriter Andy Kim's annual holiday charity concert in Montreal.
"The biggest heartbreak for me is that I won't get to see that laugh again."
As one of the few women in rock when she started out, Jordan helped make space for other woman in a male-dominated genre, he said.
"She was coming up in a time where it wasn't easy," he said. "It's nice to see a strong female poke through and really show people how it's done."
Sass Jordan says she thinks of 'music as medicine' and she still loves to connect with fans
Downham said Jordan was an inspiration to all young performers.
"I hope that people remember her for leading the way and that she led with love every time."

articles.title_orig: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.title_zh: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.content_orig:
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation .
But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.
So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks?
That is now one of the central questions facing investigators.
Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency.
He was subsequently hired by Flydubai.
A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted.
The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year.
It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.
Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera.
The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly.
In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said.
Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added.
One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.
When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.
Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction.
Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures.
As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight.
The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk.
According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise.
However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.
“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Ivy League school’s president promises action after woman alleged she was drugged ⁠and raped by fraternity members
Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling ⁠of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman , who ⁠alleges she was drugged ⁠and raped in ​2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the ⁠school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
“At ​their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish ‌individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish ‌some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying that in 2024 it launched ​a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it also imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said, adding: “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that ⁠university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but ​he did not detail ​specific initiatives that the university would take. “In ​the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our ​community to ask ‌questions and hear directly ​from university leadership,” ​he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.
As the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York attorney general, investigates, new attention has been drawn to the findings of a state-mandated sexual violence survey conducted by Cornell in 2025, which found that 35% of female undergraduates who completed the survey reported that they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact while at the university.
The 2025 version of the survey was the first to specifically include unwanted choking or strangulation in the definition of nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation that students were asked about, in addition to nonconsensual penetration and/or sexual touching.
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.title_zh: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.content_orig:
Kim Desiato, a firefighter from Tucson, Arizona, stops to look for hot spots in the aftermath of the Lewis Lake Fire in Yellowstone National Park in August 1988. The fire forced the closure of the south entrance to the park.
(CNN) — As Monica Turner trekked across the western hills of Yellowstone National Park, the cold rain was inescapable. Even the constant movement of putting one foot in front of the other as she fought through a slew of dense branches could not warm her body. It was easy to forget it was July.
Four years later in 2017, Turner made the same journey. But instead of fighting the once compact forest, she was met with a desolate clearing as the sun pounded above her. After the Maple Fire the year before, all that was left of the towering trees was a smattering of survivors looking over a sea of skinny, pencil-like sticks sprouting from the charred dirt.
In Turner’s time as a researcher, she has seen massive destruction and its subsequent regrowth as she studied the impacts of Yellowstone’s 1988 fires, which left a crown jewel of the national park system scorched. This made the level of destruction Turner witnessed in 2017 even more shocking — especially as the area had burned before without this level of loss.
Researchers across the US are seeing a similar trend — forests that are historically adapted to fire are now often being obliterated by the fast-moving, high temperature wildfires that are becoming increasingly more common with climate change . These researchers are grappling with what it will mean for our world if the trees that are the centerpiece of these landscapes we love don’t recover like they once did.
The fire itself is not inherently the problem. Every scientist CNN spoke with emphasized the need for fire on the landscapes they researched. But the lack of prescribed burning, a practice long used by indigenous people to clear out dead plants and to keep landscapes healthy, has left these trees vulnerable . It means their futures — when they encounter hotter, more vicious fires — are uncertain.
As these ecologies start to shift, it’s unclear if or when these different areas around the US will hit a tipping point where the trees won’t come back. Instead, researchers say it’s more likely there will be a gradual conversion over time, with once towering forests becoming robust scrublands or large fields of grassland.
Here’s how some places around the country are changing, and how one state is succeeding in preserving its native wildlife.
As Turner stood on the dirt field, the air was hot — much hotter than during her previous 2013 visit. Cool summers and rain had been the norm for Yellowstone during her years of research. The heat was so intense this time that a field assistant was hospitalized for dehydration during the trip, said Turner, who works at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as the Eugene P. Odum Professor of Ecology and a Vilas Research Professor.
The ash coating the former forest floor reminded her of the ash she walked through during the 1988 fires — ash that covered her face and caked her socks. For a long time, Turner thought the wildfires from that summer 38 years ago represented how forests could and would recover. Despite miles of charred trees, the research in her field showed the forest would come back, and with a high density of trees, she said. But Turner said she didn’t appreciate “how much things could change in a relatively short time.”
“We could see what we call ghost logs, which is where there had been large logs on the ground, and they were completely combusted,” she said. “And then you can see their shadows where the white ash is left behind from the hot temperatures.”
Only about 5 percent of the tree seedlings have grown back so far from the 2016 fire, compared to what burned. In place of the trees, grasses blow in the exposed meadow, now dotted with wildflowers that commonly sprout after a wildfire. Turner said she is seeing “a slow but detectable shift” to plants that are “more tolerant of warmer, drier conditions” and can grow back more easily if more wildfires come.
Slowly but surely, these changes could impact visitors to the park, Turner said. People like trees, for both how they look and the practical element of shade during hikes, she said, and the changes the forest is undergoing could impact how and when people visit the park.
The repercussions are seen in more unexpected ways as well — at one point, the park had a temporary ban on fishing, including catch and release, because the fish were already too stressed out from low water levels and the high water temperatures that were partially due to the lack of shade, she said.
“What will be the consequences for lots of other values that people care about in that region?” Turner said. “That could be wildlife habitat. It could be water availability. It could be shade if you’re hiking.”
But ultimately, it’s not yet clear what the future Yellowstone will look like.
About 100 miles northeast of California’s state capital, Derek Young stood in the middle of a clearing in Plumas National Forest. The carcasses of burnt trees that surrounded him felt like a graveyard, the remains left in the wake of the 2021 Dixie Fire.
An occasional bird would chirp in the distance, but the forest emanated an eerie stillness, said Young, a research ecologist at the University of California, Davis. Fifteen years ago, Young started studying these landscapes as a PhD student. Many of them are now unrecognizable compared to the thriving forests they once were.
“It’s really actually crazy to how much change has happened,” he said.
Many of the areas Young studies are changing from dazzling emerald trees to fields of shrubs — even years after the wildfires.
The shrubs, ranging from deer brush to white thorn shrub, are incredibly good at resprouting, Young said. While fire might lop off the shrub tops, their roots remain, helping the plants return quickly, he said. It’s stiff competition for trees to endure, which need specific conditions to grow back compared to the hardy, drought-tolerant shrubs, he said.
In just a few years, the shrubs can grow to be as tall as a person, covering the entirety of an area, Young said. “It can really feel like you’re swimming in a sea of shrubs. You can’t see more than a few feet ahead of you.”
There are a couple of factors required for trees to successfully reemerge. Some species of trees can grow in the shade, but those species are also more likely to be destroyed during a high temperature fire, he said. Others need the heat of a fire to release their seeds, while many others don’t, Young said. Those seeds then need to land in an area where they can grow and survive, which can be impacted by wind and wildlife, he added. A lot needs to happen in a short window of time in order for them to regrow.
As he sees these landscapes shift, it’s hard to weigh if this is inherently a bad change — although he noted the important services forests currently provide humans, namely capturing and holding carbon dioxide through carbon sequestration.
“As forests burn up, they release carbon, contribute to climate change, which makes it more likely for more fires to burn and convert more forests,” he said. “You could say, if you care about humanity’s well-being, that that’s actually a reason to favor maintenance and restoration of forests in place of post-fire shrub fields.”
“I do sometimes try to think from the perspective of like, what if there were no humans, and there is no society to decide what our values are,” he said. “In that scenario, I think the sort of definitive answer is the most valuable ecosystem is the one that is adapted to the site in the absence of all the human intervention.”
But he notes this change to shrubs is not happening in that theoretical vacuum without humans.
“It’s not that the system naturally wanted to be shrubs. We created that condition by suppressing fires for 100 years,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Houthis Claim Attack on Aramco as Yemen Conflict Escalates
articles.title_zh: Houthis Claim Attack on Aramco as Yemen Conflict Escalates
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_zh: Germany's chancellor arrives in Kyiv on unannounced visit to pledge more military support to Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for ​talks, we are ‌ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once ​again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from German business, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Merz pledged further military and energy assistance during his visit, with Zelenskyy announcing a German support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).
The package includes €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy said the two countries had reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), covering defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine .
According to German government sources cited by Reuters and the DPA news agency, the planned cooperation includes the development and delivery of thousands of interceptor drones capable of countering the fast, jet-powered drones Russia increasingly deploys against Ukrainian infrastructure.
The plans also envisage expanding production of long-range weapons capable of striking targets more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.
Merz emphasized that the partnership would also benefit Germany, with companies from both countries developing technology to strengthen their security.
"German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger," he said.
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron , Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin .
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

articles.title_zh: The new Fitbit Edge leaks
articles.content_orig:
Google’s midrange Fitbit Edge shows off is many sides and colors in leaked images.
Google’s midrange Fitbit Edge shows off is many sides and colors in leaked images.
We don’t know a ton about the Fitbit Edge, but it appears to be a successor to the midrange Charge line. It had leaked previously , but we can clearly see in these images posted by Android Headlines , you can see that Google’s rumored fitness tracker sort of splits the difference between the Pixel Watch and the Fitbit Air . It has a small screen that is able to display some widgets, but clearly isn’t as expansive as a proper smartwatch.
Supposedly, this fitness-first wearable will have a seven-day battery life, as well as built-in GPS and an altimeter, making it far more capable than the minimalist Air. It will also have limited app support for things like Google Maps and YouTube Music. Beyond that, not a ton is known.
The Fitbit Charge line was last updated in 2023, so a new midrange tracker is long overdue. While we don’t have any word on price or release date yet, somewhere in the $150 to $200 range seems like a safe bet. The Air costs $99.99 and the Watch starts at $399.99, so the Edge would clearly fall somewhere in the middle. The Charge 6 currently goes for $159.95.

articles.title_orig: Elder Thabo Lebethoa: ‘Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World’
articles.title_zh: Elder Thabo Lebethoa: ‘Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World’
articles.content_orig:
Elder Thabo Lebethoa , General Authority Seventy, spoke during the Sunday afternoon session of October 2026 general conference about how to receive more of the Savior’s light. The following is a summary of what he said.
The Savior said: “I am the light and the life of the world.”
“Through His Spirit, He enlightens our minds. His light is also revealed through His perfect life and teachings.”
Whatever concerns, challenges and struggles come in life, the answer is always Jesus Christ.
“Jesus Christ can bring light in our moments of darkness and restore hope where there is hopelessness.”
To receive more of the Savior’s light in one’s life: First, increase faith in Him; second, study the scriptures daily, especially the Book of Mormon; third, practice repentance daily.
“Having faith in Jesus Christ means trusting that He understands our daily difficulties and knows how to help us rise above them, because He has experienced all our pains, afflictions and infirmities.”
The method, timing and length of scripture study matter less than the consistency and sincerity of the effort.
Repentance means a change of mind and a turning of the heart to God.
“I testify that today can be a new day, and tomorrow will be a better day, for all who come unto Jesus Christ and receive His light in their lives. He lovingly beckons: ‘Come unto me, and I will give you rest.’”
“Whatever concerns, challenges and struggles we may have in our lives, the answer is always Jesus Christ.”
“Let us ponder about the changes that we need to make in our lives, and these may include how we use our time, the things we watch or listen to, and the language and tone we use as we communicate with others.”
“I testify that today can be a new day, and tomorrow will be a better day, for all who come unto Jesus Christ and receive His light in their lives.”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft shared Windows 11 26H2 Group Policy templates, settings guidance for admins
articles.title_zh: Microsoft shared Windows 11 26H2 Group Policy templates, settings guidance for admins
articles.content_orig:
Windows powers how people around the world work, learn, create, and connect every day. Today, we’re announcing the availability of the Windows 11 2026 Update, also known as Windows 11, version 26H2. Built on the same servicing foundation as recent Windows 11 releases, version 26H2 delivers the latest Windows innovations with a streamlined update experience designed to minimize disruption and help you stay secure, productive, and up to date.
As organizations and individuals continue to expect faster deployments and less downtime, Windows 11, version 26H2 takes advantage of the same modern servicing technologies that have simplified recent feature updates. For many eligible devices, moving to version 26H2 is as simple as installing a small enablement package, allowing people to start using this new release with minimal download size, quick installation, and a single restart.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is delivered as an enablement package for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
An enablement package is a lightweight update that activates new features already included in the operating system through previous monthly servicing updates. Because versions 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2 share a common servicing branch and underlying codebase, many of the components required for version 26H2 are already present on devices before the feature update becomes available.
This approach enables a significantly faster update experience compared to a traditional operating system upgrade. For eligible devices, installation is similar to a monthly update, requiring only a small download and a quick restart to transition to Windows 11, version 26H2.
As with every Windows release, version 26H2 includes the latest quality, reliability, and security improvements designed to help protect people and organizations while delivering a dependable Windows experience.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is now available for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
To be among the first to receive the update, go to Settings > Windows Update and turn on Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available . Once your device is eligible, you’ll see the option to download and install Windows 11, version 26H2.
As always, we take a measured and data-driven approach to broad availability and will be releasing version 26H2 using a controlled feature rollout. During rollout, we might place safeguard holds on devices where we detect a known compatibility issue that could impact the update experience. We will continue expanding availability over time and provide updates through the Windows release health hub.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is available now through the tools organizations use to manage Windows updates, including Windows Autopatch and the Microsoft 365 admin center [i] .
Existing management tools, update rings, policies, and deployment practices can continue to be used. We recommend that commercial and education customers begin targeted deployments to validate applications, devices, and business-critical workflows before expanding deployment more broadly throughout their organizations.
Windows 11, version 26H2 continues the annual Windows feature update cadence, with a new Windows 11 feature update released during the second half of the calendar year. As with previous annual releases, installing version 26H2 resets the support lifecycle for supported editions of Windows 11. That means 24 months of support for Home and Pro editions and 36 months of support for Enterprise and Education editions.
Select features and enhancements initially released as disabled by default in version 25H2 will be enabled by default in version 26H2. You can find more information on these features, plus guidance to help with planning and deployment, in the Windows IT Pro Blog .
We recommend updating eligible devices to Windows 11, version 26H2 to take advantage of the latest Windows innovations, quality improvements, and security enhancements.
We’ll continue to closely monitor the rollout and share information about known issues, safeguards, and rollout progress through the Windows release health hub and official Windows communications channels.
Thank you for your feedback and partnership as we continue to improve Windows for people and organizations around the world. We love to hear about your experience, so please keep your comments and suggestions coming in via Feedback Hub.
[i] Downloads in the Microsoft 365 admin center and similar channels may be delayed.

articles.title_orig: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
articles.title_zh: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
articles.content_orig:
This photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows a view outside the main venue of the 2026 Taiyuan Energy Low-Carbon Development Forum in Taiyuan, north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang)
TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies.
As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient.
The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development.
For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work.
Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer.
Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers.
The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16.
Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear.
When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder.
"With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare."
Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions.
Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao.
The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining.
On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission.
While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation.
At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake.
The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption.
Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs.
"We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd.
Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029.
The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi.
By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh.
A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy.
As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable.
Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution.
Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes.
The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand.
"When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said.
"This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added.
From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity.
Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW.
"The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said.
As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW.
Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies.

articles.title_orig: Minecraft Dungeons II Reviews Praise Local Co-Op but Fault the Open World
articles.title_zh: Minecraft Dungeons II Reviews Praise Local Co-Op but Fault the Open World
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo Life called Minecraft Dungeons II a fun but flawed sequel in its Switch 2 review, with co-operative play as the high point. A second review, from Shacknews , reached a similar verdict and said the game works best with friends sitting in the same room.
The game follows Minecraft Dungeons, which came out in 2020 as a loot-driven dungeon crawler. Families who play together on one console are the audience both reviewers had in mind.
Nintendo Life said the sequel swaps the first game's episodic progression for an open world. Its reviewer said developer Mojang stretched the appeal too thin in doing so.
Dungeons are scattered across the Overworld, and portals lead to a new biome called The Sift, which the review found lovely to look at.
The story picks up after the first game. An Illager High Council, a trio of magic users wielding soul power, invades the land, and the player's custom hero starts in the hub town of Brave Haven.
Nintendo Life put the main campaign at about 12 to 15 hours and said it is easy.
Nintendo Life said customisation remains the strongest part of the game. Loot drops steadily from enemies and chests, and all weapons and gear can be enchanted.
Artefacts grant up to three crowd-control abilities in exchange for soul power, while Talismans are new and add stat boosts and resistances. Jumping now adds variety to melee and ranged attacks.
The reviewer wrote that players mostly use those builds against the same enemies in similar-looking locations. Endermen, which appear as random encounters, were singled out as a tense source of good gear.
Shacknews writer Ozzie Mejia said he mostly played online and found it frustrating for several reasons. He enjoyed offline play with friends and family far more.
Players must choose online or offline when they create a character, and the choice cannot be reversed. A hero built for online sessions cannot be moved to a living-room game, so a new character is required.
Both modes allow players to join and leave mid-game, and online players can connect through party codes or matchmaking.
Mejia described the storytelling as minimalistic. The game has few cutscenes and almost no voiceover beyond some narration, and it leans on text.
He said the cutscenes look gorgeous in Unreal Engine 5, and that the narrated quest text reminded him of a Dungeons & Dragons campaign. He said the format grew on him by the end.
Shacknews said the sequel keeps the first game's simple loop while adding depth drawn from the Minecraft source material. Mojang developed the game with Double Eleven.
I cover what the internet is actually talking about: the new release, the viral moment, the creator beef, the product launch. My job is to explain it fast and clearly, without the breathless hype. I read the timeline…

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: FlyDubai captain reveals new details of attack in Netanyahu phone call
articles.title_zh: FlyDubai captain reveals new details of attack in Netanyahu phone call
articles.content_orig:
The FlyDubai hero captain revealed new details of his fight to save the passengers aboard flight FZ1073 in an emotional telephone conversation with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, released by his office on Saturday evening.
The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight’s captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar told Netanyahu he felt he had “one more fight left” in him when in a critical state he reached for the cockpit door once again to save the 174 passengers and 6 crew members, while the co-pilot kept attacking him and putting the aircraft in a steep defence.
He described how the attack started saying that the co-pilot asked to pray in the cockpit which he did not consider an unusual request and “and out of respect for him, I didn’t look back.”
“After 4-5 minutes, I felt a heavy blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that catastrophic damage had been caused to the plane and something was wrong, but the blows kept coming one after another, and then I realized it wasn't the plane... it was the other guy who was with me in the cockpit," the captain described the attack.
Machchhar said his vision became badly blurred from the blows and he felt how the aircraft went into a steep descent. He tried to open the cockpit door once again, but the co-pilot kept closing it while passengers were trying to get in using the access code.
Netanyahu asked him if the door was closed with a pin mechanism and the captain answered that on the inside of the cockpit the door had a twist handle and that from the outside it could be opened with a code.
Machchhar remembered hearing the whooshing sound of the aircraft plunging downwards and the passengers screaming.
Realising what was happening, he told Netanyahu how he reached for the internal twist handle and with “a sharp, quick turn” managed to finally open the door, letting the passengers in who subdued the co-pilot and stabilised the plane.
The captain said that the co-pilot "locked the cockpit door and I was lying on the floor. I heard people screaming. I realized I had one last fight left: if I don't do this, I will die with the last of my strength, I opened the door, and people were already waiting right outside and jumped in".
“I knew I couldn't let the passengers die,” Machchhar said.
The Israeli prime minister told him that he is a hero with “an unbelievable courage, inviting him and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi to light a celebratory flame on Israel’s next Independence Day, the highest honour usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
“You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel, and you are a hero of the entire world. I wish you a very speedy and complete recovery," Netanyahu told captain Machchhar.
Israeli Ambassador to the UAE Yossi Shelley was at his bedside during the call and together with Netanyahu invited Machchhar and his family to visit Israel as soon as he is able, to receive the embrace and love that the entire country wants to give him.
Dubai's Crown Prince and UAE Minister of Defence Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid also visited Machchhar in hospital hailing the captain’s bravery, stating that he “embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team, part of the story of our nation and part of what the UAE stands for a nation of compassion, a nation of peace and a nation of life,” Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed said.
In a new development on Sunday, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that the FlyDubai flight copilot, named by multiple media outlets as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, studied aviation at the UK-based Buckinghamshire New University.
The Telegraph said that during his time at the university, al-Hammami commented in social media posts that women should be “stomped on” and praised giving a woman a “pre-emptive slap.” He also appeared to praise Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Telegraph said.
The co-pilot used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday, while the UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash called the incident "a dangerous terrorist act".
Meanwhile on Sunday, regional officials said that the UAE authorities shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight, including their nationalities, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection, the Associated Press reported.
According to AP, who quoted regional officials, Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew.
Prime Minister Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev told Israel’s public broadcaster Kan that the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubenstien, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight.
Prime Minister Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk and allowed him to fly the sensitive route to Israel.
Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Miri Regev is a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party and a staunch supporter.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”
The UAE is leading the investigation and security agencies from four regional countries including Israel were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, according to the AP.

articles.title_orig: Gavin Newsom on His Life in the Wine World
articles.title_zh: Gavin Newsom on His Life in the Wine World
articles.content_orig:
This story is from an installment of The Oeno Files , our weekly insider newsletter to the world of fine wine. Sign up here.
Long before setting his sights on Sacramento, Governor Gavin Newsom had one aspiration: to make fine wine more accessible. A lifelong wine lover who first connected with the fruit of the vine through his father, the San Francisco native cofounded PlumpJack wine shop there in 1992 with a group of partners that included family friend, oil heir, and composer Gordon Getty. Named for a Shakespeare character, the PlumpJack Group has since grown to include PlumpJack, Cade, and Odette wineries in Napa, and its leadership team includes general manager John Conover and Newsom’s sister, Hilary.
Elected mayor of San Francisco in 2003, Newsom’s interest in politics was piqued when the city’s department of health required him to install a mop sink in his carpeted wine shop. He began his career in government with a role in the San Francisco Parking and Traffic Commission before earning a spot on the city’s Board of Supervisors and then moved through the ranks of political office. Newsom placed his ownership interest in PlumpJack Group’s wineries, hotels, and restaurants into a blind trust when he was elected governor in 2018. Throughout his entire career, he continues to enjoy fine wine, especially bottles from Napa, Burgundy, Chablis, and Italy.
How did you first become interested in wine? Wine was one of the things I could connect with my dad about. Food, wine, and travel were a big part of his life. Because he could sometimes be emotionally hard to reach, wine became a kind of shared language between us—a way to sit together, talk, learn, and connect without having to force the conversation.
What was your journey toward opening the PlumpJack wine shop in 1992? It really started over dinner at the Balboa Cafe with my father and Pat Kelley, who had previously owned a wine store nearby. I became fixated on this idea of making fine wine more accessible—a store that wasn’t the discount rack but also wasn’t some precious place for the initiated, where people could discover great wine at an accessible price. I was 24, raised $174,000 from 15 friends and family, quit my job, and spent nearly two years fighting through permits and scraping the business together.
What is the origin of the name PlumpJack? PlumpJack is Sir John Falstaff, Shakespeare’s irreverent, larger-than-life character, and the inspiration for Gordon Getty’s opera. I loved that Falstaff mocked stuffiness and celebrated the absurdity of life. That was precisely the attitude we wanted to bring to wine.
How did you go from having a wine shop to opening wineries? The store worked, and two years later we opened PlumpJack Cafe with the same philosophy: exceptional wines without the extraordinary restaurant markup, including great Cabernets, Pinots, and Zinfandels by the glass. I’d always had an affinity for Oakville and Napa Cabernet, so when the opportunity came in 1995 to acquire a winery there, we jumped at it and eventually expanded to four wineries.
What are some of your favorite wines? I’ve always loved Oakville Cabernet. Groth and Silver Oak were two early favorites, but my tastes have always ranged beyond Napa, including Burgundy, Chablis, Pinot Noir, and Italian whites.
Do you consider yourself a wine drinker or collector? I’ve always been more interested in drinking and sharing wine than displaying it.
Under your leadership, in what ways has the state of California addressed the glut of wine grapes in the state that caused growers to rip out a reported 40,000 acres of vines in the past year and allow 100,000 tons of grapes to remain unharvested? Government cannot manufacture consumer demand or wave a wand and correct an oversupply that developed over many years. Across the agriculture industry, we’ve supported California growers through research, pest prevention, water resilience, and market development, but I’ve also gone out of my way throughout my public career to ensure my personal history in the wine business never influences state policy. And right now, one of the worst things Washington could do is make a difficult market even harder. President Trump’s trade war with Canada has helped trigger retaliation and restrictions on American wine in what has been our largest export market. It’s exactly the opposite of what California growers need.
There is a perception that vineyards and wineries are owned by rich people who don’t need help from the government to survive. How much truth is there to that perception? The industry is incredibly diverse. Yes, there are wealthy vineyard owners, but there are also thousands of farmers, small and multigenerational wineries, farmworkers, cellar workers, truck drivers, restaurant and hotel employees whose livelihoods depend on this industry. California wine alone supports more than 422,000 jobs in our state. That’s why Trump’s tariffs are so harmful.
Why did you title your book Young Man In A Hurry ? It actually came from a 2009 Economist article about me—not exactly a compliment at the time—and years later I realized how much truth there was in it. I came to see it less as somebody else’s critique than as a self-critique: the impatience, ambition, insecurity, and constant need to keep moving that have shaped so much of my life.
If readers of your book come away with one impression, what do you hope it to be? That people are more complicated than their caricatures, including me. Writing this book forced me to scrutinize rather than sanitize my life, to understand my parents and my family differently, and ultimately to discover things about myself that I hadn’t fully understood before.
Completely theoretical, of course … but what wines would you like to see served at a White House dinner? For now, my answer is anything but Trump Wine.

articles.title_orig: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
articles.title_zh: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
articles.content_orig:
Jay Clayton testifies during a Senate Intelligence Committee confirmation hearing to be the next Director of National Intelligence on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, July 15, 2026, in Washington. Mariam Zuhaib/AP hide caption
Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar, President Trump said on Sunday.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that Clayton will lead the White House's new "Super Intelligence Force," a group that will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence."
Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence." He said his "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies."
Before being confirmed earlier this year to lead national intelligence, Clayton was United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Trump's announcement follows various statements of alarm from tech leaders over risks in the rapid development of AI, including that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed aside the warnings and attempted to reframe concerns around AI.
On Tuesday, Trump met with AI executives at the White House, and said afterwards that leaders of several artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of their work.
Meanwhile, the White House also launched a revamped government website this week, America.gov , which says it is sourced via artificial intelligence from "official government sources."
In his social media post, Trump also named other members of his "Super Intelligence Force". He said it will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael.
It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used .
During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. "I don't think any American should think that that's a good strategy," he said.
In December 2024, president-elect Trump announced he would appoint David Sacks, a Silicon Valley investor, as an AI and crypto czar , with a brief to advise the administration on policies surrounding AI.
Earlier this year, Sacks stepped down from his role and became co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He has backed AI leaders Sam Altman and Dario Amodei's warnings about the technology, and the idea of a "slow down" in AI development. Last month, Sacks wrote on social media that the tech leaders should "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to make such moves.
