articles.title_orig: Delivering Remote Audio Production Over IP
articles.title_zh: Delivering Remote Audio Production Over IP
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › Tech and Gear › Tech Tips
Distributed workflows are fast becoming the norm for radio. What does it mean for you? This is one in a series of articles.
The author is VP Sales, Americas, for Tieline .
Tieline has delivered wired and wireless IP solutions for over two decades, so it’s not a new concept for us. However, it took quite a long time for many engineers to shift to using IP, as they felt it was safer to use a wired solution like ISDN. It had always “just worked.”
When the pandemic hit in 2020, it showed everyone that we have the tools to broadcast remotely from anywhere. Since then, centralization has accelerated and new studios have become physically smaller and more flexible to stream live shows, perform audio production, create podcasts and social media videos.
Downsizing was made possible because it is common for radio show hosts, sports commentators, news readers, traffic reporters and syndicated talent and guests to broadcast partially, or entirely, from home.
As an example, Tieline users Don McDonald and Tom Cock are hosts often out on the road away from their flagship studio producing the “Talking Real Money” show. They use a ViA when on the road together, or Tom will use a Tieline codec at his home studio, and Don will use another Tieline codec at his home/mobile studio.
Both hosts can simply dial into the studio (or each other’s codec) for low-latency bidirectional links. Listeners dial into the flagship studio with questions and their audio from phone hybrids is routed to Don and Tom in real-time as a mix-minus.
Nowadays, broadcasting over IP is an accepted practice for radio and television networks around the world. Reliability is enhanced through multiple layers of redundancy with fully automated backup. Tieline employs SmartStream Plus hitless packet switching over multiple wired or wireless IP network interfaces; this technology has set a high standard for resilient IP streaming over the public internet over many years. Technology such as this, along with FEC, RIST and bonded IP, is the gold standard for broadcasting in 2026.
The ViA audio codec has become an industry standard remote codec preferred by major broadcasters on every continent.
Flexibility is paramount and that’s why Tieline’s newest product, the ViA Duo, provides even greater adaptability for a range of new use cases and workflows.
It’s driven by increasing demand for flexible platforms with professional, broadcast-quality connections for critical broadcasts. We see demand for a traditional IP codec, as well as opportunities for more flexible equipment supporting AoIP protocols including AES67, ST 2110-30, Ravenna, Dante, Livewire and NMOS. This allows the same unit to be an audio codec and provide commentary solutions by acting as an AoIP node on a network at a sports venue, or over a managed or dark fiber WAN connection back to a station in a remote integration (REMI) workflow.
More stations are expanding remote production, given how easy it is to route multiple production signals in and out of the studio. A single Tieline codec at a station can support 32 mono (or 16 stereo) signals in/out of their studio.
As an example, I was recently at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway with the group from Radio One Indianapolis. For the month of May, they weren’t just going live from the track but also producing prerecorded shows remotely for later use. I had the pleasure of seeing them deploy remote gear all over the 2.5-mile track at multiple different locations.
Radio One could handle so many live broadcasts and remote productions simultaneously because they have a large fleet of IP audio codecs back at their home studio. Each remote codec could simply dial back to the studio and be routed straight on-air, or be sent to a production room for recording and editing purposes.
Without their codec network, Radio One wouldn’t have been able to broadcast live from the track and their remote production would not have delivered a real-time solution. Felix Rosenqvist wasn’t the only Indy 500 winner, it was also Radio One’s engineering team and codec network running full speed during the entire month of May!
Audio codecs have been used for remote off-tube commentary of major events for several years. By integrating video into an audio codec like the ViA Duo, it means broadcasters can send a live gameday video feed to remote talent directly and commentators can call any event remotely from anywhere in the world.
We have all heard about new technologies merging from software-based services that allow for broadcasting anywhere using nothing more than a laptop and microphone.
However, I believe this isn’t always the most reliable or consistent experience for remote broadcast production. Laptops are truly 100% customizable by the operator and engineer, which isn’t a bad thing, but can lead to issues if not checked.
If installed software is out of place or not updated, services may become unreliable and not connect. In addition, if you are a PC user, regular updates have been known to “accidentally” disturb network and audio drivers, so a simple software update could impact your entire remote.
Of course, one can bypass this issue by either declining to update, changing registry or even opting for a “Long Term Service” edition of Windows.
Ideally, you shouldn’t have to monitor critical software updates to maintain your remote production capabilities. It makes more sense to use purpose-built hardware for which the manufacturer maintains functionality and security updates for you.
With this said, I do believe there is a time and place for software-based solutions, and Tieline itself has the Report-IT Enterprise app for reporting and similar applications. However, for reliability, nothing beats a dedicated hardware solution with multiple layers of built-in redundancy, compared to a cobbled-together PC/software solution requiring more effort to maintain.
With teams of announcers and commentators working remotely, it is critical that engineers can remote control their equipment. This helps maintain quality control and provides confidence that if issues occur at a remote site, they can be managed effectively.
For example, tools like Tieline’s built-in Toolbox Web-GUI or the optional Cloud Codec Controller are designed for comprehensive network management, configuration and control of all IP codecs, as well as Report-IT Enterprise app users. This provides confidence that people without technical knowledge can use IP codec technology and stay connected.
Read more on this topic in the Radio World ebook “Audio Production (From Anywhere).”

articles.title_orig: ‘His grace is for all,’ President Oaks declares during October 2026 general conference
articles.title_zh: ‘His grace is for all,’ President Oaks declares during October 2026 general conference
articles.content_orig:
As was foretold in the scriptures, today is a moment in history when individuals around the world are looking for God and for his eternal truths, Church President Dallin H. Oaks taught during the Sunday morning session of October 2026 general conference .
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is home to the Savior’s restored doctrine and authority, President Oaks said. In it, God’s children learn about the nature of the Godhead and the significance of the Savior’s Atonement in Heavenly Father’s plan.
“God the Father, the great Elohim, is the Father of our spirits, the framer of heaven and earth, and the author of the plan of our salvation. (See Moses 1:31–33 ; 2:1–2 ; Doctrine and Covenants 20:17–21 .) Jesus Christ is His Only Begotten Son, Jehovah, and the Messiah, ‘the God of the whole earth’ ( 3 Nephi 11:14 ),” he said.
Members of the Church both obey the invitation of the Book of Mormon prophet Amaleki and invite all others to “come unto Christ” ( Omni 1:26 ).
“As your President, I pray for what our Heavenly Father wants for each of us — to be active members of the Church of Jesus Christ, proceeding forward on the covenant path into the eternities. We need one another’s prayers.”
Each individual on the earth is a work in progress with personal trials and challenges to work through and help others to work through, he said.
“We all have present or future concerns or struggles we are trying to overcome. These may include questions or doubts. Whatever they are, the way to overcome them is to get closer to our Savior, Jesus Christ.”
Those challenges of mortality have the purpose of providing opportunities for individuals to develop faith in Heavenly Father and His Son, Jesus Christ.
“Strong faith requires more than strong desire. It means daily trying, one step at a time, with prayer and scriptural learning,” he said.
In that process of personal development, individuals need to have patience with themselves and others, President Oaks said. That patience includes allowing time for increased understanding by one’s self or a loved one. It also includes being patient with the progress of scientific understanding and the “sometimes-incomplete teachings of religion,” he said.
Reconciling the conflicts that may exist between science and religion can take time. This process may also help build faith and humility. That same faith and humility compels obedience to the Lord’s commandments to repent and be baptized.
“A major concern to your prophet leaders are those members of diminishing faith in Jesus Christ. We love you. ... So does the Lord God. He is relentless in His loving pursuit of each of you,” President Oaks said.
The Prophet invited individuals to maintain momentum in the building of their faith by keeping the commandments, keeping their covenants and avoiding the artificial limits of secular learning.
The Sunday morning general conference address was President Oaks’ second in such a conference since being sustained as Church President in a general conference solemn assembly on April 4. In the April 2026 general conference , President Oaks invited individuals to act as peacemakers at home and in all relationships.
Six months later, President Oaks invited continued learning and the study of the Book of Mormon.
President Oaks taught there are two ways to earn the necessary knowledge of life.
“There is no ultimate conflict between knowledge obtained by these different methods because God, our omnipotent Father, knows all truth and expects us to learn by both methods.”
President Oaks also invited individuals to maintain humility as they seek and obtain learning by these two methods. He referenced then-Elder Spencer W. Kimball’s 1963 address at BYU in which the member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and future President of the Church referred to humility as “teachableness.”
“Teachableness is an ability to realize that all virtues and abilities are not concentrated in one’s self. … [Humility] is forgiving others in the realization that there may be errors of the same kind or worse [that we ourselves commit],” Elder Kimball taught.
One way members of the Church can strengthen their humility is through the weekly participation in the ordinance of the sacrament and living up to the promises made in that covenant each week. For those who have made additional covenants in the temple, President Oaks invited them to attend the house of the Lord regularly.
“These simple practices will protect and strengthen you,” he said.
President Oaks also shared teachings from the Book of Mormon that can strengthen testimonies of the Savior, Jesus Christ.
First, he said the Book of Mormon teaches that Jesus, as the Creator, died “for all men, that all men might become subject unto him” ( 2 Nephi 9:5 ).
“This means that if our sins are to be forgiven through His Atonement, we must comply with the conditions He has prescribed, including faith, repentance and baptism,” President Oaks said.
Those conditions will not and cannot be compelled by the Savior or Heavenly Father, President Oaks taught. Their execution must arise from individuals’ desires, choices and actions.
Second, President Oaks taught that the Book of Mormon illustrates how the resurrected Savior ministered to some of those who did not have the chance to learn from Him during His mortal ministry in Jerusalem.
When the Savior appeared to the Nephites on the American continent, He said He was fulfilling Heavenly Father’s commandment to visit “other sheep” than those who had witnessed His teachings in and around Jerusalem (see 3 Nephi 16:1 ; John 10:16 ). The Savior was also clear in the Book of Mormon that the Nephites were not exclusively those “other sheep” to whom He would minister.
Third, the Book of Mormon includes teachings that show God loves everyone, President Oaks said.
From 2 Nephi 29:7 , President Oaks read, “Know ye not that I, the Lord your God, have created all men, and that I remember those who are upon the isles of the sea; and that I rule in the heavens above and in the earth beneath; and I bring forth my word unto the children of men, yea, even upon all the nations of the earth?”
Fourth, President Oaks said the Book of Mormon serves to correct the “erroneous assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few.”
The Book of Mormon prophet Nephi taught in 2 Nephi 26 that the Savior will receive everyone to Him regardless of their differences.
“His grace is for all,” President Oaks reiterated. And everyone who lives on this earth will have the opportunity to receive a manifestation of Christ’s reality through the power of the Holy Ghost, he said.
President Oaks said that millions of people have had personal experiences and can testify that that promise has been fulfilled in their lives.
“I invite all to believe them,” President Oaks said of those promises contained in the Book of Mormon.
The book’s purpose, as stated in its title page , is to help everyone “know of the covenants of the Lord” and “that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God, manifesting himself unto all nations.”
President Oaks concluded his message by inviting individuals to live the truths of the Book of Mormon and to share them with others. Doing so will allow all to “draw closer to Jesus Christ our Savior,” he said.

articles.title_orig: OPEC+ holds output targets steady as Middle East conflict tightens supply
articles.title_zh: OPEC+ holds output targets steady as Middle East conflict tightens supply
articles.content_orig:
OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran , with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Crude oil prices settled lower after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease surging fuel prices.
International benchmark Brent crude futures slipped 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude slid $1.76 to $91.11 a barrel.
The G7 will release 100 million barrels of reserves over the next four months "with a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the group's leaders said in a joint statement. The G7 includes France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the U.S.
Despite the G7 announcement, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven will meet next on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases, and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group, the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee, which does not set policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.
— CNBC contributed to this report .

articles.title_orig: Cornell rape accuser faces threats demanding she drop her lawsuit, attorney says
articles.title_zh: Cornell rape accuser faces threats demanding she drop her lawsuit, attorney says
articles.content_orig:
The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said Sunday.
Thomas Giuffra told CNN’s “State of the Union” that people attempting to unmask his client’s identity had also targeted at least three women mistakenly identified as her. The former Cornell student is identified as Jane Doe in court documents.
“She’s received multiple threats, and women who aren’t even Jane Doe receive threats,” Giuffra said. He added that he had received a threat Sunday morning.
Giuffra did not identify those responsible or say whether the threats had been reported to law enforcement. He did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for more information about the threats.
Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven Chi Phi fraternity members, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours on Oct. 19-20, 2024, while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
The allegations have sparked renewed scrutiny of the university’s and local authorities’ handling of the allegations. Gov. Kathy Hochul last week appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate.
NBC News reported Friday that Cornell police interviewed witnesses and received anonymous tips during their investigation in 2024, but Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten did not review that additional information before deciding not to pursue charges at the time. He has defended his decision, saying that Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement to police did not allege criminality.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the university must do better and that its board of trustees would announce an independent review of its handling of the case next week.
Maggie McCabe is a desk assistant at NBC News Washington.

articles.title_zh: Search ongoing for missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston as crews plan to scour ocean floor
articles.content_orig:
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

articles.title_orig: Even 'Bond King' Bill Gross warns 'don’t own bonds' as long-term debt enters a new ear of volatility
articles.title_zh: Even 'Bond King' Bill Gross warns 'don’t own bonds' as long-term debt enters a new ear of volatility
articles.content_orig:
PIMCO cofounder Bill Gross, who revolutionized bond investing with active trading strategies, warned the overall credit landscape has become unbalanced and cautioned against holding longer-term debt.
In a Financial Times op-ed on Wednesday, he pointed out that government, mortgage and corporate credit now totals about $84 trillion.
“Too much debt can lead to too much risk and too much equity can lead to less earnings per share growth under certain underperforming productivity cycles,” Gross wrote. “Move them both at the same pace consistent with industry standards and economic growth more than likely expands as well.”
But balance sheets have grown too lopsided, putting growth at risk, he said. The AI sector’s debt boom is an anomaly by historical standards, and federal debt has already hit peak levels for peacetime, now at 100% of GDP.
While all that debt is fueling growth now, it has led to higher inflation today and will likely slow growth in the future, Gross added.
“In such an environment, my view is: don’t own bonds, with the exception of one-year Treasury bills, which are now at 4.55%,” he said. “Be cautious with stocks at record levels as higher yields over time will contract profit margins. Be prepared for the end of ‘what you are used to’ stock markets and higher volatility in prices for the benchmark 10-year Treasury bonds.”
His admonition is notable given his career in bond investing, which earned him the moniker “Bond King .” For decades, he dominated a corner of financial markets that was considered sleepy before he arrived on the scene.
Rather than simply buying bonds and holding them to maturity to collect interest, his investment strategies generated returns well beyond what “clipping coupons” provided.
But in recent years, the market has experienced its own transformation as well. Central banks around the world no longer reliably buy and hold Treasury debt as they seek to diversify their reserves. At the same time, price-sensitive hedge funds have emerged as bigger players in the bond market and are quicker to sell.
The so-called basis trade that’s become popular among hedge funds, where they profit from small price differences between Treasury bonds and the Treasury futures, has made the market more volatile.
In fact, the basis trade has grown so much that hedge funds’ share of total Treasury holdings has almost doubled since 2023 to 8.5%, exceeding the portion that depository institutions and mutual funds command.
The new era of volatility has been on display this year, as 10-year Treasury yields have soared more than 100 basis points since the Iran war started and recently hit the highest levels in 24 years.
While hedge funds are a key source of liquidity in the market, they may weaken bonds’ reputation as a safe-haven asset, Joe Maher, markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a note in August.
“In a risk-off environment, safe-haven flows into sovereign bonds may be offset by hedge funds unwinding their leveraged trading positions as funding conditions tighten,” he wrote. “And given they have no obligation to act as market makers, the more likely it is that liquidity dries up in these markets in times of stress.”
On top of that, hedge funds could transmit stress across different assets, Maher warned. For example, a stock market selloff could force hedge funds to dump bond positions to cover their losses in equities.
For his part, Gross said he is suspicious of AI hyperscalers, unless they have price-to-earnings ratios of less than 20. And while stocks like Verizon and AT&T have decent yields, their mobile phone businesses are threatened by SpaceX’s Starlink.
Some income funds that are trading at a discount to net asset values may offer some opportunities, but they would suffer if short-term interest rates rise higher than expected, he added.
“Preserve and protect is my current investment motto,” Gross wrote.
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.title_zh: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on partners to respond decisively to Russian terror, strengthen Ukraine's air defense and impose effective sanctions on Russia's defense industry.
He said this in a post on X , according to Ukrinform.
The foreign minister said that this week marked a new chapter in Russia's campaign of all-day terror against civilians and that after targeting food depots, retail chains, pharmacy warehouses, and vital databases, Russia is now going after bridges.
"They are important lifelines that keep the country functioning, connect communities, allow people to get to work and access essential services," Sybiha said.
The minister recalled that over the past few days, Russia had struck two bridges in Kyiv six times, right when civilian traffic was using them and metro trains were crossing.
"The world cannot simply watch and wait – we urge strong reactions by our partners. Both in words and deeds. Make clear to Moscow that it must stop its escalation and terror – and engage in diplomacy and peace efforts," Sybiha said.
He also called on allies to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, impose effective sanctions on Russia's military-industrial complex, and add to sanctions lists the individuals and organizations that enable the regime to continue committing its crimes.
As reported, two people were injured in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Northern Bridge on October 4.

articles.title_orig: At 70, This Fitness Coach Says Strength Training Keeps Her Independent. Here Are the 5 Habits She Swears By
articles.title_zh: At 70, This Fitness Coach Says Strength Training Keeps Her Independent. Here Are the 5 Habits She Swears By
articles.content_orig:
If you think reaching 70 means becoming frail, slowing down and losing your independence, Carrie Sisson offers a very different picture of what aging can look like.
The fitness coach started taking strength training seriously in her 30s because she “wanted to feel good long term,” she wrote on Instagram .
Now, at 70, she's “having the time of her life”—something she largely credits to years of consistently prioritizing strength.
“I’ve always been inspired to get stronger with age—not more fragile,” she said in another Instagram post .
“I used to think 70 sounded old. Instead, I’ve found myself feeling more grateful for my life than ever. I’m strong. I’m mobile. I feel good in my body,” she wrote in a separate post .
And, she says, none of it has happened by chance.
“It’s not luck or genetics—it’s years of small deposits adding up.”
Here are the five habits Carrie recommends adopting between your 30s and 60s if you want to stay strong, capable and independent later in life.
“I promise your strength is going to matter so much more to your future than fitting into a smaller pair of jeans,” Carrie says.
Rather than chasing a number on the scales, she encourages women to celebrate getting stronger.
Research supports that approach. A 2022 review of studies involving adults aged 65 and over found that progressive resistance training significantly improved muscle strength and bone density.
“Bone density, balance, confidence—all of it is trainable, at any age,” Carrie added in another Instagram post.
Because, in many ways, it does.
“Muscle is like our insurance policy for aging,” Carrie said.
“Every time you train you are really building stronger bones, muscle you hold onto instead of lose, and a body that keeps up with you as the years pass.”
She points to everyday examples of what that strength can mean.
“You can be the friend who still gets down on the floor with her grandkids and pops back up without help, who carries her own suitcase through the airport, who says yes to the hike. It’s not luck or genetics—it’s years of small deposits adding up.”
Research backs that up. One study involving mobility-limited adults with an average age of 85 found that just 10 weeks of strength training increased leg muscle mass and improved functional performance by 7-11%.
Strength training forms the foundation of Carrie's routine, but she still makes time for cardio.
“I’ve never used cardio to maintain my weight. Not at 40, not at 50, not now at 70,” she wrote in an Instagram post.
“If you’re starting out with more body fat and not a lot of muscle yet... lifting is what makes that happen. You don’t need to run for an hour. You need to pick up something heavy and do it consistently!”
That doesn't mean cardio isn't valuable.
A systematic review involving more than 2,000 adults aged over 70 found aerobic exercise improved cardiovascular fitness, metabolic health, physical function, cognitive performance and quality of life.
Carrie also believes many of the limits we place on ourselves come from society rather than our bodies.
“Wear the clothes. Try the thing!” she says.
“You don't have to ‘act your age’ just because society has decided what 70 is supposed to look like.”
Research has linked authentic self-expression with greater wellbeing, with one study finding a positive relationship between the two.
Finally, Carrie says healthy aging isn't just about exercise and nutrition.
“The people you surround yourself with, the thoughts you rehearse and the things you give your attention to all shape the life you're creating,” she said.
Research suggests she has a point. One 2024 study found that people exposed to positive news experienced more positive emotions, while exposure to negative news had the opposite effect.
Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training , cardio , workout challenges , interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president calls gang rape allegations ‘deeply disturbing’
articles.title_zh: Cornell president calls gang rape allegations ‘deeply disturbing’
articles.content_orig:
Pedestrians walk on the campus at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption
Cornell University's president has said the institution "must do better" following a civil lawsuit filed in recent weeks alleging a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024.
In an eight-minute video statement released by Cornell on Saturday, president Michael I. Kotlikoff acknowledged questions over the university's handling of the female student's sexual assault allegations, which were reported to Cornell University police and school officials a few weeks after she said the attack happened.
"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say. We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves," Kotlikoff said in the statement. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."
Last month, a former Cornell student, identified as "Jane Doe," sued the seven alleged rapists and the university, saying she was drugged and repeatedly raped in October 2024. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.
Kotlikoff called recent days one of the most difficult weeks in Cornell's history.
"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," he said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."
Jane Doe first reported her claims to Cornell University police and university Title IX investigators shortly after the alleged incident, which happened when she was 20 years old, at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She also reported the sexual assault to the campus health clinic.
According to the lawsuit filed against Cornell, Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and other defendants, Jane Doe said she consented initially to sexual contact with two men she knew at the fraternity house while intoxicated. She alleges, as the night went on, she was then drugged and raped by multiple men, and could not give consent.
The Tompkins County district attorney declined to file charges. He has said recently he didn't receive full transcripts from Jane Doe's interview with Cornell University police, in which she clearly stated she had been raped.
"As a community, we must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent, body autonomy and prevention. We all have a role to play in keeping each other safe," said Kotlikoff in his video message.
Last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case and condemned the handling of the investigations. Kotlikoff said he welcomes the governor's decision, and that the university's board of trustees will soon announce plans for an independent review by an outside law firm into all aspects of how the case was handled.
President Trump criticized James' appointment to the Cornell case on Friday, calling the attorney general "corrupt." James' office brought a financial fraud lawsuit against Trump and his family in 2022.
"I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake," the president told reporters outside of the White House.
On CNN's State of the Union on Sunday, Jane Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra rejected Trump's statements.
"I think to politicize something like this is just wrong," Giuffra said. There are Republicans whose daughters are getting assaulted. There are Democrats whose daughters are getting assaulted. It has nothing to do with politics."
Giuffra also said his client and other women mistakenly believed to be Jane Doe have received threats.
"They said, 'we're going to shut you up," said Jane Doe's attorney, referring to the people making threats. "'You're going to pull this lawsuit out, or we're going to do something to hurt you even more.'"
In his video statement, Cornell's president vowed to push for change beyond campus.
"We will also lend our full support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws. You have my commitment that this will not be a moment that passes," he said.
Kotlikoff added the university would take immediate actions to be more transparent, strengthen sexual assault prevention and education efforts, and substance use resources. He said the university will also take a serious look at the role of sororities and fraternities in campus life.

articles.title_orig: Dabo Swinney 'absolutely' thinks Clemson can still be an ACC title contender after 41-13 loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.title_zh: Dabo Swinney 'absolutely' thinks Clemson can still be an ACC title contender after 41-13 loss to No. 4 Miami
articles.content_orig:
Clemson looked like the furthest thing from an ACC title contender Saturday night against No. 4 Miami. But that's not stopping Tigers coach Dabo Swinney from believing in his team's chances.
When asked after the 41-13 loss if he thought his team could still compete for the ACC title, Swinney was unequivocal.
"Absolutely. Absolutely. We were 3-1 coming in, we've lost to two really good teams, but we're still progressing," Swinney said. "We're just going to keep battling. We'll keep battling. Got a lot of opportunity ahead."
Yes, Clemson has lost to two really good teams in No. 4 Miami and No. 11 LSU. But it's lost to those really good teams by 69 combined points. That's not nice.
To be an ACC contender, Clemson needs to be a really good team. Or, at least show that it's capable of beating a really good team. Neither is close to happening at the moment.
Clemson's offense is being led by freshman quarterback Tait Reynolds, and it's clear that he's still learning the ropes of being a college quarterback. Reynolds was 29-of-44 passing for 295 yards and an interception against the Hurricanes. It was the first time he had thrown over 29 passes or thrown for over 215 yards in a single game.
The run game that Clemson relied on in Week 4 against Cal was nonexistent against Miami. The Tigers rushed 31 times for 55 yards on Saturday night. In its Week 1 loss to LSU, Clemson rushed 26 times for 40 yards. If you stop the Clemson run game, you have a really good chance of winning the game.
"And hey, we're 3-2; we hoped we'd be 5-0 right now, 4-1 at worst," Swinney continued. "But we're 3-2. But we're, what, 2-1 in the ACC? We're right here. We're right there. We just gotta dig in, man. Gotta go play. There's a lot of opportunity for this team."
That opportunity to make up ground in the ACC standings won't come until Oct. 24. After a bye week in Week 6, the Tigers host Charleston Southern on Oct. 17.
If there is a silver lining for Clemson, it's that there are no more ranked teams on the Tigers' schedule the rest of the season. After Charleston Southern, Clemson has Virginia Tech, Florida State, Syracuse, Georgia Tech, Duke and South Carolina. Wins in all six of those will get Clemson back to the ACC championship game … and likely set up a rematch with a far superior Miami.

articles.title_orig: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.

articles.title_orig: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.title_zh: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.content_orig:
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
Pull the lever to fan your cards with the OhSnap Wallet 2.
This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.
Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own ? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.
Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.
Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.
You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).
My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.
Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion , hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.
There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.
But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras .
OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

articles.title_orig: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.title_zh: Detecting deepfakes, in a world where even reality is suspect
articles.content_orig:
Last February, a Tomahawk cruise missile struck an Iranian elementary school, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. President Trump initially suggested that it could have been somebody else's Tomahawk: "Whether it's Iran or somebody else, the fact that a Tomahawk – a Tomahawk is very generic, it's sold to other countries, but that's being investigated right now," he said.
When Iran put out video as evidence that it was a U.S. missile, Hany Farid , one of the world's foremost experts on deepfakes, was contacted by several media outlets to determine if it was real or fake.
A professor at Dartmouth College, Farid is also co-founder of GetReal Security , a cyber security firm. "What was difficult about this case was you had very little to work on," he said. "We had a very grainy, shaky video. The missile is extremely small. And we had to reason about the physical plausibility of that missile striking the ground."
But he also had certain aspects that he could study scientifically, involving the speed of sound, the speed of light, and the size of the missile: "And those three things were enough for us to say that this is physically plausible," he said. "And this is the important part: all evidence led us to the belief that the video was authentic, and there's been no refuting of that."
But that's the world we live in: Reality itself, so perfectly mimicked by artificial intelligence, that even reality is suspect.
Farid said, "Here's the thing that makes me a little crazy, as a scientist in particular: I don't think you should be able to go into a court of law and say, 'Here is some evidence that is damning enough to put this person to death,' and then the judge says, 'Well, how do you know it's real?' And I say, 'Well, because the computer told me so.' This is not an answer
"And if I can't explain to you, to a judge, and to a jury, what is happening here – because the lighting, because the shadows, because the geometry, whatever it is – that's what we need to be able to do."
A case in point: Alex Pretti, who was killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. If you remember the scene last January 24, it was chaotic. Several ICE agents with guns surrounded Pretti.
Farid showed us a blurry photo of Pretti that was taken from the original video. "Somebody took this and 'enhanced' it," he said. According to Farid, the crispness of this "enhanced" image makes the scene feel "more real, but what it also did is when it enhanced it, it seems to have put a gun in [Pretti's] hand. If you go back to this video, the camera's panning a little bit and what's happening is, there's a shadow behind his hand on the street. And what the AI did is that it hallucinated this."
Farid says artificial intelligence has learned, "When you see photos like this with three men with guns, everybody's got a gun." And now, when you do Google searches for events like Pretti's killing, it shows the "enhanced" image.
By Farid's estimate, half of the content that's widely viewed on the Internet is fake, basically a toss of the coin. Much of it has its own sneering label: "AI slop." Footage of airplanes skidding on the tarmac, toddlers dancing a two-step, Elvis. "AI slop is a broad term that defines people generating content using AI just to grab eyeballs, video after video after video driving engagement," Farid said.
For the most part, Farid limits his examinations to the really serious stuff, the deepfakes. Even so, he's inundated. He said, "We're seeing deepfakes being weaponized in many, many different ways, from the creation of child sexual abuse material, to non-consensual intimate imagery, to full-blown state-sponsored disinformation campaigns, to what the North Koreans have done, [which] is to have their IT workers interview for jobs remotely. And they conceal their accent using AI. They can conceal their identity using a deepfake, where they change their identity from eyebrow to chin, cheek to cheek, in real time over a video call. They can conceal their geolocation. And they interview for jobs. I will tell you, just about every single Fortune 500 company has hired one or more of these, whether they know it or not.
"And now, the question you want to ask yourself is, what's next? Well, so one CEO said, 'Okay. No more virtual interviews. No more remote work.' That's insane. … We're gonna start flying people across the country? That can't be the answer. I mean it's exhausting. Let's be honest. I mean, if we're always looking at our shoulder over every email, every text message, every voicemail, every phone call, every video call? It's exhausting. I'm exhausted, and I do this for a living."
Asked if he has nightmares over deepfakes, Farid replied, "I look at content all day long. And usually the things I look at are not pleasant. I'm looking at bad things that involve horrific crimes, and when you view these things over and over and over again, they sit with you and you can't get them out of your head.
'And number two is, I don't want to be wrong. And five years ago I felt a lot more confident about our ability to distinguish real from fake. It's gotten harder. And then I worry more. I feel like the ground is constantly shifting," he said.
It builds – the stress, the pressure. After seven years on the West Coast, Farid returned to Dartmouth College, where he had previously spent 20 years on faculty. His wife, Emily Cooper, is also a professor there. The two of them bought a rural property in neighboring Vermont, where Farid mows acres of meadows, and cuts enough wood to feed their stoves through the winter. It's enough mowing and cutting to rinse some of those disturbing images away. It's isolated – there's no mail delivery, no garbage pickup –  but it's peaceful.
Certain work-related issues linger. Social media? Farid loathes it: "You can look at social media, at online platforms and say there is measurable harm coming to young kids, to adults, to seniors, across the boards. And I think we have been so mesmerized by these products which are, by design, meant to be addictive.
"I think we did an experiment on an entire generation of these young kids coming up, putting these devices in their hands. And now we've woken up and we're like, 'Oh, my God. This is terrible.' This generation right now has lower learning outcomes than any generation in history. Go to Palo Alto at the fanciest private schools where all the tech billionaires send their kids. There's no devices in those classrooms. They know."
That $17 billion settlement that Meta reached a few weeks back includes some safeguards, like a two-hour time limit for users under the age of 18. Farid thinks that's a start, but not nearly enough.
"The darkest vision I have is that everybody lives in their own information ecosystem, and nobody knows how to talk to each other anymore," he said.
On platforms where algorithms prefer fake to real content, Farid thinks all of us should stay off social media, or at the very least take those apps off our phones, to resist the temptation. As for those websites that promise to detect AI fakes, he says it's not that simple: "Here's what I think is next (and by saying next, I mean in the coming year), which is most of the deepfakes that we are seeing today have a human somewhere in the process. Somebody's hands are on the keyboard. There's still a human in the loop. But what's gonna start happening is AI agents are gonna start creating their own fakes."
And what is an AI agent? "An agent just has more autonomy, and what we have started to see is when you give it a problem to solve, it will find creative ways to do it, including creating a fake identity to interact with a human to get a human to do something and then it will lie about it," he said.
AI agents have been in the news recently for going rogue in testing trials, intensifying the global debate over AI safety and the very course of humanity . These are issues Hany Farid grapples with every day.

articles.title_orig: This NYC startup requires 4 days in office but just let everyone work remote for a whole month
articles.title_zh: This NYC startup requires 4 days in office but just let everyone work remote for a whole month
articles.content_orig:
Bruno Solari spent his August traveling all around Spain, starting with a week in Ibiza, continuing on to Madrid, Málaga, Marbella and Barcelona, before finally returning to Ibiza for a bachelor party.
He also managed to squeeze in a few meetings and client calls all throughout.
Solari, founder and CEO of the New York City-based PR firm SolComms, was among his company's 53 employees enjoying their inaugural "Work from Anywhere August." Other employees logged on from all over the U.S. (the Jersey Shore, the Hamptons, Florida) and the world (Berlin, Prague, London, Portugal).
"I was in Spain the entire month of August, and I would have felt like a hypocrite if I was going to be there and making my team be in-office," Solari, 33, tells CNBC Make It. "So I thought, 'OK, I'm doing this myself. I'm going to grant that flexibility to the entire agency.'"
The end-of-summer experiment felt like a worthwhile risk to the 3-year-old startup: Employee surveys of the trial indicate boosted productivity, work-life balance and happiness, while the business also saw a modest revenue boost. It also runs counter to several big companies scaling back on remote-work flexibility in a job market where employers have the upper hand.
"I think people were surprised that I went for it," Solari says.
Four weeks of fully remote work from anywhere in the world is a bold move for the millennial founder, who came up in PR agencies at the height of the hustle culture era and says he holds more "traditional" workplace values, like building company culture through in-person interactions rather than "through a screen" of fully remote work. Since its founding in 2023, SolComms has operated with a four days in-office requirement, with Fridays at home that end at 3 p.m. most weeks (and 12 p.m. during the summer).
Some 25% of full-time U.S. workers work in a hybrid arrangement, with the most common requirements being three days in the office, followed by four, according to a recent report from Owl Labs , a video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July. Most, 65%, work onsite full time, and 10% work remotely full time.
Solari says every year his company surveys its own employees about the perks and benefits they want, and every year they ask for more work-from-home days. Wary of granting another remote working day during the week, Solari thought to offer 100% flexibility within a one-month period instead.
He and his leadership team came up with the idea in January, announced it to employees in February, and spent the next six months coming up with best practices to make sure everyone was set up for remote success.
Among those guidelines: Stick to 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST working hours, keep cameras on for all meetings, dress for meetings as if you were going into the office, use Slack status updates liberally, take lunch and other breaks, and no sensitive calls or screens in public spaces.
SolComms also communicated their remote-August plans to the agency's 80-plus clients across healthcare, tech and AI, and consumer brands, says Natalie Valicenti, 30, the company's associate vice president of operations, who split her remote month across Rhode Island and Minnesota.
The SolComms benefit comes at a time when many company leaders are scaling back on employee flexibility and benefits, and during a tightening labor market where employers have the upper-hand.
In September, Uber announced plans to cut about 3,300 corporate jobs, as well as scale down its remote workforce and tighten in-office rules. Disney said it would require more employees to report to the office four days a week and later announced layoffs of about 300 employees.
The five-day return-to-office creep has been growing for several years. The share of Fortune 500 companies requiring five days in the office nearly doubled from mid-2024 to mid-2025, from 13% to 24%, according to research from Flex Index , a resource within the advisory firm Work Forward that analyzes office requirements data.
But for SolComms, the risks of loosening office requirements for a month seem to have paid off.
Twenty-one employees answered a survey following the inaugural remote month, with 76% saying they were more productive, 90% saying they maintained high work-life balance, and 100% saying they want Work from Anywhere August back next year, according to documents reviewed by Make It. Several say the experience helped them strengthen their communication and self-management skills, and a lot of people said cutting their commute times was the biggest draw.
There were also some downsides, like staffers saying they felt tied to their computers and found it hard to step away, whereas it felt more natural to take breaks for lunch, coffee or a walk if they were in the office.
Solari says he sees this "internal pressure to be available" as a common struggle with remote work.
"I think it's a matter of continuing to let employees know that we're flexible," he says. "You don't need to be chained to a desk to prove that you're doing a good job, and ultimately, it's not always the person who's the first to respond who's the power player in producing results."
Though not the goal, Solari says, the business also saw financial benefits: Revenue increased by a modest 4% revenue from July to August, and jumped 12% from August to September.
Solari is already committed to a return of the program in August 2027.
"[We're] 1,000% doing it again, without a doubt," he says.

articles.title_orig: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.title_zh: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.content_orig:
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.
Like the broader electorate , Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.
There are clear signs his party is paying the price.
A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.
Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.
That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.
Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.
The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.
The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.
Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”
“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”
But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.
“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.
Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.
His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.
Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.
Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.
Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.
A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.
Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.
“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”
“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.
Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.
While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.
Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.
While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.
Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.
“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.
In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.
Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.
Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.
She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”
“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.
The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

articles.title_orig: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.title_zh: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met.
On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room.
Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks.
"The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting.
Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks.
Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces.
A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.
If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war.
Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East.
"The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday.
The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs .
Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday. But prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease the burden on consumers.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel.
— The Associated Press contributed to this report.
